# D E D I C A T I O .

...our own [method], which was released to the light in the eighty-second year of the previous century <note>1682</note>, and which was rejected and, as it were, hissed off the stage by so many leaders of <term>Botany</term> <note>The study of plants</note>, to thrust it once more upon students. # P R E F A C E .

I have thought it necessary to preface this Method of Plants, which I call "improved," with a few points that I believe are in the reader's interest to know.
1. What first motivated me to treat this subject and attempt to arrange plants <term>Stirpes; a Latin term for the stocks or lineages of plants, used here to mean the plants themselves</term> into an orderly system and method.
2. How far I have progressed up to this point.
3. Why I have undertaken this new edition of my Method.

Regarding the first point: in the year 1667, the most Reverend man and our eternally honored friend *Lord John Wilkins*, Bishop of Chester—who is now among the saints <note>original Greek: ὁ νῦν ἐν ἁγίοις; a respectful formula indicating the person has died and is of blessed memory</note>—earnestly requested that I organize *Trees* and *Herbs* into a systematic method. This was to complete his *Philosophical Tables for a Universal Character* (a draft of which he was then bringing to light <note>original Latin: parturibat; literally "was in labor with," meaning he was in the process of creating or publishing the work</note>). In that work, however, I was not free to follow the natural order of things; instead, I was forced to divide each group into exactly three sub-categories, as the specific design of his project allowed for neither more nor fewer. Nevertheless, not daring to refuse anything to such a great Man and such a great Friend, I completed the task as a hurried work <note>original Latin: tumultuario opere; work produced in haste or under pressure</note> and almost spontaneously.

By this matter, *Lord Robert Morison, a Scotsman from Aberdeen and a Doctor of Medicine*, was deeply offended. Perhaps he feared that it might somehow diminish the fame and authority he held among Botanists—which was not small—nor

# P R E F A C E .

...[might] diminish the reputation he had undeservedly acquired for himself by publishing specimens of that Method, which he boasted he had not drawn from books, but had been taught by nature herself. Taking it poorly that I had dared to put my sickle into his harvest <note>original Latin: "in messem suam falcem immittere"; a common idiom meaning to interfere in another's field of expertise or business</note>, he tore those Tables to pieces in shameful ways, while keeping the author's name silent. Although I acknowledged that the Method was subject to criticism, and was not only imperfect but in many ways erroneous and flawed; yet, when I saw myself held in contempt and plainly made a laughingstock by a man who was self-willed <note>original Greek: αυθάδει (authadei); meaning stubborn or arrogant</note> and full of himself—not to say anything harsher, or disturb his spirit <note>original Latin: manes; referring to the spirits of the dead, as Morison had passed away by this time</note>—I decided to see what I could achieve in arranging plants and establishing a system by following the lead of nature freely, so that I might provide somewhat for my own reputation.

At last, after weighing the matter long and hard (as I have said * elsewhere), and by comparing my own observations with those of others, I carved out that distribution which I later published under the title *A New Method of Plants* in the year [16]82 of the previous century. I foresaw that this work would be far from perfection—I do not mean absolute perfection, but such as the nature of the subject allows (which indeed turned out to be the case)—for reasons cited in the preface to that small work. Namely, that such a task was not the work of one man or one lifetime. Furthermore, I was neither strong enough in intellect to perfect it, nor was I equipped with the proper resources <term>adminiculis; technical supports, such as extensive libraries or botanical collections</term>,

...[not] were, as one who lived in the country far from London and Oxford, where there was neither a botanical library nearby which I might consult in a doubtful matter, nor a Physic Garden <term>Hortus Medicus: a garden dedicated to the study of plants for medicinal use; the most famous were at Oxford and Chelsea</term> which I might visit to inspect plants not yet sufficiently explored; and for whom neither leisure nor resources were available for seeking out, buying, and cultivating plants. For these reasons, I had not rarely been forced to follow probable conjectures, and what I might suspect rather than what I had found for certain.

It follows in the next place that I show how far I have progressed in improving or defending my Method. Four years after that Method was published, I brought to light a general *History of Plants* <note>original Latin: *Historia Plantarum*; Ray’s massive three-volume work published between 1686 and 1704</note>, in which I arranged herbs according to that system, with a few changes. However, when it came to Trees, I noticed that *Palms* differ from other trees in almost the same way as *Grasses* and *grass-leaved plants* <note>original: *Graminifolias*; this reflects Ray’s early recognition of the distinction between Monocots and Dicots</note> differ from other herbs. Seeing that they agree among themselves in their whole habit and external appearance, the texture of their parts, and their manner of germinating, and differ from other trees, I recognized that they should be separated from them and all referred to their own proper genus. This was despite the fact that they differ in fruit—being dry in some and moist in others—and were therefore pulled apart into different categories, namely the *stone-fruit bearing* <note>original: *Pruniferarum*</note> and the *nut-bearing* <note>original: *Nuciferarum*</note> groups, in that earlier Method. Furthermore, since I saw that the position of the flowers with respect to the fruit was of great importance to...

<meta>This page continues the Preface of John Ray’s work on the classification of plants. # PREFACE

...[was] decided that a new Method for distinguishing trees—which had not been properly accounted for in that earlier system—needed to be investigated and substituted for it, one more in conformity with Nature than what I had pursued in that small work. This I have performed to the best of my ability in the aforementioned *History*.

Later, in the year 1690, the most distinguished Mr. ***Augustus Quirinus Rivinus***, Professor of Physiology at the University of Leipzig, published a new Method for plants <term>Stirpium: a Latin term for plants, stocks, or lineages; here referring to the plant kingdom</term> based on the differences between flowers, both in respect to the number of petals and their regular or irregular shape. Having been asked what I thought of this work in very kind letters from Mr. ***Rivinus*** himself, I disclosed my views in the preface to my *Collection of European Plants growing outside the British Isles* <note>original: *Stirpium Europæarum, extra Britannias nascentium Syllogen*; published 1694</note>, and I added the reasons why his system seemed less acceptable or less preferable to my own. Not long afterward, in a *Letter* addressed to me, Mr. ***Rivinus*** defended his views and sought to vindicate them from my objections.

While I was preparing a response to him, there came into my hands the *Elements of Botany* (as he calls them) by Mr. ***Joseph Pitton Tournefort***, a Doctor of Medicine from Paris and Professor of Botany. This work was written in French, and in it he claims to derive the characteristic marks of genera from the shape or structure of the flower; nevertheless, in his primary division, he distinguishes herbs into ***Monopetalous*** <term>flowers with a single petal forming a tube or bell shape</term> and ***Polypetalous*** <term>flowers with several distinct, separate petals</term>. In this work, I found myself mentioned frequently, and almost as often singled out and criticized.

--- Page 17 ---
<meta>This page continues John Ray’s preface, where he has just introduced the botanical systems of his contemporaries, Rivinus and Tournefort. # PREFACE

These circumstances impelled me to investigate more inquisitively and to look more deeply into the origin, nature, and use of <term>Method: the systematic classification of plants into groups based on shared characteristics</term> in general, and to compare our own system more diligently with the Methods of others, so that I might more clearly discern and more certainly judge which should be preferred.

Having finally weighed all these factors properly, I discovered that it is impossible to divide all plants into genera or classes based on any single part alone—whether that be the flower or the fruit—without doing violence to Nature; that is, without separating plants that are clearly related, or grouping those that are foreign to one another. Consequently, neither the *Rivinian* Method—which is taken from the number of petals in a flower and its regularity or irregularity—nor the *Tournefortian*—which takes the differences of genera from the diverse structure or form of the flower—satisfies us. Nor are we satisfied by the method followed by ***Dr. Hermann*** <note>Paul Hermann (1646–1695), a German physician and botanist</note> in the distribution of <term>vessel-bearing: plants that produce seed pods or capsules (Latin: *Vasculiferarum*)</term> plants, which is sought from the simplicity of the seed vessel and its division into two, three, four, or six cells or compartments.

I. For, in the first place, the *Rivinian* Method pulls apart the plants we call *Bulbous* herbs and their relatives into different genera. Yet no one—unless they are a slave to a hypothesis <note>original Greek: *ὑποθέσει δουλεύει* (hypothesei douleuei)</note>—would fail to recognize that these are of the same kind. For some of them possess a regular flower, others an irregular one; likewise, some are single-petaled <note>original: *monopetalon*</note>, and others many-petaled <note>original: *polypetalon*</note>. Nor is this true only of the *Bulbous* plants,

<summary>Ray argues that no single plant part, such as the flower or fruit, is sufficient for a natural classification system. He specifically begins to critique the systems of Rivinus, Tournefort, and Hermann for separating closely related plants like bulbous herbs.</summary>

<keywords>botanical method, plant classification, Augustus Quirinus Rivinus, Joseph Pitton de Tournefort, Paul Hermann, bulbous plants, petals, seed vessels, taxonomy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues John Ray's critique of contemporary botanical systems. # PREFACE

...not only that, but the species of other genera also differ either in the number of petals in the flower, or in the regularity and irregularity of the flower’s shape. Thus, most species of ***Cinquefoil*** <note>Latin: *Pentaphylli*, literally "five leaves"</note> have a five-petaled flower, yet some have four petals, such as the *smaller green Cinquefoil with a golden flower* which sends down little roots into the earth from its joints (see *Morison’s History* <note>Robert Morison (1620–1683), a Scottish botanist and Ray's contemporary</note>). Indeed, ***Tormentil*** <note>Latin: *Tormentilla*</note>, a plant of the same family, has a four-petaled flower. One species of ***Herb-Paris*** <note>Latin: *Herbæ Paris*</note> has a four-petaled flower, while another has a three-petaled one. The plants called ***Rough-leaved*** <note>Latin: *Asperifoliæ*, the family including borage and forget-me-nots</note> have a regular flower, except for ***Viper’s Bugloss*** <note>Latin: *Echium*</note>, which has an irregular flower. Among the ***Four-petaled Pod-bearers*** <note>Latin: *Tetrapetalis Siliculoſis*, the mustard and cabbage family</note>, which are all clearly of the same genus, ***Candytuft*** <note>Latin: *Thlaſpi Creticum*</note> and its related species have an irregular flower, while the rest are gifted with a regular one.

II. The ***Tournefortian*** Method <note>The classification system of Joseph Pitton de Tournefort (1656–1708), who focused on the shape of the flower corolla</note> can in no way be reconciled with ***Bulbous*** herbs. For what does the number of cells into which the fruit is divided contribute to the structure of the flower, unless you establish that the fruit is actually a part of the flower? Yet *Dr. Tournefort* <note>See *Elements of Botany*, Page 41</note> distinguishes the flower from the fruit as separate things, and makes the fruit and the flower two distinct essential parts of the plant. However, according to his own teaching, the fruit is actually a part of the flower—namely, it is either the <term>Calyx: the outer, usually green part of a flower that protects the bud</term> or the <term>Pistil: the central, seed-bearing organ of the flower</term>. For he generally affirms that either the *Calyx* or the *Pistil* turns into the fruit. But they do not turn into something other than what they were before, since the fruit from the...

<meta>This page continues John Ray's critical evaluation of Joseph Pitton de Tournefort’s botanical system. On the previous page, Ray began arguing that Tournefort’s method fails to account for bulbous plants, specifically regarding how the plant is already structured within the bulb. ...is perfectly formed from the beginning, and thereafter only increases in size; indeed, in the embryo, all parts of the fruit can be discerned even before the flower unfolds. Furthermore, I am not pleased by the arbitrary Classes to which he refers herbs of different genera—that is, those provided with flowers of different forms—such as the First, Second, and Third Classes of his *Elements of Botany* <note>Latin: *Elem. Bot.*, referring to Tournefort’s 1694 work *Éléments de botanique*</note>. I call these Classes "arbitrary" because, by his own choice and because it so seemed fit to him, he assigns three genera of herbs of a different character to each of them; whereas by equal right, had it pleased him, he could have assigned either two or even four. Perhaps this seemed convenient to him for equalizing the number of species within each Class. But if this be permitted to **Mr. Tournefort** <note>Latin: *D. Tournefort*; the "D." stands for *Dominus*, a title of respect for a learned man</note>, why should it not be for any other Botanist? If so, there will be as many Methods as there are Teachers.

Finally, the differences between genera taken from the structure of the flower cannot but be uncertain and obscure, since scarcely two people will agree on the similarity of flowers. Indeed, if we grant that a similarity exists between some, who, I ask, shall determine how far this similarity must be extended in establishing genera? Who will decide where the boundary should be set between flowers of different forms—as, for example, between the ***Clove-like*** <note>Latin: *Caryophylleos*, referring to the Dianthus or Pink family</note> and the ***Rose-like*** <note>Latin: *Rosaceos*</note>, or between either of these and the ***Four-petaled Pod-bearers*** <note>Latin: *Tetrapetalos Siliquosarum*, the family containing mustard and cabbage</note>?

# PREFACE.

...having turned these matters over in his mind, he was most thoroughly convinced that both the mode of growth and the **habit** <term>the general appearance or architecture of a plant</term> of the whole plant, and the remaining arrangement of its accidental features, must necessarily be summoned not only to establish subordinate species, but even to define **genera** <term>the plural of genus; a rank in biological classification</term>. This is our own opinion, as delivered in the *Dissertation on Methods* and elsewhere.

It remains, in the last place, for me to explain why I have undertaken this new edition of the *Method* <note>Referring to Ray's *Methodus Plantarum Emendata*</note>. Let the Benevolent Reader know, therefore, that I was moved by two primary reasons to do so.

First, that I myself noticed, and was also advised by others, that the Method which I used in the *History of Plants* <note>original: *Historia Plantarum*</note> for the arrangement of **plants** <note>original: *stirpibus*</note> suffered from its own defects and faults. It does not become an honorable man and a **lover of truth** <note>original: *φιλαλήθη* (philalēthē)</note> to hide or disguise an error once it has been recognized; rather, so that he may devote himself to the truth, he ought to disclose and correct it, even to the detriment of his own reputation. This I have done in this little work, so that I might adapt the Method—of which I am not yet ashamed—to be as accurate and purged of errors as possible for the use of students.

Second, because I have found that some who drew the **Characteristic Marks of the Genera** <note>original: *Notas Generum Characterišticas*</note> from our *Method* and *History* very often erred in describing them, and omitted certain of the principal Marks; namely, because they were not sufficiently attentive and diligent in following the guidance and divisions of the **Tables** <term>taxonomic charts used to identify plants by their features</term>.

# NECESSARY PRELIMINARY KNOWLEDGE

->Concerning<-

# THE METHOD OF PLANTS

## IN GENERAL.

<image-desc>Ornate woodcut initial letter 'D' decorated with floral and leaf motifs.</image-desc>A perfect definition is constructed from the **nearest genus** <term>the next highest category in a hierarchy</term> and the **essential difference** <term>the specific trait that distinguishes a species from others in that genus</term>. Yet the true essences of things are unknown to us, and consequently, their essential differences are as well. However, since the same qualities, functions, and other accidental features flow from the same essence, there can be no more certain mark of essential or generic agreement than the possession of many common attributes—that is, having many similar parts and features, or the same overall appearance, **habit** <term>the general shape or architecture of a plant</term>, and texture. Indeed, what the Logicians call a **proper accident** <term>a quality that belongs to all members of a group and only that group</term>—which they insist should be used as the "essential difference" when one is missing—is granted to very few things. It is not easy, not to say impossible, for us to investigate what those specific traits are. Therefore, I do not fear to reduce plants that have many similar parts and features, or which agree in their total habit and texture, to the same **genus** <note>original: *genus*</note>, even if they differ in the shape of the flower, the number of its petals, whether the seed is naked or enclosed in a vessel, the number of cells into which such a vessel is divided, or any other accidental feature. 

Thus, for example, I refer **Honeywort** <note>original: *Cerinthen*</note> to the **Rough-leaved plants** <note>original: *Asperifolias*; a group including modern Borages</note>, although instead of four separate seeds it has two vessels divided into as many cells, in each of which a single seed is contained. Likewise, I count **Cachrys** <note>original: *Cachryn*</note> and the **Sea Parsnip** <note>original: *Pastinacam marinam*</note> among the **Umbelliferous Herbs** <term>plants like carrots or parsley that have umbrella-like flower clusters</term>, although their fruit appears to be a seed vessel with the seed contained inside, rather than a "naked" seed; this is contrary to the usual rule of other **Umbellifers** <note>original: *Umbelliferarum*</note>.

# NECESSARY PRELIMINARY KNOWLEDGE.

For the **generic character** <term>the set of features that defines a group</term>, some single property or mark common to all already known species and unique to them alone must be chosen, wherever it can be found. That mark is most conveniently taken from the Flower or Fruit in plants that have these parts, because these parts usually vary less within the same genus than others, and they are notable, conspicuous, and easily observable due to their color, shape, and other **accidental features** <term>qualities like color or size that do not change what a thing is, but help describe it</term>. If, however, some plant should occur in the future which agrees with other species of a genus in its other parts and features, but lacks this single mark which we have adopted as the Characteristic; despite this, we establish that it should be referred to that genus with which it has more common attributes.

In my *Letter to Mr. Rivinus* <note>Augustus Quirinus Rivinus (1652–1723), a German botanist who argued for a simpler classification system based solely on the number of flower petals.</note> and my *Dissertation on the Various Methods of Plants*, I decided that in those genera where such a notable property—common to all species contained within them and unique to them alone—is lacking, a "complex of several common attributes" should be taken as the Characteristic. This complex would consist of features that all together would belong to all the species contained under those genera, and to no others besides. But when I consider how—I do not say difficult—but impossible it is to assign a certain number of such accidental features, unless one knows every species of plant growing throughout the whole world (For how can one be certain that among those which still lie hidden unobserved, some will not be found which agree in their whole **habit** <term>the general appearance or growth form of a plant</term> and other marks with a certain described species, yet lack one or another mark from the assigned Characteristics?), since this is so, I judge it sufficient that all the assigned attributes belong to most species of a genus, and most of them to all. Nor should any species be excluded from fellowship or participation in a genus because it lacks one or another mark from those which [make up] the characteristi- <meta>catchword: cam (completing 'characteristicam' or 'characteristic')</meta>

<summary>John Ray explains that while botanists should look for a single defining feature (usually in the flower or fruit) to group plants, a "complex of attributes" is often more practical because nature is too diverse to fit into rigid, single-trait definitions.</summary>

Nor, however, do I think it should be excluded from the *Clover* genus because of this diversity, because that difference is not noticeable except to those alone who curiously examine and dissect plants and their parts."

In my *Dissertation on the Various Methods of Plants* <note>original: *Dissertatione de variis Plantarum Methodis* (1696).</note>, I conceded that complete agreement in both the Flower and the Fruit simultaneously is an indubitable sign of generic relationship. Accordingly, the opposite would follow: that those things which differ in Flower and Fruit, differ in genus. However, I see that this must not be admitted when the appearance, habit, and texture of the whole plant are opposed to it. Thus, the *Great Rush or Bulrush* <note>original: *Juncum seu Scirpum maximum*</note>, the *Rush with Horsetail heads* <note>original: *Juncum capitulis Equiseti*</note>, and their relatives—which produce scaly heads, and under each individual scale produce single, three-sided <note>original: *triquetra*</note>, naked seeds—and the *Common Smooth Rush with a scattered panicle* <note>original: *Juncum levem vulgarem paniculâ sparsâ*</note> and others—which produce a stamen-like flower provided with a six-leaved calyx, and a triangular fruit divided into three cells (or certainly opening <note>original: *dehiscentem*</note> into three parts) containing many seeds—these I do not separate. Rather, on account of the similarity in their whole external appearance, constitution, and texture, I reduce them to the same genus, by the unanimous consent not only of all Botanists, but of the entire human race. ...[due to the] dissimilarity of its parts, I separate the *Hairy Wood-grass* <note>original: *Gramen nemorosum hirsutum*; likely a species of *Luzula* or Wood-rush</note> and count it among the *Grasses*, with which it agrees in these features. Thus, I consider the *Small Yellow Water-lily with a fringed flower* <note>original: *Nymphæam luteam minorem flore fimbriato*</note> of Caspar Bauhin [C. So Mr. Magnol <note>Pierre Magnol (1638–1715), a French botanist after whom the Magnolia is named.</note> says in the Preface to his *Catalogue of the Montpellier Garden*: *“It is necessary,”* he says, *“to count among the true and genuine Toadflaxes <note>original: *Linarias*</note> both those which have flat seed and those which have round seed.”* <insert>The same is to be said concerning the species of Spurrey <note>original: *Spergulæ*</note>.</insert> *“And whether the Bird’s-foot Trefoil <note>original: *Lotus*</note> has pods divided into cells or not, they are genuine species of Bird’s-foot Trefoil.”* So (these are the words of Mr. Volckamer <note>Johann Georg Volckamer (1662–1744), a German physician and botanist.</note> in the Preface to the *Flora of Nuremberg*): *“Every single member of the Mallow and Hollyhock family known to us so far boasted a single-petaled flower divided into five parts; nonetheless, we possess from the famous Cape of Good Hope in Africa a rarer Marsh-mallow <note>original: *Althæam*</note> with a golden and almost spiral flower, which as it withers, breaks apart into five petals that are truly separated from one another.”* Likewise (the same author in the same place), the *African Berry-bearing Chrysanthemum* is *enangiospermon* <note>vessel-seeded; seeds enclosed in a fruit or vessel</note>, whereas the rest of the plants of this genus, by everyone’s common consent—and rightly so—are referred to the *Gymnosperms* <note>naked-seeded; seeds appearing to be "naked" rather than enclosed in a fleshy fruit</note>.

To speak briefly, the best *Method of Plants* is one in which all genera—whether the highest, the intermediate, or the lowest—share several common attributes, or agree in several parts and characteristics. However, Nature, I believe, does not allow for a Method of this kind. The next best thing is a method in which all plants that share several common attributes are referred to their own genera; while the rest, among which no agreement or similarity of multiple parts or characteristics is found, are distinguished by more general marks based on their agreement in one particularly notable part—namely, the structure of the Flower, its regularity, or the number of petals...

# PRELIMINARY KNOWLEDGE.

[by the] number [of seeds], the simplicity of the fruit, or its division into cells, as is most convenient, they are distinguished into genera. The species of these genera, however, are often not joined by any true affinity, nor united by any similarity or agreement, except in that general characteristic from which the name of the genus is taken. For what similarity is there between the *Rose*, the *Poppy*, *Rue*, *Buttercup*, and the *Rock-rose*, which Mr. Tournefort <note>Joseph Pitton de Tournefort (1656–1708), a French botanist whose system Ray both admired and critiqued.</note> reduces to the same Class, except for a certain agreement in the form of the Flower? What else are the *Many-petaled plants with an irregular flower* <note>original: *Polypetala Flore irregulari*</note>, which compose the eleventh Class of the same Mr. Tournefort’s *Elements of Botany*, but a dissolved broom <note>original: *scopæ dissolutæ*; a Latin idiom referring to a loose bundle or a disorganized collection of things.</note>? I do not, however, condemn or criticize his Method for this reason. For whoever wishes to establish a Method encompassing all plants must necessarily do the same.

For the sake of clearer understanding and memory, it is appropriate to connect the highest genera or Classes among themselves by some method to show a general view of all plants.

Our Method in arranging the highest genera proceeds gradually from the more imperfect to the more perfect, or from the lowest order of Plants to the higher.

1. In the first place, therefore, we present those which Botanists <term>Botanici<gloss>students or experts of plant life</gloss></term> commonly call *imperfect*, which lack both Flower and Fruit simultaneously, or at least lack a Flower; namely *Seaweeds* <note>original: *Fucos*</note>, under which name I here include all underwater plants, *Mushrooms* <note>original: *Fungos*</note>, *Mosses* <note>original: *Muscos*</note>, and those called *Capillary Herbs* <note>original: *Herbas Capillares*; a historical term for ferns, named for their hair-like stems.</note>.

2. Then, (after the division of the remaining Herbs into those with *Two seed-leaves* <term>Dicotyledones<gloss>plants whose seeds have two embryonic leaves</gloss></term> and those with *One seed-leaf* <term>Monocotyledones<gloss>plants whose seeds have only one embryonic leaf</gloss></term>), we attach to the plants lacking Flowers those provided with an *imperfect*, *petal-less* <term>Apetalo<gloss>lacking petals</gloss></term>, or *stamen-bearing* <term>Stamineo<gloss>consisting primarily of stamens without a colorful corolla</gloss></term> flower.

3. We assign the third place to those which have a perfect Flower, that is, one that is petal-like or bract-bearing, but [whose] seeds

He introduces the fundamental division of plants into Dicotyledons and Monocotyledons based on their seed leaves.</summary>

### PRELIMINARY KNOWLEDGE.

->** 5<-

<note>This text continues from the previous page's description of a plant category</note> naked, that is, enclosed or contained by no vessel except for the perianth <note>original: *perianthium*; the outer envelope of a flower, often the calyx</note>.

4. In the fourth place, we arrange those which have both a petaloid flower <note>original: *Florem Petaloden*; a flower with visible petals</note> and seeds enclosed in vessels.

Finally, I proceed to the *monocotyledons* <term>monocotyledons: plants whose seeds contain a single embryonic leaf, such as grasses or lilies</term>, and I distinguish them equally into those gifted with an apetalous or staminous flower <note>original: *Apetalo seu Stamineo Flore*; flowers lacking petals where the stamens are the most visible part</note>, and those enjoying a petaloid or bracteate flower <note>original: *Petalode seu bracteato*; flowers with petals or leaf-like structures called bracts</note>.

*Note*, as has already been noted above, that all the characteristic marks of a Class do not always apply to every single genus of each Class; among some, perhaps not even that mark from which the name of the Class is taken. For example, among the *four-petaled plants with pods* <note>original: *Tetrapetalas siliquosas*</note>, one or another five-petaled <note>original: *pentapetalon*</note> genus is found. It is enough that most marks agree with each and every one. Nor is there a need for us to be excessively scrupulous about admitting a plant into a share of some genus with which it has many marks or common attributes, even if it lacks that more distinguished mark which is used as the characteristic of the genus. I do, indeed, occasionally rebuke Mr. Tournefort <note>Joseph Pitton de Tournefort (1656–1708), a French botanist and Ray's contemporary rival</note> because he not infrequently subjects some genus to a certain section even though the characteristic mark of that section does not apply to it. Not that I disapprove of the action itself, but to show that he does the very thing for which he reproaches me, and sometimes—incautiously or perhaps overcome by the evidence of the matter—he comes around to our opinion; namely, that the most certain mark of generic agreement in plants is the whole similar habit <note>original: *habitum*; the general appearance or growth form of a plant</note> or several common attributes. We do, however, concede that the mark which is assumed as the characteristic of any genus should be very general and ought to apply as closely as possible to all species contained under that genus.

Furthermore, the reader must be advised that this Method of ours is intended especially for arranging European plants and

# RULES
### To Be
## OBSERVED IN ESTABLISHING A METHOD OF PLANTS.

-> I. <-

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap letter 'Q' containing a face (likely a lion or sun motif) within the circular part of the letter.</image-desc>
*As little innovation as possible should be made; neither should names received by common usage and frequently found in the writings of Physicians <note>original: "Medicorum"; at this time, botany was closely tied to medicine, as most doctors relied on herbal remedies</note> be changed, nor should their meanings, in order to avoid confusion and error. Those even moderately well-versed in the History of Plants <note>original: "Historia Plantarum"; this refers to the study of botany as a whole</note> know what great darkness and what great uncertainty the multiplication of names has introduced.*

-> II. <-

*The characteristics <note>original: "Notæ"; identifying features or "marks" used for classification</note> of genera <note>original: "generum"; the categories used to group plants</note>, both the highest <term>summa genera: Broad, primary categories, such as the distinction between trees and herbs</term> and the subordinate <term>subalterna genera: Lower-level groupings, similar to modern families or genus levels</term>, should be clear, distinct, and exactly defined—not obscure or indeterminate, where the extent of their meaning is uncertain. Hence, those characteristics derived from size or from a resemblance to other things seem less commendable; for it is not easy to determine what the boundary of size is (where those exceeding it are called "greater" and those falling short are called "lesser"), or how far a resemblance should be extended. Nevertheless, one must very often use these by necessity. Care must be taken, however, that the difference in size is not so small that it is not easily observed by anyone, or that the resemblance*

### III.

*Characteristics <note>original: "Notæ"; the physical features used to identify a plant</note> should be obvious, manifest, and easily observable by anyone. For since the primary use of a Method is to lead the unlearned and beginners <note>original: "rudes & Tyrones"</note> into the knowledge of plants <note>original: "Stirpium cognitionem"</note> concisely, without boredom or difficulty, one should not propose characteristics of a kind that require an attentive and anxious observer, or for which it would be necessary for someone to carry a microscope around with them.*

### IV.

*Genera <term>Genus: (plural: genera) A category used to group species that share similar characteristics. Ray is arguing for keeping groups that "feel" natural to the eye.</term> that are already accepted and approved by almost all botanists should be preserved—for example, the Umbellifers <term>Umbelliferae: Plants like carrots or parsley that have flower clusters shaped like umbrellas.</term>, the Verticillates <term>Verticillatae: Plants with leaves or flowers arranged in whorls or circles around the stem, like mint.</term>, those endowed with a Butterfly-shaped flower <note>original: "Flore Papilionaceo"; referring to the pea and bean family, whose flowers resemble butterflies</note>, etc.—and the Method should be adapted to them. Nor do we advise this without reason, since, as I have said elsewhere, among the highest genera <note>original: "summis generibus"; the primary, broad divisions of the plant kingdom</note> known thus far, the best are the genera of: Seaweeds <note>original: "Fucorum"</note>, Fungi, Mosses, Ferns <note>original: "Capillarium"; literally "hair-like" plants, a common term for ferns at the time</note>, Umbellifers, Verticillates, Rough-leaved plants <note>original: "Asperifoliarum"; the borage family</note>, Star-leaved plants <note>original: "Stellatarum"; the madder family</note>, Apple-bearing plants, Berry-bearing plants, Downy-seeded plants <note>original: "Papposarum"; plants whose seeds have fluffy "pappus" to fly in the wind, like dandelions</note>, Headed plants <note>original: "Capitatarum"; plants with flowers in dense heads, like thistles</note>, Corymb-bearing plants <note>original: "Corymbiferarum"; daisies and similar plants</note>, Four-petaled pod-bearing plants <note>original: "Tetrapetalarum Siliquosarum"; the mustard family</note>, Bulbous plants, and Grass-leaved plants. These constitute a good portion of those categories into which the more skilled botanists of the last century divided plants. For the species of these groups do not merely agree in one general characteristic,*

<meta>This page continues Ray's discussion on Rule IV, focusing on how natural groups of plants share multiple characteristics beyond their namesake features. -> # RULES <-

...they agree, but they also possess other common attributes besides. Thus, the plants called **Umbellifers** <term>Umbelliferae: A family of plants, like carrots, parsley, or hemlock, where the flower stalks sprout from a single point like the ribs of an umbrella.</term> agree not only in the arrangement of their flowers and seeds (from which they take the name "Umbellifer"), but also in their compound leaves, which are situated alternately on the stem; in their five-petaled flowers, which are small relative to the size of the plants and sit atop the fruit; and in their seeds, which are joined together in pairs. 

The **Rough-leaved plants** <term>Asperifoliae: An old name for the Borage family (Boraginaceae), known for having coarse, hairy leaves.</term> agree not only in having rough leaves (from which the name is derived), but also in those same leaves being attached to the stems alternately or without a specific order; in their single-petaled flowers with a five-parted margin; in their flower spikes which, before the flowers open, are curled back like a scorpion’s tail <note>This refers to a "scorpioid cyme," a type of flower cluster that uncurls as it blooms, typical of forget-me-nots and borage.</note>; and in having four seeds for every flower, and so on. 

The **Four-petaled pod-bearers** <term>Tetrapetalae siliquosae: Now known as the Brassicaceae or Mustard family; plants with four petals arranged like a cross and seed pods called siliques.</term> agree not only in those characteristics from which the name is taken, but also in that they have many flowers opening one after another at the tips of the stems and branches, with no small leaves <note>referring to bracts</note> placed at the base of the flower stalks. Their leaves are placed on the stems alternately or in no specific order, and the flower cups <note>the calyx</note> fall off along with the petals. It would be easy to show the same thing by running through each individual point in the remaining groups.

### V.

Care must be taken that plants which are kindred and of the same kind are not separated, and that those which are dissimilar and foreign—or of a different genus—are not grouped together. Hence, I cannot approve of **Dr. Rivinus’s Method** <note>Augustus Quirinus Rivinus (1652–1723) was a German botanist who classified plants strictly by the number and shape of their petals. Ray argues this is too simple and breaks up natural families.</note>, although it is very convenient for teaching, because it suffers from this fault—as I have shown in the cases of **Cinquefoil** <note>original: "Pentaphyllo"</note>, **Tormentil**, **Viper’s Bugloss** <note>original: "Echio"</note>, and **Sword-lily**...

## VI.

*The characteristic marks of genera must not be multiplied without necessity, nor should more be heaped together than are needed to determine the genus with certainty, lest the memory be burdened, and lest we appear to offer a full description of the plant instead of its defining characteristic marks.* <note>Ray is arguing for "parsimony" in science—the idea that a definition should be as simple as possible. He warns that if a list of traits becomes too long, it stops being a useful definition and becomes a tedious description.</note>

DRY-FRUITED TREES, NOT POD-BEARING, 157. <term>Fructu Sicco non Siliquosae: Trees that produce dry fruits—such as nuts, capsules, or winged seeds—rather than fleshy fruit or pods.</term>

POD-BEARING TREES WITH NON-BUTTERFLY-LIKE FLOWERS, 160. <term>Siliquosae Flore non Papilionaceo: Trees that produce pods (legumes) but have flowers with regular, symmetrical petals, unlike the irregular shape of a pea flower.</term>

POD-BEARING TREES WITH BUTTERFLY-LIKE FLOWERS, 162. <term>Flore Papilionaceo: Trees with "papilionaceous" flowers, named for their resemblance to a butterfly (Latin: *papilio*). This is the classic shape of flowers in the pea and bean family.</term>

ANOMALOUS TREES, 165. <term>Arbores Anomalae: A "catch-all" category for trees that do not fit neatly into the established botanical groups due to irregular or unique characteristics.</term>

## JOHN RAY’S
# METHOD OF PLANTS
### IMPROVED AND ENLARGED.

---

->*On the Primary Division of Plants.*<-

**W**e treated the division of plants into *Perfect* and *Imperfect* in the Dissertation *on the various methods of plants* page 16. To which add, that strictly speaking no plant at all is found to be imperfect, but all, even of the lowest order, obtain the perfection due to their natures, and each is perfect in its own kind. Those plants which others call *imperfect*, I might (as I think) more rightly call of a lower order. <note>Ray is arguing against the medieval idea of a "Great Chain of Being" where some organisms were seen as "incomplete" or "mistakes"; he argues every creature is perfect for its specific purpose.</note>

Moreover, some plants (although they should not be called *Imperfect* for this reason) lack some principal part, namely either the *fruit* or the *flower*. Whether any besides the *Fungus* (if indeed the *Fungus* is to be excepted) is destitute of all flower and fruit or seed, I doubt, and I judge it more likely that none exists: But it is certain that very many lack a flower, namely: 1. All *Submarine* plants, *Corals*, *Algae*, *Seaweeds*, *Sponges*, etc. <note>In the 17th century, corals and sponges were still classified as plants because they were stationary.</note> 2. Those *perpetually submerged in fresh waters*: for whatever aquatic plants bloom, they raise the top of the stalk that carries the flowers above the surface of the water; 3. *Fungi*. 4. *Mosses*, and perhaps also, 5. <term>Capillary plants<note>fern-like plants, specifically those that reproduce via spores on the underside of leaves</note></term>, which Mr. *Tournefort* <note>Joseph Pitton de Tournefort (1656–1708), a contemporary French botanist and rival of Ray.</note> counts among those destitute of flowers: to which must be added certain miscellaneous ones such as *Jointed Glasswort*, *Adder's-tongue*, etc., joined by no affinity either among themselves or with the rest of the flowerless ones.

Therefore, having rejected that division of plants into *Imperfect* and *Perfect*; we shall distribute them into *Flowerless* and *Flowering*. *Flowerless* we shall again divide into those *Immersed in water*, whether *Salt* such as *Seaweeds* etc. or *fresh*; and those *Born out of water* such as *Fungi* and *Mosses*.

The *Flowering* plants we shall divide into <term>Dicotyledons<note>Plants whose seeds produce two initial leaves (seed-leaves) upon germinating, like beans or oaks.</note></term>, whose sown seeds emerge from the earth with two irregular leaves, called <term>Seed-leaves<note>original: "foliis seminalibus"</note></term>, which serve the purpose of *Cotyledons*, or at least are divided into two lobes, even if they do not produce them above the ground in the form of leaves: and <term>Monocotyledons<note>Plants whose seeds produce a single initial leaf, like grasses or lilies.</note></term>, which neither produce two seed-leaves nor hide two lobes.

<summary>In this introduction, John Ray rejects the classification of "imperfect plants" and introduces his groundbreaking division of flowering plants into Dicotyledons and Monocotyledons based on their seed leaves.</summary>
<keywords>John Ray, taxonomy, botany, Dicotyledons, Monocotyledons, plant classification, Tournefort, seed leaves, flowerless plants</keywords>

<page-num>2</page-num>
<header># METHOD OF PLANTS</header>

->Plants are either:<-

<image-desc>A botanical classification diagram using nested curly brackets to illustrate a hierarchical taxonomy. The tree branches from non-flowering and flowering plants into various aquatic and terrestrial categories, including specific genera and types of seeds (dicotyledonous and monocotyledonous).</image-desc>

**Those lacking flowers**, and these are either:
*   **Immersed in water**:
    *   In saltwater, such as all submarine plants: **CORALS**, **SEAWEEDS**, **SPONGES**, etc. <note>original: "CORALIA, FUCI, SPONGIÆ". In the 17th century, corals and sponges were classified as plants because they were fixed in one place like vegetation.</note>
    *   In freshwater.
*   **Growing outside of water**:
    *   **FUNGI**.
    *   **MOSSES**.
    *   Those called **<term>Capillary plants<note>Ferns and their relatives; the name "capillary" comes from the hair-like appearance of some species' stems or the ancient belief they could heal hair.</note></term>**; to which must be added certain scattered or miscellaneous types, such as jointed **GLASSWORT**, **ADDER'S-TONGUE**, etc. <note>original: "KALI geniculatum, OPHIOGLOSSUM".</note>

**Flower-bearing**; which are either:
*   **<term>Dicotyledons<note>Plants that produce two seed-leaves upon germination. Ray was the first to realize this was a fundamental way to group plants.</note></term>**, whose seeds, when sown, emerge from the earth with two "anomalous" leaves (called seed-leaves), or at least are divided into two lobes, even if they do not carry them above the ground in the form of leaves.
*   **<term>Monocotyledons<note>Plants that produce only a single seed-leaf upon germination, such as grasses and lilies.</note></term>**, which neither produce two seed-leaves nor contain two lobes.

This division can also be extended to **Trees**: since *Palms* and their relatives differ from other trees in this respect in the same way that Monocotyledons differ from other herbs.

Among the Mosses, some (such as, for example, *Lycopodium* <note>Clubmoss</note>) seem to have a stamen-like flower; however, since they resemble Mosses in their entire appearance, they should not be separated from them.

## FIRST GENUS
### Of Plants Lacking Flowers, or
# SUBMARINE PLANTS.

I call "Submarine Plants" those which are born on the seafloor or upon marine rocks, and are either perpetually immersed in the waters or at least reached by each incoming tide. (Those plants which are born in the vicinity of the sea are called *maritime* plants.)
I divide these into three types:
The *first* consists of those which are composed of a very hard and stony substance, which crunch under the teeth when chewed or feel gritty; they are fragile and emit a clear ringing sound when struck against a hard body. For this reason, they may be called <term>Lithophyta<note>From the Greek for "stone-plants." In Ray's time, corals were considered plants because they grew in fixed positions like trees.</note></term>.
The *second* consists of those which are of a woody, tough, and somewhat horn-like substance; these are called <term>Corallines<note>original: "Corallinæ." These are distinguished here from stony corals by their flexible, leathery texture.</note></term>.
Finally, the *third* consists of those which are of a softer and herbaceous substance, such as *Algae*, *Seaweeds*, *Sponges*, *Mosses*, and so on.

---

->Of Submarine Plants<-
->First Genus<-
->or<-

# LITHOPHYTA.

1. **Coral**, or the *Stone-tree* <note>original: "Lithodendron."</note>, the characteristics of which are a stony substance, solid and not at all porous, nor pierced with small holes, having the form of a small tree or a leafless shrub.
2. **Porous-coral** <note>original: "Porus."</note> is very close in substance to the Corals, differing from them only by the frequent pores or holes with which it is pierced or interrupted. I refer the so-called **Star-stones** <note>original: "Lapides Astroites & Stellares." Fossilized or living corals with star-shaped patterns.</note> to this group, as well as the **Brain-stones** <note>original: "Encephalites." Corals whose surface patterns resemble the folds of a human brain.</note>.
3. **Eschara** are "stone-plants" that imitate leafy fronds; some are even beautifully netted, called **Leafy-pore** and **Netted Leafy-pore** <note>original: "Frondipora" and "Frondipora reticulata." These are likely bryozoans, colonial animals that form lacy, fan-like structures.</note>.
4. **Stony Mushrooms** imitate **terrestrial mushrooms** in their shape, and some even in their gills <note>original: "lamellis."</note>.
5. **Stony Sea Mosses**, some of which are joined together like little boxes, such as, for example, the **Apothecary's Coralline** <note>original: "Corallina Officinarum." This is a calcium-coated seaweed used historically in medicine.</note>. The nodes or joints are threaded inside by a certain "nerve" or fiber, about the thickness of the thread used to sew clothes...

## Second Genus of Submarine Plants,

->or<-

->Those of a harder and tenacious, woody, or horny substance,<-

# CORALLINES according to some.

The reticulated Coralline, called the "Sea-fan" <note>original: "Flabellum marinum."</note> by some. It is covered with a certain tartar-like crust that can be easily scraped off, which seems to be formed from the silt at the bottom of the sea and grows onto the plant. Once the outer crust is scraped away, the inner substance appears hard, blackish, etc.

1. The coral-like marine shrub of Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a foundational Flemish botanist.</note>.
2. Purple shrubby coralline of C. B. <note>Caspar Bauhin (1560–1624), a Swiss botanist who classified thousands of plants.</note>.
3. Rough woody coralline, with the appearance of Heath, of Park. <note>John Parkinson (1567–1650), the last of the great English herbalists.</note>.

## Third Genus of Submarine Plants,

->which are<-

->Of a softer consistency, approaching that of herbs.<-

1. **Algae**, or **Seaweeds** <note>original: "Fuci."</note> with grass-like leaves, containing seeds within the folds <note>original: "sinu."</note> of the leaves.
2. **Pod-bearing Seaweeds**, mostly forked <note>original: "dichotomi."</note> and seed-bearing; they have two types of pods—some are bladdery <note>original: "ventosos."</note> and filled only with air, others are full of seeds.
3. **Greater Seaweeds**, neither blistered nor forked. Their seeds, if they have any, have not yet been discovered.
4. **Sea Mosses**, **Lichens**, etc. are of the smallest kind, and as far as has been discovered until now, are sterile or devoid of seeds.
5. **Sea-figs** <note>original: "Alcyonia."</note>, or plants resembling Mushrooms.
6. **Sponges** are very close to Fungi, or hover between Mosses and Fungi; they have a soft and somewhat woolly substance, full of small holes and endowed with an elastic power, which easily drinks up and retains water or other liquids.

# SECOND GENUS
## Of Plants Lacking a Flower, or
# F U N G I .

Fungi have almost nothing in common with the more perfect <note>By "perfect," Ray refers to higher vascular plants that have clearly defined parts like leaves, stems, and seeds.</note> plants: for they commonly lack the green color of herbs, nor do they have a similar texture, nor any *Flower* or *Seed* that we have known until now, if you except one or two species; nor do they even have a *Leaf* properly so called. In short, there is very little distinction of parts in them. Most of them arise in a very short space of time and are likewise of a brief life span. However, many of those that grow on trees last for a long time.

I divide Fungi into two Genera, namely into the *Gilled* <note>original: "Lamellatos."</note>, or those having something analogous to small plates <note>The gills on the underside of a mushroom cap.</note> under their caps or heads: most of which have a stalk <note>original: "pediculum."</note> bearing a cap or head; and those *Lacking Gills*. In the former genus, the heads consist of a dual substance: the *Upper* part is uniform and undivided, usually of the same color inside as the stalk; the *Lower* part is often of a different color and divided into gills; sometimes this substance is not divided into gills but mimics the comb of wood <note>Likely referring to a porous or honeycombed structure.</note> with larger pores coming between.

Each Genus is either *Terrestrial* or *Arboreal* <note>Growing on trees.</note>. In the second Genus, there is also a *Subterranean* type, called the *Earth Tuber* <note>original: "Tuber terra," referring to Truffles.</note>. In the Genus of tree-dwelling fungi lacking gills, the Samucus-fungus <note>Elderberry fungus.</note> is given the specific name *Jew’s Ear* <note>original: "Auricula Judæ"; now commonly called the Jelly Ear (Auricularia auricula-judae).</note>, and the Larch-fungus is denominated *Agaric* <note>original: "Agaricus."</note>.

Fungi lacking gills are of various forms: some are *membranous* or like *leather*, such as the *Jew’s Ear* and *Pliny’s Pezicae* <note>Cup fungi.</note>; others are *globose* or thick, such as the *Lycoperdon* or *Dusty Fungus* <note>The Puffball; "Lycoperdon" literally translates to "wolf's fart," as noted in the list below.</note>; others are *branched*, called *coralloids* <note>Coral fungi.</note> by some; others are *Capped* or *Headed*, such as the *Phalloid Fungus* <note>Stinkhorns.</note>, the *Honeycombed Fungus* or *Merulius* <note>Likely referring to Morels (Morchella).</note> etc.

<image-desc>A hierarchical classification scheme for fungi. A large curly brace divides Fungi into two main categories: 'Lamellati & pileati' (Gilled & capped) and 'Lamellis carentes' (Lacking gills). These are further subdivided by smaller nested braces. 'Gilled' are split into 'Arborei' (Tree-dwelling) and 'Terrestres' (Land-dwelling). 'Lacking gills' are subdivided into a list of eight types including 'Clavati' (Club-shaped), 'Capitati' (Headed), 'Globosi' (Globular), 'Membranacei' (Membranous), 'Ramosi' (Branched), 'Seminiferi' (Seed-bearing), 'Subterranei' (Underground), and 'Variarum formarum' (Of various forms).</image-desc>

{ **Gilled & capped**, or consisting of a dual substance.
{ { **Arboreal** [Tree-dwelling].
{ { **Terrestrial** [Land-dwelling].
{ **Lacking Gills**.
{ { **Club-shaped** <note>original: "Clavati."</note>, resembling clubs.
{ { **Headed or capped**: such as the fungus **MERULIUS**, **PHALLOIDES**.
{ { **Globose or dusty**, called **WOLF’S FART** <note>original: "CREPITUS LUPI," the common name for puffballs.</note>.
{ { **Membranous**; such as **JEW’S EAR**, Pliny’s **PEZICAE**.
{ { **Branched**, **CORALLOIDS**.
{ { **Seed-bearing**.
{ { **Subterranean**. **EARTH TUBERS** [Truffles].
{ { **Of various forms**.

# THIRD GENUS

->Of plants lacking a flower<-

->or<-

# M O S S E S.

Mosses, although they are recognized by anyone—even among the common folk—at first glance, yet to define them exactly would not be easy even for the <term>Philosophers</term> <note>In this period, "philosophers" or "natural philosophers" refers to scientists and naturalists.</note> themselves.

They are distinguished from other plants by their smallness, or by their drier and less succulent <note>meaning juicy or fleshy</note> substance, or by their easy revival upon being placed in water after they have almost dried out—in the manner of the <term>Thlaspi</term> <note>original: "Thlaspeos," an old botanical name for a group of cruciferous plants.</note> called the *Rose of Jericho* <note>original: "Rosa Hierichuntina." The Rose of Jericho (*Anastatica hierochuntica*) is famous for its "resurrection" properties when moistened.</note>—or by their native habitats, which are wretched, dry, and scorched by excessive cold or heat, such as on trees, wood, and rocks where other plants cannot live or endure; or finally, by their way of producing fruit.

Some of these seem to approach Fungi in color and texture, which is why they are named <term>Moss-fungi</term> <note>original: "Musco-fungi." Ray is likely referring to Lichens, which were often categorized between mosses and fungi at this time.</note> by some.

<summary>John Ray introduces the third category of his botanical system, the Mosses, noting that while they are easily recognized by sight, they are difficult to define scientifically due to their unique survival traits and habitats.</summary>
<keywords>Mosses, Musci, Rose of Jericho, plant classification, extremophiles, Moss-fungi, Lichens, botanical history</keywords>

## Mosses are either:

<image-desc>A taxonomic classification of mosses organized as a hierarchical tree structure using large nested curly braces to group characteristics and types.</image-desc>

*   Drier and juice-less <note>original: "exsucci"</note>, and not at all herbaceous, producing small circles <note>original: "orbiculos," likely referring to the cup-like fruiting bodies or apothecia found on lichens</note> which perhaps contain seeds, though they are commonly considered sterile; called **Moss-fungi** <note>original: "Musco-fungi"</note> by some: which are either
    *   More upright and branched, such as **Coral-like mosses**, **Branched tree moss**, **Shield-bearing or scutellar moss**.
    *   Crust-like or lichen-like <note>original: "Licheniformes"</note>, such as Moss growing in the manner of a crust on trees and rocks—yellow, ash-grey, dark, etc.
    *   **Cup-moss** <note>original: "Muscus pyxidatus"</note>, etc.
*   More succulent and herbaceous, which are clearly fertile or fruit-bearing, whose surface consists either of
    *   **Leaves**, mostly of an indeterminate shape, sending out roots and thus spreading themselves out, such as **Earth-lichens** of various species.
    *   **Stems**, covered with leaves of a determinate shape, which are either
        *   **Larger**,
            *   Shrubby and woody, which although they resemble mosses in their leaves, belong rather to the tree-like genus <note>Ray notes that despite their appearance, these larger plants are structurally closer to woody plants</note>.
            *   Club-shaped and flower-bearing, producing seeds in spikes resembling clubs, such as **Lycopodium** <term>Lycopodium</term> <note>commonly known today as clubmoss</note> and the **Wild Savin of Tragus** <note>original: "Sabina Sylvestris Tragi," referring to the 16th-century botanist Hieronymus Bock, who went by the name Tragus</note>.
            *   Producing seeds in the axils <note>original: "alis," literally "wings," the angle between the leaf and the stem</note> of the leaves, such as the **Fir-shaped land moss**, etc.
        *   **Smaller**, producing fruit in little heads <note>original: "capitulis," referring to the spore-bearing capsules</note> or little horns, which have stems that are either
            *   **Scaly**, mostly trailing on the ground and creeping, weak, whose capsules emerge from the axils of the leaves or scales along the stems and branches; these I call **Land Mosses**.
            *   **Leafy**, more upright, less branched, or creeping, but mostly gathered into dense tufts <note>original: "cespites"</note>, whose capsules emerge either from the tips of the branches, or from the roots or the shoots of the previous year; these have leaflets that are either
                *   Surrounding the stems on all sides, with capsules
                    *   Sitting on longer stalks <note>original: "pediculis"</note>, covered by a little cap or lid <note>original: "pileolo seu operculo," the calyptra and operculum that protect the developing spores</note>
                        *   Hairy; **Greater Golden Maidenhair** <note>original: "Adiantum aureum majus," usually referring to the Haircap moss, *Polytrichum commune*</note>.
                        *   Membranous; **Lesser Golden Maidenhair**, with heads that are ->Erect.<-
                            ->Reflexed.<- <note>meaning bent backward or downward</note>
                    *   Sessile <note>sitting directly on the stem</note>, without stalks.
                        *   Capped and striated <note>marked with narrow lines or grooves</note>.
                        *   Naked, called **Apocarpi** <note>original: "Apocarpi," a term meaning "without fruit stalks"</note>.
                *   Arranged in the manner of **Ferns** <note>original: "Filicinorum modo," referring to mosses where the leaves are arranged in two flat rows like a fern frond</note>.

Ray further divides them by their growth habits, the shape of their stems and leaves, and the structure of their reproductive capsules.</summary>

## THE FOURTH GENUS

->Comprising the plants called<-

# C A P I L L A R Y  P L A N T S . <note>Capillary plants is the historical term for ferns, so named because some species have very fine, hair-like stems.</note>

In my *Method* and *History of Plants*, I established the distinguishing mark for the genus of Capillary plants <note>original: "Capillarium stirpium"</note> as lacking a stem, as if their entire surface consisted of nothing but leaves. This definition fits all European plants of this genus that I have known until now. However, it is clear from the testimony of reliable authors that some Indian and American species are actually found to be stem-bearing; indeed, I myself have seen several dried specimens of these collected on the island of *Jamaica* in the possession of the most learned and friendly man, **Sir Hans Sloane**. <note>Hans Sloane (1660–1753) was a physician and naturalist whose massive collection later formed the foundation of the British Museum.</note> Therefore, a common mark or generic character for the Capillary plants is still lacking. For if, along with **Mr. Tournefort**, you take "lacking flowers" and "being dorsiferous" <term>dorsiferous: from the Latin 'dorsum' (back) and 'ferre' (to bear), referring to plants that carry their seeds or spores on the back of their leaves</term> together as the distinguishing mark, you will exclude the **Royal Fern** <note>original: "Osmundam Regalem"</note> and any similar relatives from the fellowship or membership of this genus, if you follow the common opinion of herbalists; for to us, even these appear to be dorsiferous. 

Yet it is not certain that Capillary herbs lack all flowers, since **Mr. Rivinus** attributes small, granulated flowers to them—of the kind I myself thought I saw in the **Polypody** <note>a common type of fern</note>, distinguished by a yellow color. Furthermore, in his description of the Tree Fern, **Mr. Plumier** <note>Charles Plumier (1646–1704), a French botanist known for his work in the West Indies</note> says that before the seed-bearing tubercles turned into fine dust, he saw very small, grayish, single-petaled flowers precede them, hollowed out in the manner of a tiny hemispherical calyx and filled with many very small grayish filaments.

The mark of the *Capillary plants* should therefore be: the seed is a very tiny powder, born on the leaves and usually on their backs. I added "usually" so that I might avoid all dispute regarding the **Royal Fern**, although in that plant the so-called "flower-bearing shoots" are actually part of the leaves, which (it seems to me) have been contracted because of the seeds growing upon them, with their margins turned upward or rolled back.

As for the method of classification, I judge that to be best which I proposed in my letter to **Mr. Rivinus**, which is taken from the placement of the seeds.

<summary>Ray redefines the "Capillary" genus (ferns) to account for tropical species with stems and debates whether ferns possess flowers, ultimately focusing on seed placement as the primary taxonomic trait.</summary>

<header>REVISED AND ENLARGED.</header>

### *Where the seeds of Capillary plants originate.*

<note>This section outlines the diverse ways fern spores appear on the plant, which was the primary way early botanists classified them.</note>

- *In special little forks (which are nevertheless part of the leaves) packed together like clusters of grapes in the so-called Flowering Herbs, such as the **Royal Fern**.* <note>original: "Osmunda regalis"</note>
- *On the backs of the leaves, and this either:*
    - *From their margins, as in the common **Female Fern**, the true **Maidenhair**, etc.*
    - *On the middle or interior part of the surface, and this either:*
        - *1. In rusty spots or warts, usually in a double row, as in **Polypody** and most species of the so-called **Male Fern**.*
        - *2. In small worm-like lines, as in **Hart's Tongue**, **Black Maidenhair**, etc.* <note>original: "Phillitide, Adiantho nigro"</note>
        - *3. In a somewhat broad line drawn along both sides of the middle nerve or rib of the leaf lengthwise, as in the **Spleenwort** described by Plumier as "powdery near the nerve."* <note>Charles Plumier (1646–1704) was a French botanist who explored the West Indies.</note>
        - *4. Over the entire surface of the leaf; as in **Scolopendria**.* <note>A term historically used for various ferns, often Hart's Tongue.</note>

---

These Genera, however, can be further subdivided by size, the division of the leaves, the form of the roots, and other accidental features.

This *Method*, I say, seems to me the best of all; but since so many new and unnamed species of *Capillaries* <note>ferns</note> in the *East Indies* but especially in *America* have been discovered and described through the auspices and industry of most famous men living today or recently deceased—**Mr. Hendrik van Rheede**, **Mr. John Banister**, **Mr. Charles Plumier**, **Sir Hans Sloane**, and others of lesser note—so many indeed that I would scarcely have believed could be found in the whole world; and since either their *living roots*, or carefully dried branches stored between papers, or images drawn from life have been sent to Europe or brought in and shown to the curious, and afterwards even *engraved in copper*, exhibited publicly, and exposed to the eyes of all: yet in many of them, the placement of the seeds has not been observed, or certainly not described. Since, I say, these things are so, I see it is plainly impossible for me to reduce them all to this *Method*; rather, the old way taken from the shape and division of the leaves must be entirely retained, though in some respects changed and improved.

Whether, therefore, this genus of plants truly bears stems, or less so, I am little concerned; I shall take their differences from the simplicity or division of their leaves.

First of all, however, I will set forth the definitions of *Stem* and *Leaf*.

*Stem*, therefore, as defined by **Jungius**, *is a part of the plant so extended in length that the front parts do not differ from the back, nor the right from the left; or such that from its shape it cannot be known which part is the front and which is the back.* <note>Joachim Jungius (1587–1657) was a German philosopher and naturalist. Ray admired his precise, almost mathematical approach to defining plant parts.</note>

<meta>catchword: *Folium* (Leaf)</meta>

<meta>Continuity: Following the previous page where John Ray categorized ferns (Capillary plants) based on the location of their seeds or spores, he now moves on to define the nature of the leaf itself and how it is used to further classify these plants into groups of different sizes and structures.</meta>

<page-num>10</page-num>
-> # METHOD OF PLANTS <-

A leaf is that which possesses a front (or upper) surface distinct from its back (or lower) surface.

Rushes, Horsetails, Onions, etc., which have a hollow and rounded leaf, seem to be exceptions here, unless you consider the interior surface of the tube to be the upper part and the exterior to be the lower part. <note>Ray is struggling with "terete" or cylindrical leaves that don't have the typical flat top and bottom of most foliage.</note>

*A leaf is either simple or composite.*

**Simple** is that which is not divided into several leaves or lobes.

**Composite** is either *pinnate* <note>Arranged like the vanes of a feather</note> or *branched*.

I call leaves **simple** not only when they are completely whole or undivided, but also however they may be cut or fringed, provided that the fringes or incisions are not very deep, nor reach close to the middle rib or rachis <note>term: rachis (the central axis of a leaf)</note>, nor correspond to each other in equal numbers on both sides along the length of the leaf in an opposite or alternating arrangement.

**Composite** leaves are those which, along the length of the total leaf, are divided either into several fringes reaching close to the middle rib, or into several pinnules or leaflets attached to the middle rib, or into several pinnate shoots, or finally into several twiggy branches attached to the middle rib in equal numbers, in the manner I have described, in either an opposite or alternating position.

Tree ferns <note>original: "Filices arboreæ"</note> differ from other stalk-bearing plants in their size and stature, and because their trunks consist of a woody substance.

I divide the Capillary plants <note>term: Capillary plants (an archaic term for ferns, from the Latin 'capillus' meaning hair, referring to their fine stems or roots)</note> into **Major** and **Minor**.

The **Major** are: **Hart’s Tongue**, **Mule Fern**, **Holly Fern**, **Fern**, and **Royal Fern**. <note>original: "Phyllitis, Hemionitis, Lonchitis, Filix, Osmunda"</note>

The **Minor** are: **Spleenwort**, **Maidenhair Spleenwort**, **Wall Rue**, and **Maidenhair**. <note>original: "Asplenium, Trichomanes, Ruta muraria, Adiantum"</note>

Although I by no means approve of this division of plants taken from differences in size—since nature has fixed no certain limit or boundary of size between them, such that those exceeding it should be called *major* and those falling short should be called *minor*—I am nevertheless sometimes forced to use it when a more convenient one does not occur. It is sufficient for the present to assert this division, so that the greatest part of the Capillary plants which we call **major** exceed the greatest of the **minor** in size; and if any smaller species are found, they can easily be reduced to their proper genera by their similarity or agreement with the larger ones. Furthermore, these **minor** Capillary plants differ from the larger ones not only in their smallness, but in their texture, the shape and division of their leaves, the smoothness and shine of their stems, and other peculiar characteristics.

<summary>John Ray defines the botanical difference between simple and compound leaves and explains his pragmatic, if imperfect, system for categorizing ferns by size and leaf structure.</summary>

<page-num>II</page-num>

### Large Ferns <note>original: "Plantae Capillares"; in Ray's time, ferns were called "capillary" plants because many were used as hair treatments or had hair-thin stems.</note> are categorized by their Leaves:

{ **Simple**, meaning whole and not at all divided into wings; such as **HART'S-TONGUE** and **MULE-FERN**.
{ **Composite**, or divided:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;{ By a **Single** division into wings, leaflets <note>term: pinnulae (small leaflets that make up a fern frond)</note>, or deep segments, such as **POLYPODY** and **ROUGH WORT**.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;{ By a **Double** division: first into wings, and then into leaflets.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;{ By a **Triple** division: first into branches, then into wings, and finally into leaflets; plants of this kind are called *branched*.

### The first Genus of the larger Ferns, possessing a simple or whole leaf that is not at all divided into wings.

1. **Hart's-tongue** <note>original: "Phyllitis"</note> is a fern with a simple, long, straight leaf that is neither hollowed out at the base nor eared. 
In the *European Hart's-tongue*, the seeds <note>Historically, the spores on the back of fern leaves were referred to as seeds.</note> grow onto the back part of the leaves in oblique lines or patches.
I consider the Hart's-tongue with a wavy or curled leaf, as well as the one with a fingered leaf, etc., to be accidental variations of the Hart's-tongue, not distinct species.

2. **Mule-fern** <note>original: "Hemionitis"</note> agrees with the Hart's-tongue in having simple leaves, but differs from it either by a hollowed-out notch at the base of the leaf—usually with two appendages standing out like ears—or by a leaf that is in some way jagged at the base and shorter than the former. **Mr. Bobart** <note>Jacob Bobart the Younger, a contemporary botanist at Oxford.</note> adds that the leaves of the *Mule-fern* expand into ivy-like angles, whose veins are distributed from the top of the leaf-stalk <note>term: petiole (the stalk that joins a leaf to a stem)</note> or center toward the edges.

To this Genus, people usually add **Dr. Sloane's** <note>Sir Hans Sloane, whose collection became the foundation of the British Museum.</note> *Asarabacca-leaved Mule-fern*; the deeply jagged *Mule-fern* with powdery edges described by **Plumier**; and the beautiful *American Mule-fern* resembling the shape of a Roman axe described in **Plukenet's** *Almagestum*. However, since these plants produce stalks (these are the words of **Mr. Bobart**) that are a shining, splendid black and have powdery edges, we have judged that they belong by better right to the *Maidenhair* <note>original: "Adiantum"</note> family, and it has pleased us to call them *Single-leaved Maidenhairs*. I am not opposed to this opinion myself, although I think they should be called "simple-leaved" rather than "single-leaved" Maidenhairs.

It should be noted that among the *Hart's-tongue* and other types of Ferns found in **America**, there are some species that creep or climb by sending out straps <note>term: stolons (horizontal connections between plants)</note> in the manner of **Strawberries**. These should be counted among the stalk-bearing plants, since those straps or cords seem to be nothing other than prostrate stems—unless one preferred to refer them to the roots and call them "exposed roots."

# The second Genus of the larger Ferns <note>original: "Capillarium majorum"; ferns were traditionally called "capillary" or hair-like plants because of their thin, dark stems or their use in hair-strengthening remedies.</note>,
## *With leaves composed only of segments, leaflets, or wings.*

1. **Polypody** <note>original: "Polypodium"</note> is a capillary herb with leaves divided into oblong segments reaching nearly to the middle rib, and in most species, these segments have even margins.

It is distinguished from Rough Wort <note>original: "Lonchitis"</note> and other pinnate <note>term: pinnate (a leaf shape where leaflets are arranged like the barbs of a feather on either side of a central stem)</note> ferns by this most certain sign: that the leaf segments are not contracted into a small stalk <note>term: pediculus (the stem of an individual leaflet)</note> as they are in those others, by which they would be attached to the leaf's rib; instead, they are connected or continuous with the rib along their entire base. In most species, the incisions of the segments do not reach all the way to the central spine <note>original: "rachin"</note> of the leaf, but the leaf remains continuous along the rib. It differs from Spleenwort <note>original: "Scolopendria"</note> in its size, which is greater, and in its leaf segments, which are longer, narrower, and sharper. Add to this that in Spleenwort, the seed-like eruptions <note>original: "seminalia exanthemata"; historically, the spore-cases on the back of ferns were mistaken for seeds or skin-like spots.</note> occupy the entire underside of the leaves, whereas in Polypody, they are divided into a double row of dots or spots on each segment.

2. *Rough Wort* <note>original: "Lonchitis"</note> differs from the remaining pinnate or, if you prefer, winged ferns, because its leaflets <note>term: pinnulae (the small, individual leaflets that make up a fern frond)</note> are eared <note>term: auriculate (having a small, ear-shaped lobe at the base of the leaflet)</note> at the base.

**Mr. Bobart** <note>Jacob Bobart the Younger (1641–1719) was a prominent English botanist and curator of the Oxford Botanic Garden.</note> distinguishes Rough Worts into those that are simply eared (on one side only) and those eared on both sides. The latter might perhaps more correctly be called *pinnate Mule-ferns* <note>original: "Hemionitides pinnatæ"</note>.

3. *Fern with only pinnate leaves*, or *non-branched Fern* with whole wings that are not divided into smaller leaflets.

# The third Genus of the larger Ferns,
## *With leaves subdivided once: first into wings, and then those wings into leaflets or segments.*

**Mr. Bobart** divides these into: 1. Those whose wings are not divided all the way to the nerve; 2. Those whose wings are dissected into distinct leaflets all the way to the nerve. One may see the full list of all these in his work, *The History of Oxford [Plants], page 576* <note>original: "Hist. Oxon. pag. 576."</note>.

# The fourth Genus of the larger Ferns,
## *With leaves subdivided twice, known as the Branched kind.*

**To this** Genus belong the *Common Female Fern* <note>likely referring to the Bracken fern</note>, whose distinguishing marks are its remarkable size, its creeping root, its non-toothed leaves, and its seed-vessels growing all around the edges of the leaves; also the *Flowering Fern* or *Royal Fern* <note>original: "Osmunda regalis"</note>, and many others.
