# METHOD OF PLANTS

4. **Lavender Cotton** <note>original: *Santolina*</note> or **Female Southernwood** <note>original: *Abrotanum fæmina*</note> is distinguished from other genera by having fairly large, individual flowers at the ends of each small branch. **Mr. Tournefort** <note>Joseph Pitton de Tournefort (1656–1708), a hugely influential French botanist before the time of Linnaeus.</note> observes that the seeds are separated from one another by tiny leaves bent into the shape of a channel.

5. **Water Hemp-Agrimony** <note>original: *Cannabina aquatica*</note>, called **Bidens** <note>meaning "two-toothed," referring to the bristles on the seeds. Today known as Bur-marigold.</note> by some. Its characteristics are a "horned" or two-toothed seed, leaves arranged in pairs on the stem, and flowers that are sometimes radiate <note>having outer petals</note> but usually naked <note>lacking petals</note>. We placed this above among the corymb-bearers with naked flowers because it possesses flowers of both types.

6. **Daisy with a naked yellow flower** <note>original: *Bellis flore luteo nudo*</note>.

7. **Clusius’s Valentine Chrysanthemum** <note>original: *Chrysanthemum Valentinum Clus.* Carolus Clusius was a famous 16th-century botanist.</note>. This also has flowers that are sometimes radiate and sometimes naked, which is why it can be referred to the **Chrysanthemums**.

8. **Garden Costus** <note>original: *Costus hortorum*</note> or **Costmary** <note>original: *Balsamita mas*</note>. Its characteristics are naked yellow flowers clustered in an umbel <note>an umbrella-like arrangement</note> at the tops of the stems; the leaves are broad and whole, with notched edges.

9. **Tansy** <note>original: *Tanacetum*</note>. Its characteristics are golden, naked flowers clustered in an umbel at the tops of the stems; the leaves are finely divided <note>laciniated</note> with the segments arranged almost in pairs along the rib. It has a powerful but not unpleasant scent.

10. **Tarragon** <note>original: *Draco* herba</note>. **Mr. Tournefort** refers this to **Southernwood** under the title "Male Southernwood with a sharper and scented flax-like leaf" <note>original: *Abrotani maris Lini folio acriore & odorato*</note>. **Mr. Hermann** <note>Paul Hermann (1646–1695), a physician and botanist who worked in Ceylon and Leiden.</note> identifies its characteristics as smaller, naked, disk-shaped flowers arranged in spikes along the length of the stems and branches; the leaves are alternate and resemble those of **Hyssop**, with the lowest leaves divided and the rest whole. This plant is not currently at hand, and therefore I have nothing further to say about it.

11. **Sweet Maudlin** <note>original: *Ageratum*</note>. According to the observations of **Mr. Tournefort**, it has a radiate flower and therefore seems it should be referred to **Sneezewort** <note>original: *Ptarmica*</note>. For my part, I have not yet been able to discern that kind of crown of small petals surrounding the central disk; nor have others whom I consulted on the matter. The plant they call "white-flowered Ageratum" does indeed possess a flower surrounded by such a crown of petals; consequently, it is rightly referred to **Sneezewort**.

12. **Sea Cudweed** <note>original: *Gnaphalium maritimum*</note>. **Mr. Breyn** <note>Jacob Breyne (1637–1697), a Polish botanist.</note> observed long ago that the female plant does not have a winged <term>pappus</term> <note>the tuft of hairs on a seed that allows it to float on the wind</note>. **Mr. Tournefort** observed that the flowers and seeds are separated from each other by tiny leaves bent into a channel, and the fruit is composed of two parts: a curved grain and a sort of pointed little cap covering its head. It is usually referred to the **Cudweeds** <note>original: *Gnaphalium*</note> because of its woolly <note>tomentose</note> leaves.

## Corymb-bearing herbs <note>Plants that produce flower clusters where the outer stalks are longer than the inner ones, creating a flat-topped appearance, such as daisies or tansy.</note> with naked flowers <note>Flowers that lack ray-florets or "petals" around the edge, appearing as button-like centers.</note> are classified by their stems and branches.

*   *Indeterminate* <note>In botany, this means the main stem continues to grow rather than ending in a flower.</note>, where the flowers do not terminate the growth, but emerge from the leaf axils <note>the angle between the leaf and the stem</note> along the stems and branches; with flowers:
    *   *Nodding downward*; with leaves:
        *   *More greyish-white*, with a notable bitterness; **WORMWOOD** <note>original: *Absinthium*</note>.
        *   *Less grey and bitter*; **SOUTHERNWOOD** <note>original: *Abrotanum*; often called Male Southernwood.</note>.
    *   *More upright*; **MUGWORT** <note>original: *Artemisia*</note>.
*   *Determinate* <note>Growth that ends with a flower head at the tip of the stem.</note>, which the flowers terminate; and these have flowers that are either:
    *   *Scattered*, running out individually on long stalks on each small branch, and somewhat large; **LAVENDER COTTON** <note>original: *Abrotanum femina*; literally "Female Southernwood."</note>.
    *   *Gathered into umbels <note>umbrella-shaped clusters</note> at the tops of the stems*; with leaves:
        *   *Entire* <note>having a smooth, undivided edge</note>;
            *   *Downy and greyish-white*; **SEA COTTONWEED** <note>original: *Gnaphalium maritimum*</note>.
            *   *Smoother and greener*, saw-toothed around the edges; **COSTMARY** <note>original: *Balsamita*</note>.
        *   *Cut into segments arranged in opposite pairs or coupled*; **TANSY** <note>original: *Tanacetum*</note>.

<header>PLANT METHODOLOGY</header>

# NINTH GENUS,

->*or*<-

## The Fourth Genus of herbs with a composite flower,

->*Whose flowers are composed of tubular florets mostly divided into long segments, otherwise known as*<-

### THE HEADED PLANTS.

They are called "Headed" <note>original: *Capitatæ*</note> because their calyxes <term>the cup-like base of the flower</term> containing the seeds swell out into a scaly belly resembling a head, especially after the flower has fallen away.

1. *Thistle* <note>original: *Carduus*</note>. We call all herbs of this genus "thistles" if they are provided with prickly leaves, even if their flower heads are not prickly at all.

2. I call the *Artichoke* <note>original: *Cinara*</note> a type of thistle with a very large, scaly head resembling a pine cone, where the bases of the scales and the bottom of the flower are fleshy and edible.

*Tournefort* <note>Joseph Pitton de Tournefort (1656–1708), a French botanist and contemporary of the author.</note> identifies the *Thistle* by its prickly head, whether the leaves are prickly or smooth; for this reason, he classifies all *Knapweeds* <note>original: *Jaceas*</note> with prickly heads as Thistles. He identifies *Cirsium* <note>Plume-thistles</note> by leaves armed with short prickles, and *Knapweed* as having neither a prickly head nor prickly leaves.

We define the *Thistle* as a headed plant with feathery seeds <term>pappose; seeds with hair-like tufts for wind dispersal</term>, where at least the leaves—and sometimes also the head and stems—are armed with stiffer prickles:

3. *Cirsium* <note>Plume-thistle</note>, a headed plant with leaves surrounded by softer and shorter prickles:

4. *Knapweed* <note>original: *Jacea*</note>, a headed herb with leaves lacking spines. Add to this that the leaf margins are even—that is, they are neither notched <term>crenate</term> nor toothed <term>dentate</term>.

5. *Great Centaury* <note>original: *Centaurium majus*</note>, a plant with non-prickly leaves, saw-toothed <term>serrated</term> margins, and a larger flower.

6. We distinguish *Saw-wort* <note>original: *Serratula*</note> and the *Winged Plumeless Thistle* <note>original: *Crupina Belgarum*</note> from *Great Centaury* by the smallness of all their parts, but especially their flowers.

And this division certainly seems more suited both to the nature of things and to the accepted meaning of the names than that of Mr. Tournefort, who distinguishes these genera by the prickliness of the flower head. For thistles with prickly heads and those without agree in their overall appearance and habit; likewise, Knapweeds with prickly heads and those lacking spines also agree with one another; whereas the latter group differs from the former in their entire growth habit and constitution.

By the common acceptance and use of the word, not only among the common people but among all botanists, a *Thistle* is a plant where at least the leaves, if

<meta>This sentence continues on the next page, likely concluding "...if not the heads, are prickly."</meta>

The author also argues for his classification system over that of his contemporary, Tournefort, prioritizing the plant's overall growth habit over single features like prickly flower heads.</summary>

# AMENDED AND ENLARGED.

...it does not signify a plant provided with both a prickly stem and a prickly head. What of the fact that *Mr. Magnol* <note>Pierre Magnol (1638–1715), a French botanist after whom the Magnolia is named.</note> observed a Knapweed <note>original: *Jaceam*</note> with purple heads that was not prickly, which differed from the purple thin-leaved Knapweed with prickly heads described by *Jean Bauhin* <note>original: *J. B.*; a Swiss botanist (1541–1613).</note> only in the fact that it had no spines (*Garden of Montpellier, page 103*)? I see no suitable reason, therefore, why *Mr. Tournefort* <note>Joseph Pitton de Tournefort (1656–1708), a major figure in botanical history who disagreed with the author on classification methods.</note> should innovate without necessity and against the consensus of all botanists by changing the meanings of words.

I consider the Star-thistle <note>original: *Carduum stellatum*</note> or Calcitrap <note>original: *Calcitrapam*</note> to be a species of Knapweed with a prickly head, characterized by scales ending in rigid, straight spines pointing forward.

I do not insist on that conjecture regarding the Centaury with Artichoke-leaves <note>original: *Centaurio Cinaræ folio*</note> described by *Cornut* <note>Jacques-Philippe Cornut (1606–1651), a French physician and botanist.</note>—namely, that all garden varieties of Artichokes arose from that seed being sown and cultivated in gardens. Rather, after second thoughts, I approve and embrace the opinion of *Mr. Plukenet* <note>Leonard Plukenet (1642–1706), a British botanist.</note>: that those garden varieties owe their origin to the wild prickly Artichoke cultivated and domesticated in gardens, in the same way that the cultivated Apple <note>original: *Malus sativa*</note> comes from the wild one.

7. The markers of the *Cornflower* <note>original: *Cyani*</note> are: the marginal florets of the flowers are larger and longer than the inner ones, less deeply divided, and with the mouth expanded wide.

The plant commonly called the Greater Cornflower, or Broad-leaved Mountain Cornflower, or the Cornflower-like Mullein <note>original: *Verbasculum Cyanoides*</note> by *Caspar Bauhin* <note>original: *C. B.*; brother of Jean Bauhin and author of the influential *Pinax*.</note>, is not a true and genuine species of Cornflower according to the characteristic marker just provided, but is a species of Knapweed <note>original: *Jaceæ*</note>; for although the marginal florets are larger and longer than the rest, they are nonetheless more deeply divided into long and narrow segments.

In the Greater Black Knapweed, and even in the Common Black Knapweed, the marginal florets are sometimes larger and longer than the others.

8. *Greater Burdock* <note>original: *Lappa major*</note> or *Bardana* is distinguished from the rest by its very large leaves and the scales of its flower heads ending in hooked points.

9. *Tournefort* makes the characteristic marker of *Cnicus* <note>a genus including the Blessed Thistle</note> the flower heads being fortified by a circle of leaves; he refers the *Blessed Thistle* <note>original: *Carduum benedictum*</note>, the *Yellow Atractylis*, *Tragus's Meadow Thistle*, and *Bauhin's Small Thistle* to this group. Nor do we reject this marker, and we ourselves made it the characteristic for the Blessed Thistle in the *Table* of this genus in the *History, page 298*; therefore, we admit the genus of *Cnicus*. However, why this marker should be sufficient to establish a genus in one class but not in another—for example, in the Hawkweed <note>original: *Hieracio*</note> with heads like Blessed Thistle—I do not see the reason, and I ask this of *Mr. Tournefort*.

10. For *Carthamus* <note>Safflower</note>, he makes the marker the seed being destitute of down <term>pappus; the tuft of hairs or feathers that allows seeds to fly</term>, which I also gladly admit: though one might rightly ask why he makes it a distinct genus because the seeds lack down, yet does not do the same for the Thistle with Wallflower-leaves <note>original: *Carduo Leucoii folio*</note>, which, according to our observation, produces seeds of that very kind.

# METHOD OF PLANTS

->Herbs with flowers composed of tubular florets, or the Headed plants<-
->are defined by their heads as follows:<-

*   The largest heads, scaly, resembling pine cones <note>original: "Pini conorum æmulis"</note>; the base of the scales and the floor of the flower are fleshy and edible; the leaves are sometimes spiny, sometimes smooth; **ARTICHOKE** <note>original: *CINARA*</note>, *Scolymus*.
*   With smaller heads; the leaves are:
    *   Spiny; with prickles that are:
        *   Frequent and quite rigid; **THISTLE** <note>original: *CARDUUS*</note>.
        *   Gentler and softer; with the flower heads:
            *   Surrounded by a circle of leaves; **BLESSED THISTLE** <note>original: *CNICUS*</note>, under which name we include—along with Mr. Tournefort—the *Blessed Thistle*, the yellow *Distaff-thistle*, the *Meadow Thistle* of Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock (1498–1554), a German botanist known as Tragus.</note>, and the *Small Thistle* of Jean Bauhin <note>original: *J. B.*</note>.
            *   Not surrounded by any such circle; with seeds that are:
                *   Lacking a pappus <term>pappus: the tuft of hairs or bristles on a seed (like a dandelion "clock") that aids in wind dispersal</term> and smooth; **SAFFLOWER** <note>original: *CARTHAMUS*</note>.
                *   Crowned with a pappus; **PLUMED THISTLE** <note>original: *CIRSIUM*</note>.
    *   Lacking spines;
        *   Serrated <note>toothed like a saw</note> along the margins, with smooth flower heads:
            *   The Greater; **GREAT CENTAURY** <note>original: *CENTAURIUM MAJUS*</note>.
            *   The Lesser;
                *   With leaves divided into few and large jagged segments; **SAW-WORT** <note>original: *SERRATULA*</note>.
                *   Or divided into thin segments; **CRUPINA** <note>original: *CRUPINA Belgarum*</note>.
        *   Even (not toothed) along the margins; with flower heads that are:
            *   Burdock-like, with scales ending in hooked points, and very large leaves; **GREAT BURDOCK** <note>original: *LAPPA MAJOR*</note>.
            *   Spiny; with prickles that are:
                *   Straight; **STAR-THISTLE** <note>original: *CALCITRAPA*</note>, or *Prickly Knapweed*.
                *   Reflexed <note>bent backward or downward</note>; **MURICATE KNAPWEED** <note>original: *JACEA MURICATA*</note>.
            *   Smooth; with the outer florets of the head:
                *   Less deeply cut, with the mouth of the flower spreading wide; **CORNFLOWER** <note>original: *CYANUS*</note>.
                *   Deeply cut into long and narrow segments; **KNAPWEED** <note>original: *JACEA*</note>.

Note: To unburden the genus of Thistles <note>original: *Cardui*</note>, which is overwhelmed by an excessive multitude of species, two distinct genera of spiny herbs can be established for the woolly and hoary thistles, and those marked with white lines and spots, under the names **MILK THISTLE** <note>original: *Sylibi*</note> and **COTTON THISTLE** <note>original: *Acanthii*</note>.

<meta>This page continues the systematic classification of plants with composite or grouped flower heads, moving from the standard "Headed" plants (like Thistles) discussed on the previous page to "Anomalous" types that share characteristics with Corymb-bearing plants (like Daisies) but possess unique structural differences.</meta>

<header>CORRECTED AND AUGMENTED.</header>

## Anomalous herbs with composite flowers,

### RELATED TO THE CORYMB-BEARING PLANTS.

1. **Scabious** <note>original: *Scabioſa*</note>, which differs from the corymb-bearing plants <term>corymbiferous: plants where flowers form a flat-topped cluster, often used then for the Aster family</term> in this: it possesses florets that are all irregular, each also gifted with its own individual calyx <note>original: *calicibus privatis*</note> or one peculiar to itself. Furthermore, the marginal florets, in most species, are larger and longer than those in the interior.

2. *Teasel* <note>original: *Dipſacus*</note>, the total flower of which does not have a "calyx" properly speaking, but rather leaves mimicking a perianth <term>perianth: the outer envelope of a flower</term> surrounding the base of the head; moreover, small oblong leaves bent into a hollow socket embrace each individual floret, arranged like scales.

3. *Globe Thistle* <note>original: *Carduus ſphærocephalus* or *Echinopus*</note> differs from herbs with composite flowers properly so-called in that the total flower—if one may so call the spherical head by which it is easily distinguished from any other plant at first sight—does not have a perianth. The individual florets are divided at the top into four narrow segments <note>original: *lacinias*</note> and are supported by a scaly calyx.

4. *Globe-daisy* <note>original: *Globularia*</note>. The florets gathered into a small globe gave this plant its name; each of these is supported by an individual calyx containing a single seed remaining after the flower has fallen. As described by Tournefort <note>Joseph Pitton de Tournefort (1656–1708), a French botanist</note>, the florets are perforated at the bottom, expanded at the top, and divided into two lips, as it were; the upper lip is missing, and the lower is split into three segments.

This plant is more closely related to the *Whorled* plants <note>original: *Verticillatis*; the Mint family</note> than the *Corymb-bearers*; for it produces a single-petaled, lipped flower held in a calyx, containing a single seed remaining after the flower has fallen.

5. *Sea Holly* <note>original: *Eryngium*</note>, the marks of which are the leaves—at least the upper ones on the stalks—and the prickly heads; the flowers at the tops of the stalks and branches are crowded into heads, beneath which sit radiating leaves. Tournefort attributes flowers that are generally five-petaled to this genus, and a fruit composed of two grains joined before maturity, in some species terminated by two or three leaves; for this reason, he refers it to the genus of *Umbellifers* <note>original: *Umbelliferarum*; the Carrot or Parsley family</note>. Truly, however, its agreement with the *Teasel* in the form of its heads does not allow them to be separated from one another.

<header>METHOD OF PLANTS</header>

# THE TENTH GENUS
->or Herbs<-

# WITH A PERFECT SIMPLE FLOWER AND A SOLITARY NAKED SEED
->FOR EACH INDIVIDUAL FLOWER.<-

This genus belongs to that group whose species have almost no natural affinity with one another, nor do they agree in any matter other than those traits which we have used for the generic characteristics: namely, having a perfect <term>perfect flower: a flower containing both male (stamens) and female (pistil) reproductive parts</term> simple flower, and naked seeds that are solitary for each individual flower.

1. **Valerian** <note>original: *Valeriana*</note>, the characteristics of which are: leaves on the stems in opposite pairs; monopetalous <term>monopetalous: a flower where all petals are fused into a single tube or shape</term> tubular flowers, divided into five parts at the edges, clustered into bundles at the tops of the stems and branches; and seeds winged with an emerging pappus <term>pappus: a downy or feathery appendage on a seed, like that of a dandelion, which aids in wind dispersal</term> upon which the flower sits.

2. **Cornsalad** <note>original: *Valerianella*</note>, which differs from Valerian by having seeds that lack a pappus; it also differs from almost all other plants by its dichotomous <term>dichotomous: a branching structure where the main stem divides repeatedly into two equal parts</term> stems.

The plants to which this name is assigned do not agree in either flower or fruit (please consult *Mr. Tournefort’s Elements of Botany, page 108, Plate 52*); hence, if the defining traits of genera are to be taken from the flower and fruit, they will not agree in genus, but ought to be referred to different genera. Therefore, the generic trait (if indeed they belong to the same genus) seems most correctly taken from nothing other than the forking of the stem and branches.

But if in **Lamb’s Lettuce** <note>original: *Lactuca agnina*</note> two seeds should follow each individual floret (as *Mr. Rivinus* asserts), a fact which I have not yet been able to distinguish for myself, it could be removed from this section and sent to the Umbelliferous genus <term>umbelliferous: plants like carrots or parsley that bear flowers in umbrella-like clusters</term>.

3. **Leadwort** <note>original: *Dentellaria*</note>. According to *Mr. Hermann*, the characteristics of this plant are oblong, hairy fruit armed with bristles; flowers expanded from an oblong tube into five segments and gathered into spikes; and alternate leaves. *Mr. Tournefort* attributes a flower commonly divided into six parts to Leadwort. However, I do not see the reason why he places this plant under Class II, Section 4—a category defined by the style being composed of four embryos which turn into as many seeds enclosed in the calyx <term>calyx: the outer protective layer of a flower, often green and leaf-like</term>—since in this plant only a single seed follows or sits beneath each flower.

4. **Sea Lavender** <note>original: *Limonium*</note>. We have established its characteristics as its maritime habitat, naked and branched stems, flowers arranged along the stems, and seeds in individual...

...one per calyx <term>calyx: the outer protective part of a flower that holds the petals</term>. *Tournefort* <note>original: *Tournefortius*</note> attributes to this mostly five-petaled flowers, though in some species they are single-petaled <term>monopetalous: a flower where all petals are fused into a single tube or shape</term> and divided into five parts, with a funnel-shaped calyx.

Hermannus*</note>: oblong-round seeds, furrowed, five-sided, and navel-like <term>umbilicata: having a central depression or 'belly button'</term>, containing a floury kernel; flowers arranged in a five-sided circle emerging from a tube; and leaves and branches that grow in joined pairs.

**Jalap** <note>original: *Jalapium*</note>: this is the root of the **Marvel of Peru**, as noted by *Mr. Plumier* <note>original: *D. Plumier*</note> and *Munting*.

6. **Bastard Toadflax** <note>original: *Linaria adulterina*</note>, noted for leaves like those of Toadflax and five-petaled flowers sitting atop the fruit.

7. **Tragus's Sparrow-wort** <note>original: *Passerina Tragi*</note>. The fruit grows in the axils <term>axils: the "armpit" or angle between a leaf and the stem</term> of the small leaves in pairs or threes together, upon which sit four-petaled yellow flowers.

8. **Agrimony** <note>original: *Agrimonia*</note> or **Grecian Eupatorium** <note>original: *Eupatorium Græcorum*</note> is distinguished from others of this genus by its five-leaved flowers growing on top of the fruit, its seeds (or, if you prefer, burr-like seed vessels) which often contain two seeds or rather kernels, and its lobed or feathered <term>pinnate: leaves arranged like a feather on either side of a stem</term> leaves.

For a long time, I was doubtful whether **Agrimony** properly belonged to this genus, because its burrs often contain two seeds. But when I saw that these seeds—or more correctly, kernels—were not separated by two distinct cells, but lay hidden in the same cavity, and that this cavity often contains only a single kernel, I decided this plant should no more be considered two-seeded than the **Hazelnut**, which we sometimes find bearing two kernels by some playful trick of luxuriant nature.

9. **Salad Burnet** <note>original: *Pimpinella sanguisorba*</note>, the characteristics of which we identified as feathered leaves, thick spikes composed of densely packed florets and seeds, and four-sided seeds upon which four-petaled florets sit.

However, *Mr. Tournefort* <note>original: *D. Tournefortius*</note> reproached me for saying the flower has four petals <note>original: *quadrifolium*</note>, since it is a single unit <note>original: *integer*</note>, and for taking the capsule for a seed.

To the first point, I reply: I considered single-petaled flowers—whose petals are divided almost to the base into four segments mimicking four leaves—as four-petaled, as botanists commonly do.

To the second, I say: because the fruit falls off whole and does not open by itself, I considered it a "naked" seed. Examining it later with curiosity, I often found it pregnant with two seeds, yet they were not hidden in distinct cells, so they should be considered kernels rather than separate seeds. But see more on this above among the **Petal-less** <note>original: *Apetalas*</note> plants.

<header>AMENDED AND ENLARGED.</header>

# THE ELEVENTH GENUS
## or Herbs
### UMBELLIFEROUS <term>Umbelliferous: plants that produce flowers in an "umbel," a cluster where all flower stalks radiate from a single point like the ribs of an umbrella; now known as the Apiaceae or Carrot family</term>

->Those which are Gymnodispermous <term>gymnodispermous: from the Greek, meaning "producing two naked seeds"</term>, or bearing two naked seeds after each individual flower.<-

Umbelliferous herbs are so named because most of them bear flowers arranged in the shape of an Umbel <note>original: *Umbella*</note>, like the parasols by which women shield the rays of the Sun from their faces. In Umbelliferous plants, the top of the stem and the topmost branches are divided into several rays arising from the same point, and then each individual ray is divided into several smaller stalks <note>original: *pediculos*</note>, which support a secondary Umbel. Together, however (both the rays and the smaller stalks), they are fitted into the shape of an inverted cone.

Master Tournefort <note>Joseph Pitton de Tournefort (1656–1708), an influential French botanist</note> counts Umbelliferous herbs among those gifted with a rose-like <term>rosaceous: having petals arranged in a circle like a wild rose</term> flower; yet he attributes to a large part of them a lily-like flower ("Fleurdelisée" <note>French: lily-flowered</note>, that is, with petals arranged in the form of a *Fleur de Lis of France*), which he himself distinguishes from the rose-like, while ascribing "Fleur en Rose" (that is, rose-like) to the rest in his *Elements of Botany* <note>original: *Elem. Bot.*</note>.

->I.<-

->*Umbelliferous plants with a compressed leaf-like seed, or one encircled by a leaf-like wing.*<-

1. *Sphondilium* [**Hogweed**], the characteristics of which are broad leaves, white flowers with two-cleft <term>bifid: divided into two parts by a deep notch</term> and seemingly horned petals (the outer ones being much larger than the others), seeds that are two-cleft at the top with a furrowed back, and on the inner surface—where the two seeds touch each other—marked by two black radiating lines.
2. *Pastinaca latifolia* [**Broad-leaved Parsnip**], the characteristics of which are pinnate leaves <term>pinnate: a leaf shape where leaflets are arranged on either side of a central stem, like a feather</term>, or as Master Tournefort prefers, composed of large enough "wings" supported by a thick rib; yellow flowers, similar in form to rose-like ones; thick, fleshy, edible roots.
3. *Panax Heracleum* [**Hercules’ All-heal**] differs from the Broad-leaved Parsnip by its more branched leaves and a sap-bearing root.
4. *Tordylium* [**Hartwort**], the characteristics of which are leaf-like seeds, encircled by a raised or sometimes granulated margin or border, and flower petals that are two-cleft nearly to the base, with the outer petals larger than the inner ones.
5. *Anethum* [**Dill**], the characteristics of which are leaves [divided] into very thin segments of **Fennel**...

6. **Peucedanum** <term>Peucedanum: commonly known as Hog's Fennel</term>, whose characteristics are leaves finely dissected like Fennel (whence it is commonly called "Hog's Fennel"), though with segments wider than those of Dill, divided and subdivided into three parts; the petals of the flowers are equal.

->*Umbelliferous plants provided with a seed having many leaf-like wings*<-

**Laserpitium** <term>Laserpitium: Laserwort, historically associated with the prized ancient medicinal resin "silphium"</term>, whose characteristics are four leaf-like wings running lengthwise on each individual seed; in certain species, these are curled or wavy. These wings are membranous; while the two seeds are still green and joined together, only six wings are visible, as those two at the base of each seed are closely joined to one another. Our Morison <note>Robert Morison (1620–1683), a Scottish botanist and contemporary of the author</note> not ineptly compares these seeds to the wheel of a watermill floating in a river.

->*or elliptical.*<-

**Cachrys** or *Libanotis cachryophora*; whose characteristics are finely dissected leaves and swollen seeds, the size and shape of a small Nutmeg, with a spongy substance surrounding the kernel (which is usually similar to a grain of Barley, according to Master Tournefort).

<header>CORRECTED AND ENLARGED.</header>

### IV.

### Umbellifers with a simple or twin spherical fruit.

**Coriander** <term>Coriandrum: Coriander</term>. In this genus, the two seeds grow together into a perfectly spherical shape in some species; in others, each individual seed assumes a globose shape, so that two small spheres follow each individual flower. The lower leaves are broad, while the upper ones are finely divided; the scent is foul and offensive, like that of bedbugs <note>original: *odor teter & odiosus cimicum*. The name Coriander actually derives from the Greek *koris*, meaning "bedbug," due to the smell of the unripe fruit and foliage.</note>.

### V.

### Umbellifers with a beaked seed.

**Scandix** or **Venus's Comb** <term>Pecten Veneris: a plant named for its long, comb-like seed pods</term>, the distinguishing marks of which are the beaked seeds—specifically, the upper end is drawn out into a sharp point, resembling the "beaks" of the Musky Crane's-bill <note>original: *Geranii moschati*</note>. The petals of the flowers are undivided and have a somewhat rounded tip, with the outermost petal being longer than the others.

### VI.

### Umbellifers with a long, narrow seed somewhat resembling a bird’s beak.

->1. Smooth-seeded.<-

**Chervil** <term>Chærophyllum: a genus of fragrant herbs</term>, of which there are two kinds: 1. **Garden Chervil**, with an annual root, more finely dissected leaves, and bifid <note>split into two parts</note> petals, or petals notched in the middle. 2. **Wild Chervil**, called "Wild Myrrhis with smooth seeds" by Caspar Bauhin <note>original: *C. B.* refers to Caspar Bauhin’s botanical catalog</note>; this plant has leaves divided into larger segments—though still narrow and sharp for their size—a perennial root, and irregular flowers where the outermost petal is larger and longer than the rest.

->2. Rough-seeded, but not striated,<-
->as far as we have been able to discern.<-

**Knotted Cretan Wild Myrrhis**, with rough seeds. The stems of this plant swell into prominent nodes <note>bumps or joints</note> below the points where the leaves emerge.

->3. Striated-seeded.<-

**Myrrhis with striated seeds**, also known as "Wild Chervil" by Caspar Bauhin. The characteristics of this plant are solid stems (or stems filled with pith) that swell into prominent nodes below the joints; the small flowers are white with a faint purple tint, having equal, bifid petals; the seeds turn a lemon-yellow color when mature. <header>THE METHOD OF PLANTS</header>

**Mr. Tournefort** <note>Joseph Pitton de Tournefort (1656–1708), a French botanist whose system of classification based on flower shape was highly influential before Linnaeus.</note> describes the **Bulbous Chervil** <term>Cicutaria bulbosa: now known as Chaerophyllum bulbosum</term>, which Caspar Bauhin <note>original: *C. B.*</note> also notes. Its stalk swells into very large nodes just below the joints; it is the tallest of all the Umbellifers <note>Plants with umbrella-like flower clusters.</note> I have observed, reaching nearly twice the height of a man in richer soil. Yet the root is a small bulb, possessing few fibers and not set deep in the earth.

He also brings the white and red **Marsh Chervil** <note>original: *Cicutariam palustrem albam & rubram*</note> into this same genus.

->VII.<-

### Umbellifers with long, large, furrowed seeds.

**Garden Myrrh** <term>Myrrhis sativa: commonly called Sweet Cicely</term>. The whole leaves resemble those of a fern, which is why our common folk call it "Sweet Fern," that is, the Scented Fern <note>original: *Filix odorata*</note>.

->VIII.<-

### Umbellifers with striated seeds of medium length and thickness.

1. **Spignel** <term>Meum: also known as Baldmoney</term>. It is distinguished from other Umbellifers by its extremely fine leaves and its rather large, oblong, striated <note>marked with fine parallel grooves</note> seed.

2. **Fennel** <term>Foeniculum</term>. It is distinguished from the rest of the Umbellifers of this genus by its leaves, which are divided into hair-like segments; its striated, oblong seeds; its small, pale yellow flowers; and its blunt petals that end in a nearly straight line rather than being split in two. It differs from Spignel by having longer leaf segments. <gloss>See Page 120, Line 17</gloss>

4. **Common Lovage** <term>Levisticum vulgare</term>. It has very large leaves like those of Celery <note>original: *Apii*</note>, a somewhat long seed, a root that lives for many years, and a strong scent. Mr. Tournefort assigns the Common Lovage to the **Angelica** genus, to which he attributes the characteristic of large leaves attached to a branched stalk that ends in a single leaf. **Broad-leaved Herb-Frankincense** <term>Libanotis latifolia</term>, which has a leaf like a Columbine <note>original: *Aquilegiae folio*</note>, differs from the previous plant by these leaves.

5. **Cumin** <term>Cuminum</term>. It is distinguished from Spignel by its annual root, its leaves being divided into less frequent and less delicate segments, and its smaller, narrower, curved seed.

->IX.<-

### Umbellifers with narrower, smaller, and very small striated seeds.

->1. With a tuberous root.<-

1. **Earthnut** <term>Bulbocastanum: also known as the Pignut</term>. Its identifying marks are a tuberous root consisting of a single tuber, and a longish seed which is smooth in some species and striated in others.

2. **Water Dropwort** <note>original: *Oenana*, likely a variant of *Oenanthe*</note>

2. **Water Dropwort** <term>Oenanthe</term>, the characteristics of which include tuberous roots composed of many small glands. Add to this its habitat in marshes. Mr. Tournefort <note>Joseph Pitton de Tournefort (1656–1708), a French botanist whose system of classification based on flower shape was highly influential before Linnaeus.</note> rejects these traits and substitutes them with flowers composed of unequal, two-cleft <note>original: *bifidis*</note> petals, and somewhat long, rounded seeds that are grooved on the back and tipped at the top with certain points, the middle of which is the largest and sharper than the rest. While these [new traits] should be accepted, the former [roots] should not be rejected.

3. **Skirret** <term>Sisarum; original text: Sifari</term>, its traits are the leaves and scent of the Broad-leaved Parsnip, narrow striated seeds, and several roots like those of a small turnip <note>original: *Napi*</note> hanging as if from the same neck.

->2. *With a fibrous or stalk-like root.*<-

1. **Water Parsnip** <term>Sium or Pastinaca aquatica</term>. Its traits are the leaves and scent of the cultivated Broad-leaved Parsnip; its roots are harder and more woody than that variety, and the petals of the flowers are equal, two-cleft, and white. Here should be referred the **German Amomum** <term>Amomum Germanicum: also known as Bastard Stone Parsley</term> and the **Selinum with Sium-like leaves**.

2. **Burnet Saxifrage** <term>Pimpinella saxifraga</term>, having the leaves of Salad Burnet <note>original: *Pimpinellæ sanguisorbæ*</note> and a pungent, warming root. Mr. Tournefort attributes unequal and two-cleft flower petals to this genus. But in our observations, at least in the smaller species, there is no significant difference in the size of the petals, nor do the petals appear two-cleft except very slightly.

3. **Caraway** <term>Carum</term> is recognized by its oblong, narrow, striated seeds and its pinnate leaves <note>Leaves arranged like a feather</note>, with the leaflets cut into many segments and attached without stalks <note>original: *fine pediculis*; likely a printer's error for *sine*, meaning "without".</note>.

### X.

->*Umbellifers with shorter, broader, and larger striated seeds.*<-

1. **Angelica**, whose traits are very broad leaves and large, thick, striated seeds with a more swollen back. The flowers of **Garden Angelica** <note>original: *Angelicæ Sativæ*</note> are arranged in a spherical shape or "corymb"; this arrangement is so unique that it rightly constitutes a distinct genus. Mr. Tournefort makes Garden or Officinal Angelica a species of **Masterwort** <term>Imperatoria</term> and thus confuses the names.

2. **Masterwort** <term>Imperatoria</term> differs from Angelica by having leaves that are less branched, divided and subdivided into three parts, white flowers arranged in umbels, and thick, slanted, perennial roots.

3. **Alexanders** <term>Smyrnium</term>, the traits of which are a large, swollen, and somewhat round seed, which turns black upon ripening.

4. **Mountain Laserwort** <term>Siler montanum</term>. Its traits are the leaves of **Seseli** <note>Meadow Saxifrage or Moon-carrot</note>, with the topmost segments divided into three parts, and a rather large seed with a leafy fringe.

5. **Hemlock** <term>Cicuta</term>, its traits are leaves divided many times over into minute particles,

6. **Fine-leaved Water Dropwort** <term>Phellandryum</term> or Marsh Hemlock. Its traits: a very thick stem, very large leaves divided into many tiny particles much like Hemlock <term>Cicuta</term>, and flower petals that are equal and two-cleft.

7. **Meadow Saxifrage** <term>Seseli pratense</term>. Its traits: leaf segments are narrow and sharp, the flowers are a pale yellow with somewhat round petals, and the seeds are short, slightly swollen, and turn reddish when mature.

8. **Anise** <term>Anisum</term>. It differs from others in that the lowest leaves on the stem are whole and broad, while the upper ones are finely divided; the seeds are somewhat round with a very pleasant smell and taste; and it is a small, annual plant.

### XI.

->*Umbellifers with very small, shorter, and more swollen striated seeds.*<-
->*very small.*<-

1. **Bishop's Weed** <term>Ammi</term>. Its traits: leaves divided into long, narrow ribbons <note>original: *lacinias*</note> with notched <note>original: *crenata*</note> edges, flower petals that are two-cleft and unequal, and very tiny seeds. Matthioli’s <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–1577), an Italian physician and botanist who published a famous commentary on Dioscorides.</note> fourth "Samphire" <term>Crithmum</term>—or Meadow Eryngium with saw-like leaves—is not inaccurately referred here to Bishop's Weed.

2. **Celery or Parsley** <term>Apium</term>. Its traits: a very small, yellowish flower; triangular leaves with fewer, broader, and more blunt segments; and seeds that are striated <note>meaning marked with parallel grooves or ridges.</note>, short, and very tiny. It differs from Bishop's Weed <term>Ammi</term> by having flower petals that are whole and not at all two-cleft.

5. <note>Note: The numbering in the original text skips from 2 to 5.</note> **Picktooth** <term>Gingidium</term> or **Toothpick-plant** <term>Visnaga</term>. Its traits: the umbel <note>the umbrella-like flower cluster characteristic of this family.</note> closes up after the flowers have fallen, and its rays are very long and rigid; the seeds are very tiny, like those of Celery <term>Apium</term>. <note>The rigid rays of this plant were historically used as toothpicks, giving it its common name.</note>

### XII.

->*Umbellifers with hairy or shaggy seeds.*<-

1. **Candy Carrot** <term>Daucus Creticus</term> with hairy seeds. Its traits: leaves are very finely divided, and the seed is long, grayish-white, shaggy <note>original: *villosum*</note>, and pungent.

2. **Macedonian Parsley** <term>Apium or Petroselinum Macedonicum</term>. Its leaves are similar to garden parsley; the seed is small, oblong, and hairy.

3. **White Mountain Parsley** <term>Apium petræum</term> or *Apium montanum album* of Jean Bauhin <note>Jean Bauhin (1541–1613), a Swiss botanist and physician whose works helped standardize botanical descriptions.</note>. Its traits: leaves are divided into opposite wings, mimicking the whole leaves of the Lesser Burnet Saxifrage; the stem is notably grooved <note>original: *canaliculatus*</note>; the seeds are striated, hairy, and reddish at the top.

4. **Fine-leaved Parsnip or Carrot** <term>Pastinaca tenuifolia</term> or **Carrot** <term>Carota</term>. It differs from other Umbellifers by its finely divided leaves, shaggy seeds, and umbels that close after the flowers fall—forming a shape like a bird's nest—and by its fleshy root.

The outer petals are longer and larger than the inner ones, and sometimes appear to have an appendage at the side. Surrounding the base of the rays for both the primary and secondary umbels <note>An umbel is a flower cluster where the stalks spread from a common center like umbrella ribs; the "primary" is the main cluster and the "secondary" is the smaller cluster on each stalk.</note> are somewhat broad leaves, divided into several very long, hair-like segments.

### XIII.

->*Umbellifers with prickly or thorny seeds.*<-

<margin>+</margin>
1. **Bur Parsley** <term>Caucalis</term> is abundantly distinguished from other umbellifers by its prickly, thorny, or rough seeds, so that there is no need to seek out other identifying marks.

I include **Wild Chervil** <term>Myrrhin sylvestrem</term> with rough seeds here. It has soft leaves, divided almost like **Hemlock** <term>Cicuta</term> but paler; the stem is like Hemlock, and the umbels sit at the leaf axils <note>original: *alas*; literally "wings," referring to the junction where the leaf meets the stem.</note> in the manner of **Smallage** <term>Paludapium</term>. The flowers are white; the seeds are oblong, rounded, and rough, with an oblong tip. **Tournefort** <note>Joseph Pitton de Tournefort (1656–1708), a French botanist whose system of classification was widely used before Linnaeus.</note> refers this plant to the **Chervil** genus <term>Chaerophyllum</term>.

2. **Sea Parsnip** <term>Pastinaca marina</term>, called **Secacul** by some and **Spiny Samphire** <term>Crithmum spinosum</term> by Jean Bauhin <note>J. B. refers to Jean Bauhin (1541–1612), a Swiss botanist.</note>. It differs from other umbellifers not only in its seeds but also in its spiny leaves. **Mr. Tournefort**, in his *Institutes*, calls this plant **Prickly-Parsnip** <term>Echinophora</term>, and describes the flower and fruit thus: It has a rose-like flower growing in an umbel-shaped head, sitting on a common calyx <note>the green outer part of a flower that holds the petals</note>, which then turns into a fruit with a single capsule containing an oblong seed.

### XIV. & XV.

->*Umbellifers with simple or non-branching leaves.*<-

These either have whole leaves or cut (lobed) leaves.
The **Whole-leaved** plants <term>Integrifolia</term> are either those where the stem passes through the leaf, called **Perfoliate** <term>Perfoliata</term>; or those where the leaves merely attach to the stem without surrounding it. These latter are either shrubby, bearing a true umbel at the summit, such as the **Ethiopian Shrubby Hartwort** <term>Seseli Æthiopicum frutex</term>; or herbaceous, producing less typical umbels, such as **Hare's Ear** <term>Auricula leporis</term> or <term>Bupleurum</term>.

Those with cut leaves can be divided by their seeds into those that produce smooth seeds, called **Masterworts** <term>Astrantiæ</term>, and those that bear rough or bur-like seeds, such as **Sanicle** <term>Sanicula</term>. The tiny flowers of Sanicle have five petals, with the petals folded back on themselves and split into two <note>original: *bifidis*</note> at the point where they fold, as Tournefort observed.

The same author [Tournefort] joins **Sea Holly** <term>Eryngium</term> to Sanicle because its flower has five petals and produces two seeds joined together for each flower, which in some species end in two or three small leaves. I leave these points for further observation.

# THE TWELFTH GENUS,
->or<-
# THE STELLATE HERBS.

They are so called because their leaves surround the stems at intervals in the manner of a radiating star. <note>This "star-like" arrangement is known in modern botany as "whorled" leaves.</note> Their flowers are monopetalous <term>monopetalous</term> <note>Meaning the flower consists of a single petal or a single piece, rather than separate petals.</note>, but they are divided into four segments that imitate four distinct leaves. In most species, two seeds <note>The OCR reads "femina" (females), which is likely a transcription error for "semina" (seeds), as these plants are characterized by their "twin" seeds.</note> naturally follow and sit below each small flower. An exception must be made for the Spiked Sea-Madder and the Spiked Cretan Madder, in which only a single seed sits below each flower.

## STELLATE HERBS WITH A SHORTER FLOWER TUBE.

### I.

->*Four-leaved: having four leaves arranged at each joint of the stem in the form of a cross.*<-

1. **Crosswort** <term>Cruciata</term>, whose identifying marks are flowers arranged in whorls <note>Clusters that encircle the stem at the same level.</note> at the nodes of the stems: these are white in the **Smooth Madder of Turin** <note>original: *Rubia lævi Taurinensium*</note> and yellow in the remaining species.
2. **Four-leaved Madder** <term>Rubia quadrifolia</term>, with flowers at the tops of the stems.

### II.

->*Many-leaved: or those with more than four leaves situated at each joint.*<-

**Tournefort** <note>Joseph Pitton de Tournefort, a contemporary botanist.</note> distinguishes these by the fruit, which in **Dyer’s Madder** <note>original: *Erythrodano* or *Rubia tinctorum*</note> is soft and juicy like a kind of berry. I have instead taken the red root—useful for dyeing—as the characteristic identifying mark.

->*Many-leaved Stellates, with fruit that is dry at maturity.*<-

->*1. With leaves that are smooth or less rough.*<-

1. **Common Bedstraw** <term>Gallium vulgare</term> <note>Now known as *Galium verum* or Lady's Bedstraw.</note>; it differs from the others by its thin, dark green leaves and small yellow flowers.
2. **Hedge Bedstraw** <term>Mollugo</term>; this has white flowers and broader leaves.

## THE THIRTEENTH GENUS,

->or Herbs<-

# THE ROUGH-LEAVED PLANTS,

->*In which usually four naked seeds follow each individual flower.*<-
<note>original: "Asperifoliæ"; a group characterized by coarse, bristly hairs on their leaves and stems.</note>

---

The identifying marks of this genus are leaves positioned on the stems in an alternating pattern or with no specific order, single-petaled flowers <term>monopetali</term> with five-parted edges, open five-cleft calyxes <term>calices quinquifidi</term> <note>The calyx is the outer protective green "cup" of a flower.</note>, the tips of the flower spikes reflected or curled back like a scorpion's tail before the blossoms open <note>This spiral shape is known to modern botanists as a "scorpioid cyme."</note>, and four seeds following each individual flower.

1. **Spotted Lungwort** <term>Pulmonaria maculosa</term>, whose identifying marks are a long, whole perianth <note>The outer envelope of a flower.</note>; and in most species, leaves variegated with white spots.
2. **Hound’s Tongue** <term>Cynoglossum</term>, whose identifying marks are leaves that are woolly or rough in most species; the seeds are rough, bur-like, and flattened, with their sharp edges directed upward toward the style <note>The central stalk of the flower's female reproductive part.</note>. The fruit is so structured that it represents a four-sided pyramid. **Tournefort** <note>Joseph Pitton de Tournefort (1656–1708), an influential French botanist.</note> refers **Sea Bugloss** <term>Echium marinum</term>—called by others "Our Small Sea Hound’s Tongue" <note>original: "Cynoglossum marinum minus nostras"</note> because of its somewhat tubular flower, bluish-green <term>glauca</term> leaves, and smooth seeds—to the **Bugloss** group. Perhaps it might more correctly be placed under **Honeywort** <term>Cerinthe</term>, says **Mr. Hermann** <note>Paul Hermann (1646–1695), a German physician and botanist who worked in Leiden.</note>, with whom we also agree.
3. **Borage** <term>Borago</term>, having larger star-shaped flowers, divided into five sharp segments all the way to the base, with the tips coming together into a sharp point <term>umbonem</term>; the seeds are wrinkled and resemble the head of a viper.
4. **Bugloss** <term>Buglossum</term> <note>From the Greek for "ox-tongue," referring to the rough texture of the leaves.</note>; its smaller, tubular flowers, expanding at the top into five blunt or circular segments, distinguish it from Borage. The seeds resemble a viper’s head.
5. **Alkanet** <term>Anchusa</term> <note>Historically prized for the red dye extracted from its roots.</note>, differs from Bugloss and its other relatives by the blood-red juice of its root. **Tournefort** classifies Alkanet under Bugloss. However, the blood-red juice of the root seems sufficient to us, as it did to the ancient authors, to distinguish this as its own genus.
6. **Viper’s Bugloss** <term>Echium</term>, differs from the rest of this genus by its horn-shaped or curved flower, which expands from a narrow base into a wide opening, with the upper part extending further and the lower part shorter.
7. **Gromwell** <term>Lithospermum</term> <note>The name literally means "stone seed" in Greek, referring to the hard, nut-like seeds.</note>, whose identifying marks are a stony, shiny seed of an oval shape, and a flower expanding into five somewhat round segments. It differs from Bugloss (as **Mr. Tournefort** correctly notes) in the shape, hardness, and polish of its seeds.

**Mr. Tournefort** refers **Scorpion-tail Viper’s Bugloss** <term>Echium Scorpioides</term> to **Gromwell** <term>Lithospermum</term>—

It carries [them]. But it differs from **Gromwell** <term>Lithospermum</term> by its very long flower spikes, with no leaves mixed in. 8. **Heliotrope** <term>Heliotropium</term> is distinguished from others of this class by its flowers extending into long spikes, divided into five larger parts, between which usually as many smaller parts intervene, folded back into a star shape around the center (as observed by **Mr. Tournefort** <note>Joseph Pitton de Tournefort, the prominent French botanist mentioned previously.</note>).

9. **Pliny's Great Cleavers** <term>Aparine major Plinii</term> or **Madwort** <term>Asperugo Tournef.</term> is distinguished from its relatives by its rough stems and leaves, which cling to clothing; leaves sometimes growing three or four together, and small compressed seeds in bivalve <note>Two-valved</note>, compressed, three-cornered, and toothed pods. 10. **Comfrey** <term>Symphytum</term>, whose identifying marks are hanging cylindrical flowers, and polished, shining seeds like those of **Gromwell**.

11. **Honeywort** <term>Cerinthe</term>, whose identifying marks are hanging cylindrical flowers, which resemble **Comfrey**; two seeds, or rather seed-vessels, follow each flower. What are commonly thought to be seeds, as **Mr. Tournefort** observes, are actually capsules divided into two cells, each containing a single seed: in this respect the plant is unusual <term>anomala</term>, but should be referred to this group due to its agreement in other characteristics.

12. **Navelwort** <term>Linum umbilicatum</term> <note>Now usually referred to as *Omphalodes* or *Cynoglossum* species.</note> differs from others by its fruit being navel-shaped <term>cotylode</term> or resembling a cup.

**Mr. Tournefort** calls this genus **Navel-seed** <term>Omphalodes</term>, and makes **Small Comfrey with the appearance of Borage** a relative to it, under the name "Dwarf Spring Navel-seed with a Comfrey leaf" <note>original: "Omphalodis pumilæ vernæ Symphyti folio"</note>. This is correct, as I have been informed by **Dr. Charles Preston, M.D.** <note>Charles Preston (1660–1711), a Scottish physician and botanist who corresponded with the leading scientists of his day.</note>, who has seen its fruit.

# THE FOURTEENTH GENUS,
->or<-
## WHORLED-FLOWERING HERBS.

The more certain characteristics by which these are distinguished from other plant genera are: leaves growing in pairs opposite one another on the stem; single-petaled lipped flowers <term>monopetali labiati</term> <note>flowers where the petal is fused into a tube that opens into "lips," typical of the mint family</note>, and in most cases also hooded <term>galeati</term> <note>original: "galeati," referring to a helmet-like upper lip</note>; and four seeds for every flower, for which the calyx <term>perianthium</term> serves as a small protective vessel.

**Mr. Tournefort** <note>Joseph Pitton de Tournefort (1656–1708), a hugely influential French botanist whose system rivaled the author's.</note> defines the characteristic of whorled-flowering herbs as having flowers *en gueule* <note>French for "in the throat" or "gaping"</note>, which I interpret as being "masked" <term>larvatos</term>. Truly, the flowers of **Mint** <term>Menthae</term>, **Pennyroyal** <term>Pulegii</term>, and **Water Horehound** <term>Marrubii aquatici</term> bear no resemblance to a mask, but are divided into four nearly equal segments. The same author refers herbs with "gaping" flowers <note>original: "en gueule"</note> and "snouted" flowers <note>original: "en muffle"</note> to different classes; however, he says they ought to be distinguished primarily by the seed capsule. For gaping flowers have a style composed of four embryos, which turn into just as many seeds for which the calyx serves as a vessel. But snouted flowers, such as **Eyebright** <term>Euphrasia</term>, **Lousewort** <term>Pedicularis</term>, **Cow-wheat** <term>Melampyri</term> etc., leave behind a capsule distinct from the calyx. But indeed, since they agree perfectly in the form of the flower, in **Tournefort’s** method, as far as I can see, they should not have been referred to different genera. For what do seeds or fruits have to do with the structure of the flower? <note>This highlights a major 17th-century botanical debate: whether to classify plants based on their reproductive fruits or their floral appearance.</note>

->I.<-

->*Shrubby whorled plants, whose stems are perennial and consist of a woody substance.*<-

1. **Sage** <term>Salvia</term>, whose characteristics are large, gaping flowers in loose spikes composed of whorls <note>rings of flowers around the stem</note> somewhat distant from each other, wrinkled leaves, and a strong, powerful scent. Add to this, the lip of the flower is divided into three segments, of which the middle one is not at all split <term>bifida</term>, as far as I could discern in **Common Sage** <term>Salvia vulgari</term>.

**Mr. Tournefort** classifies **Sticky Yellow Clary** <term>Horminum luteum glutinosum</term> (also called **Jupiter’s Beard** <term>Colum Jovis</term>) as a species of **Sage**.

The same author separates that plant which we (following **Parkinson** <note>John Parkinson (1567–1650), the last of the great English herbalists.</note>) made a species of **Sage**—under the title of **Shrubby Yellow Broad-leaved Sage**—and its relatives from **Sage** <term>Salvia</term>, **Clary** <term>Horminum</term>, and **Mullein** <term>Verbascum</term>, and makes a unique genus of them

2. under the title of **Jerusalem Sage** <term>Phlomis</term>, whose characteristic marks are a tubular flower,

...[the flower is] divided above into two lips, the upper of which hangs down over the lower; the calyx <term>calix</term> <note>the outer green cup of a flower</note> is composed of five flat segments.

Of this genus, he identifies the following species: 1. **Mullein with broad Sage-like leaves** <note>original: *Verbascum latis Salviæ foliis*</note> by **Caspar Bauhin** <note>C. B., a famous Swiss botanist (1560–1624)</note>. 2. **Mullein with narrow Sage-like leaves** <note>original: *Verbascum angustis Salviæ foliis*</note> by the same author. 3. **Shrubby Portuguese Jerusalem Sage with a purple flower** <note>original: *Phlomidem Lusitanicam fruticosam flore purpureo*</note> from the *Elements of Botany* <note>original: *El. Bot.*, referring to Tournefort’s 1694 work</note>. 4. **Long-leaved Black Horehound** <note>original: *Marrubium nigrum longifolium*</note> by **Caspar Bauhin**; that is, the **"Wind-herb" of Montpellier** <note>original: *Herbam venti Monspeliensium*</note>. 5. **Very white shrubby Spanish Jerusalem Sage with a rusty-colored flower** <note>original: *Phlomidem Hispanicam fruticosam candidissimam flore ferrugineo*</note> from the *Elements of Botany*. 6. **Very white herbaceous Spanish Jerusalem Sage** <note>original: *Phlomidem Hispanicam candidissimam herbaceam*</note> from the *Elements of Botany*.

3. **Lavender** <note>original: *Lavendula*</note>, the characteristics of which are flowers arranged in quite dense whorls <term>verticillis</term> into thin spikes that mimic ears of wheat, sitting upon long stalks. Add to this: the upper lip of the flower is two-cleft <term>bifidum</term> and bent back, while the lower lip is divided into three parts.

We recognize four species of this genus: 1. **Broad-leaved Lavender** <note>original: *Lavendulam latifoliam*</note> by **Caspar Bauhin**. 2. **Narrow-leaved Lavender** <note>original: *Lavendulam angustifoliam*</note> by the same. 3. **Broad-leaved Indian Lavender with a shorter, ash-colored spike** <note>original: *Lavendulam latifoliam Indicam spicâ subcinereâ breviore*</note> from the **Royal Garden at Paris** <note>original: *H. R. P.*</note>. 4. **Lavender with many-cleft leaves** <note>original: *Lavendulam folio multifido*</note> by **Jean Bauhin** <note>J. B., brother of Caspar and also a renowned botanist</note>. To these, **Mr. Tournefort** adds 5. **Broad-leaved Spanish Woolly Lavender** <note>original: *Lavendulam latifoliam Hispanicam tomentosam*</note> from his *Elements of Botany*. The same author considers **French Lavender with saw-toothed leaves** <note>original: *Stœchadem serrato folio*</note> to be a species of Lavender.

4. **French Lavender** <note>original: *Stœchas*</note>, whose spikes are more robust than those of common Lavender, overlapping with hairy scales <note>original: *pilosis squamis imbricatæ*</note>, with small leaves at their very summit. Add to this the smallness of the flowers, which appear as if cut into five nearly equal parts. **Tournefort**, **Rivinus** <note>Augustus Quirinus Rivinus (1652–1723), a German botanist who also proposed a system based on flower shape</note>.

5. **Rosemary** <note>original: *Rosmarinus*</note>; the characteristics of this are its notable size and stature, with flowers mixed among the leaves at the nodes of the stems; the leaves are narrow and oblong, gray on the underside and a darker green on the upper side. Add to this the hood <term>galeam</term> <note>the upper part of the lipped flower</note> of the flower, which is bent back and two-cleft, and the lip which is divided into three parts, with the middle segment hollowed out in the shape of a spoon. **Tournefort**, *Elements of Botany*.

6. **Hyssop** <note>original: *Hyssopus*</note>; this also has long, narrow leaves; it is distinguished from its relatives by long spikes of flowers composed of rather sparse whorls, mostly facing one direction, with a two-cleft flower hood that is bent upward, and a small lip divided into three parts, the middle of which is hollowed like a spoon and two-cleft.

7. **Savory** <note>original: *Satureia*</note> agrees with **Hyssop** in having long, narrow leaves, and with **Thyme** in the shape of its flowers, from which it differs because the flowers are scattered in the axils <term>alis</term> <note>the angle between the leaf and the stem</note> of the leaves; whereas in **Thyme** they are crowded into more robust little heads. I believe these genera should be distinguished by the shape of the leaves: those of Savory are long and narrow, while those of **Common Thyme** <note>original: *Thymo vulgari*</note> are shorter and broader. **True Thyme** <note>original: *Thymus legitimus*</note> differs from Savory by having flowers crowded into oblong heads.

**Mr. Tournefort** makes **Thymbra** <note>a plant similar to Savory or Thyme</note> a distinct genus from Savory, and determines that it differs from Thyme because the whorls are not crowded into heads at the tops of the stems, but are born at intervals along the stems and branches.

The author frequently engages with the systems of contemporary botanists like Tournefort and Hermann.</meta>

8. **Common Marum** <note>original: *Marum vulgare*; likely Spanish Mastic Thyme (*Thymus mastichina*)</note> differs from **Thyme** by its larger leaves, its woolly whorls or flower heads, and the intensity of its scent. **Tournefort** <note>Joseph Pitton de Tournefort (1656–1708), a French botanist who developed an early system of plant classification</note> includes *Marum* among the species of **Thymbra** <note>a genus of savory-like plants</note>. However, it differs from every other species of whorled plant known to us by such a remarkable characteristic—namely, its woolly heads and whorls <term>verticillis</term> <note>circular clusters of flowers around a stem</note>—that it deserves to constitute its own distinct genus. In having flowers crowded into thicker heads at the tops of the stems and branches, it agrees with **Thyme** and **Wild Thyme**; it does not agree with *Thymbra*, as far as I can discern.

9. **Thyme** <note>original: *Thymum*</note>. Its known characteristics are short and somewhat broad leaves, and flowers crowded into thicker heads at the tops of the stems; the "helmets" <term>galeæ</term> <note>the arched upper part of a tubular flower</note> of these flowers are raised and split in two, while the lower lips are divided into three parts. The lower whorl is located further away from the main head. **Hermann** <note>Paul Hermann (1646–1695), a German-born physician and botanist</note>.

The "legitimate" **Thyme** of **Dioscorides** <note>original: *Diofc.*; referring to the 1st-century Greek physician who wrote *De Materia Medica*</note> is not round-leaved, but resembles **Savory** <note>original: *Satureiam*</note> in its leaves, and bears a crowded flower head.

10. **Wild Thyme** <note>original: *Serpyllum*</note> differs from **Thyme** in that it is lower-growing, less shrub-like, and has trailing branches; otherwise, it agrees with it in its flowers, seeds, and overall appearance.

That which is called **Goat's Oregano** <note>original: *Tragoriganum*</note> does not seem to differ in genus from **Thyme**.
Furthermore, the flowers of **Savory**, **Common Marum**, **Thyme**, **Wild Thyme**, **Marjoram**, and **Oregano** <note>original: *Origani*</note> agree so closely in their shape and notches that a distinction of genera cannot be sought from those parts.

11. **Poly-mountain** <note>original: *Polium*</note>. **Mr. Tournefort** rejects our identifying marks taken from the whitish-grey color <term>canitie</term> of the leaves and foliage and their notched edges; he establishes the mark of *Polium* (by which it differs from **Germander** <note>original: *Chamædri*</note>) as having flowers that lack a "helmet" or upper lip, crowded into oblong heads at the tops of the stems and branches. The lip of the flower is divided into five parts, a trait it shares with **Germander**.

However, the etymology of the name <note>The Greek *polios* means "grey" or "whitish," supporting the author's focus on the leaf color</note> favors our marks regarding the whiteness of the leaves; and as for the notches, they characterize the species of *Polium* properly so called.

12. **Teucrium** <note>Tree Germander</note> differs from **Germander** chiefly in its stature and size, though it agrees with it in having leaves and flowers that lack a "helmet." **Tournefort** assigns the same marks to *Teucrium* and **Germander**, except for the tubular shape of the flower's cup <term>calicis</term> in **Germander**.

13. **Germander** <note>original: *Chamedrys*</note>; the marks of this are leaves with the divisions of an oak, as the name indicates <note>from the Greek *chamai* (on the ground) and *drys* (oak)</note>. It differs from **Teucrium** chiefly by its smallness and the shape of its leaves. **Tournefort** distinguishes these genera by the shape of the calyx and by the position of the flowers in the leaf axils <term>alis</term> <note>the angle between the upper side of a leaf and the stem</note>. The flower lacks a "helmet," and a five-parted lower lip hangs down, the middle portion of which is spoon-shaped and split in two in some species. Additionally, the flowers are born in the axils of the leaves, specifically in pairs along the stems and branches. **Mr. Hermann**.

**Mr. Tournefort** refers the **Pharmacists' Water Germander** <note>original: *Scordium Officin.*</note>, the **Wood Sage** or **Wild Sage** <note>original: *Scorodoniam seu Salviam agrestem*</note>, and **Cortusus’s Marum** to the **Germander** genus. I do not see why these individual plants should not constitute their own proper genus—

...they should constitute [their own genus], since **Wood Sage** <note>original: *Scorodonia*; *Teucrium scorodonia*</note> differs from **Germander** <note>original: *Chamædry*</note> and **Teucrium** by a notable mark: it has single flowers in each of the leaf axils <note>original: *alis*; the angle between the leaf and the stem</note>. ### II.

#### *Whorled herbaceous plants, with a flower that is barely hooded, but divided into almost equal segments.*

1. **Mint** <note>original: *Mentha*</note>, which has a four-parted flower, where the hood <term>galea</term> <note>the arched upper part of a tubular flower</note> and the lip <term>labello</term> are barely distinguishable from the side segments; it has a sweet scent (as the Greek name *hedyosmos* <note>original: ἡδύοσμος; literally "sweet-smelling"</note> indicates) and creeping roots.
2. **Pennyroyal** <note>original: *Pulegium*</note> differs from Mint by its denser whorls <term>verticillis</term> <note>circular clusters of flowers around a stem</note> and its small size. Master **Rivinus** <note>Augustus Quirinus Rivinus (1652–1723), a German botanist who classified plants by flower shape</note> adds that the segment which serves as the hood is whole, whereas in Mint it is usually split in two, an observation we have also confirmed.
3. **Water Horehound** <note>original: *Marrubium aquaticum*; likely *Lycopus europaeus*</note> is distinguished from Mint by its denser, more widely separated whorls, its wrinkled leaves that are jagged at the base, and its lack of scent. The flower resembles a funnel with a four-parted rim and rounded segments.
4. **Vervain** <note>original: *Verbena*</note> has wrinkled leaves and flowers spread out into five nearly equal parts; these are arranged in spikes that are not divided into whorls, with no leaves mixed in among the flowers. Additionally, the seeds entirely fill the seed-vessel <term>perianthia</term>.

### III.

#### *Whorled plants with scaly heads.*

1. **Dittany** <note>original: *Dictamnus*</note>, the distinguishing marks of which are very woolly and gray-white leaves and smooth, scaly heads <term>capitula fquamata</term>. These scales are larger than those of Marjoram and more loosely packed together. Individual flowers emerge from the hollows of each leaf, just as in **Marjoram**.
2. **Marjoram** <note>original: *Majorana*</note> has scaly heads composed of several pairs of small leaves which overlap like scales because of their closeness; these are smaller than those of Dittany. Individual flowers emerge from the axil of each leaf. These small leaves sometimes differ from the other leaves on the stem in their shape, smoothness, and small size.
3. **Oregano** <note>original: *Origanum*</note> differs from Marjoram chiefly by its longer scaly heads that extend into spikes. **Tournefort** <note>Joseph Pitton de Tournefort (1656–1708), a French botanist</note> and **Rivinus** observed that Marjoram differs from Oregano by having flower segments that end in sharp points, while in Oregano they are more rounded; in my opinion, this distinction is too subtle.

### IV.

->*Whorled herbaceous plants with whorls arranged into spikes; that is, those where the leaves beneath the whorls have a different shape from the rest of the leaves.*<-

1. **Basil** <note>original: *Basilicum*</note> or **Ocimum**; this has leaves like Marjoram <note>original: *Amaraci*</note>, a pleasant scent of lemon or cloves <note>original: *Caryophylli*</note>, and flowers arranged in loose spikes composed of more spaced-out whorls <term>verticillis</term> <note>circular clusters of flowers around a stem</note>. But to tell the truth, there is a more certain characteristic which I owe to Master **Rivinus**, namely the shape of the flower, in which the beard <term>barba</term> <note>the lower lip of the flower</note> is simple and undivided, while the hood <term>galea</term> <note>the arched upper part of the flower</note> is divided into four parts (scalloped <note>original: *crenata*</note> according to **Tournefort**) and is larger than the beard or lip.
2. **Clary Sage** <note>original: *Sclarea*</note>, whose characteristics are a flower hood much larger than its lip and sickle-shaped (curved like a hook according to Rivinus); the lip is three-parted, with the middle portion split in two <note>original: *bifida*</note> and hollowed out. Refer **Ethiopian Sage** <note>original: *Æthiopin*; *Salvia aethiopis*</note> to this group, as well as **Meadow Sage** <note>original: *Horminum pratense*; *Salvia pratensis*</note> with saw-toothed leaves described by **Caspar Bauhin** <note>original: *C. B.*; a Swiss botanist whose work was a standard reference in this era</note>.
3. The upper lip of the **Sage** <note>original: *Hormini*</note> flower (which we usually call the hood) truly resembles a hood, etc.
4. **Spiked Ironwort** <note>original: *Sideritis spicata*</note>; beneath each of its whorls are two broad, roughly round leaflets, armed with small spines, clutching the flowers within their folds <note>original: *sinubus*</note>.
5. **Self-heal** <note>original: *Prunella*</note>, whose characteristics are short, stockier spikes. Add to this: the upper lip of the flower is cut into the shape of a hood, and the lower is three-parted, with the middle segment wider and more extended, hollowed out like a spoon <note>original: *in cochlearis formam*</note>. The flower cups <term>calices</term> are divided into two lips, the upper of which is not clearly divided into spines (Tournefort asserts it is cut into three sharp segments), while the lower, which sits beneath the flowers, ends in two spines.

### V.

->*Whorled herbaceous plants, where the leaves beneath the whorls are of the same shape as the rest.*<-

1. **Wood Betony** <note>original: *Betonica*</note>, whose characteristics are flowers arranged in stockier spikes, stems that do not branch, and scalloped <note>original: *crenata*</note> leaves. Add to this: the upper lip or hood of the flower is raised and usually split in two, and the lower lip is three-parted, with the middle part split in two.
2. **Catmint** <note>original: *Nepeta*</note> or **Catnip** <note>original: *Mentha cataria*</note>; the leaves are like Nettle or Betony, usually grayish-white <note>original: *incana*</note>, with a scent stronger than Mint; the flowers are arranged in stockier spikes, with a raised and split hood, and a three-parted lip where the middle segment is hollowed out like a spoon, and the two side segments stand out like wings. According to Master **Tournefort**. The middle segment of the beard, as observed by Rivinus, is lightly saw-toothed.
3. **Hemp-nettle** <note>original: *Galeopsidi*</note> has leaves like a Nettle, a foul odor, and small seeds, [which are] thoroughly

...black at maturity; the upper lip of the flower is hollowed out like a spoon, while the lower lip is divided into three parts, with the middle segment being blunt, long, wide, and turned back on both sides, and the side segments being small and short. **Tournefort** refers the plant called **False Hemp** <note>original: *Cannabin spuriam*</note> to this group. However, in my opinion, he does so incorrectly, since in **Hemp-nettle** <note>original: *Galeopsi*</note> the flowers run out into long, narrow, or slender spikes composed of fewer whorls <term>verticillis</term> <note>circular clusters of flowers around a stem</note>—usually six flowers—whereas in **False Hemp** the spikes are quite thick and more robust, formed from denser whorls; furthermore, the segments of the calyx <note>the green outer cup of the flower</note> extend into long, sharp, rigid spines. Related to **Hemp-nettle** is the **Strumous-rooted English Ironwort** described by **Parkinson** <note>original: *Sideritis Anglica strumosa radice Park.*</note>, and also the **Common Yellow Dead-nettle**, as noted by **Master Tournefort**.

4. **Lamium** <term>Dead-nettle</term>, whose characteristics are nettle-like leaves and rather large seeds that fall out of the wide, short calyxes immediately upon ripening, and a foul odor. Add to this: the upper lip of the flower is concave in the shape of a spoon, the lower lip is split almost like a heart, and the throat of the flower is also bounded on both sides by a "wing" or small leaf-like part.

5. **False Hemp** <note>original: *Cannabis spuria*</note>, which **Caspar Bauhin** calls the **Stinging Nettle with saw-toothed leaves** <note>original: *Urticam aculeatam foliis serratis*</note>, is distinguished from all its relatives by this single trait: the segments of the calyx extend into long and rigid prickles. The tube of the flower is oblong, the hood <term>galea</term> <note>the arched upper part of the flower</note> is concave, and the lip is divided into three parts, with the middle segment being longer and somewhat scalloped.

6. **Marrubium** <term>Horehound</term>; its features are blunt, wrinkled leaves and flowers in dense whorls around the nodes of the stems; the upper lip is raised and split as if into horns, the lower lip is divided into three parts, with the middle portion usually being cleft in two. The flower calyxes end in as many small spines as there are ridges in each—up to twelve. Add to this the white, woolly appearance of the whole plant. The **White-leaved Broad-leafed Foreign Horehound** of **Caspar Bauhin** <note>original: *Marrubium album latifolium peregrinum C. B.*</note> has a cup <note>original: *perianthium*</note> divided into only five segments.

7. **Master Tournefort** established a new genus under the name **Marrubiastrum** <term>Bastard Horehound</term>, whose species include: 1. **Ironwort with Chickweed and Germander leaves** <note>original: *Sideritis Alsines Trissaginis folio C. B.*</note>; 2. **Marsh Dead-nettle with Balm leaves from the Belgian garden** of **Hermann** <note>original: *Lamium Melissæ folio paludosum Belgicum Hort. Lugd. Bat. Herman.*</note>; 3. **The kind of Ironwort with thorny whorls** of **John Bauhin** <note>original: *Sideritidis genus verticillis spinosis J. B.*</note>. The characteristic features are the upper lip or hood of the flower, which is hollowed out like a spoon, and the lower lip, which is divided into three notches.

8. **Stachys** <term>Hedge-nettle or Woundwort</term> differs from the others by its dense whorls and the white, woolly down of its leaves. Add to this: the upper lip of the flower is raised, cleft in two, and concave like a spoon, while the lower lip is three-parted, with the side segments being so small that they look more like notches. Thus says **Master Tournefort**.

9. **Sideritis** <term>Ironwort</term>. Under this name I include several plants of different forms, to which botanists have given this name because of their effect in healing wounds inflicted by iron <note>The name comes from the Greek 'sideros' meaning iron</note>; these agree in scent with **Dead-nettle** but do not have the leaves of a **Nettle**. I admit this is less "philosophical" <note>meaning the grouping is based on medicinal use rather than strict physical structure</note>. **Master Tournefort** describes the upper lip of the **Ironwort** flower as standing upright...
