# METHODUS PLANTARUM

...turned back, and divided into three parts below, which serves as a distinguishing mark. But this is common to many genera of whorled plants. It adds flowers arranged in whorls <term>verticillatim</term> <note>arranged in a circle around the stem</note> along the stems and branches; each whorl is supported by two nearly round leaves, which are often notched like a cock’s comb, differing from the other leaves growing lower down on the stem. These characteristics apply to the **Spiked Ironwort** <note>original: *Sideritidi spicatæ*</note> mentioned above, but not to this entire genus.

10. **Ballote** or **Black Horehound** <note>original: *Marrubium nigrum*</note> resembles **Dead-nettle** <note>original: *Lamium*</note> in its leaves and foul odor, but it differs in its flowers: many are crowded together on individual stalks emerging from each leaf axil <term>alis</term> <note>the angle between the leaf and the stem</note>, and the calyxes <note>the green outer cup of the flower</note> are less open and longer. Add to this the shape of the flower: the upper lip is concave like a spoon, and the lower lip is divided into three parts, with the middle segment split in two.

11. **Clinopodium** <term>Wild Basil</term> bears leaves like **Wild Marjoram**. The flowers are in dense whorls around the nodes of the stems (which distinguishes it from **Balm** <note>original: *Melissa*</note> and **Calamint**), and their tubes are longer than in **Horehound**; the upper lips are rounded, raised, and usually split in two, while the lower lips are divided into three parts, with the middle segment being the widest.

12. **Acinos** <term>Basil Thyme</term> has leaves like **Wild Thyme** <note>original: *Serpylli*</note> or **Small Basil**. The small calyxes of the flowers are oblong and striped, with a narrow neck and a bulging middle. The flowers come out from the leaf axils along the stems and are not gathered into heads at the tops of the stems, which distinguishes it from **Wild Thyme**.

13. **Motherwort** <note>original: *Cardiaca*</note>, whose distinguishing marks are leaves that are somewhat round in outline and deeply jagged. Add that the upper lip of the flower is bent into a channel and is much longer than the lower one; the lower lip is divided into three parts; the calyx is very short and filled with seeds right up to the top.

14. **Lion's Tail** <note>original: *Leonurus*</note>; the flower matches the **Motherwort** flower in shape, though the hood <term>galea</term> <note>the upper, helmet-like petal of the flower</note> is much longer, and it differs in having a more elongated calyx. The plant itself is distinguished from **Motherwort** by its leaves, stature, and the size of all its parts. Furthermore, it produces woody stems. For this reason, it could also be classified among the shrubby whorled plants. <insert>See Page 190, Line 23.</insert>

15. **Bells of Ireland** <note>original: *Moluca*</note> is easily distinguished from other whorled plants by the very large, wide calyx of its flower, which rivals a shallow bowl <note>original: *acetabuli*</note>. For although **False Dittany** <note>original: *Pseudodictamnus*</note> also enjoys larger flower calyxes, they do not match those of **Moluca**; for **Moluca** bears its seeds <note>original: *semina* — the transcription reads 'femina,' likely a clerical error for seeds</note> quite naked compared to the others, whereas on the contrary, **False Dittany** hides them very well, as **Master Rivinus** <note>Augustus Quirinus Rivinus (1652–1723), a German physician and botanist who proposed a classification system based on the number of petals</note> notes. Add that the upper lip of the flower is concave like a spoon, and the lower is divided into three parts, with the middle segment usually split in two.

16. **Moldavian Balm** <note>original: *Moldavica Melissa*</note>, whose characteristics (as noted by **Master Tournefort** <note>Joseph Pitton de Tournefort (1656–1708), an influential French botanist known for the concept of the genus</note>) are a flower opening bounded by two wing-like parts, and an upper lip that is slightly arched or vaulted and split into two raised parts;

# CORRECTED AND AUGMENTED.

...farther down it is also divided into two parts (*Mr. Rivinus* <note>Augustus Quirinus Rivinus (1652–1723), a German botanist who classified plants by their petals.</note> makes it four parts). The leaves are longer, narrower, and more deeply notched <term>crenata</term>.

17. **Calamint** <note>original: *Calamintha*</note>, whose marks are several flowers sitting together on long, branched stalks <term>pediculis</term> emerging from the leaf axils <term>finubus</term>; they are sparse and scattered, gaping from a long tube into two lips, of which the upper is split <term>bifidum</term>, rounded, and raised, and the lower is divided into three parts.

18. **Lemon Balm** <note>original: *Melissa*</note> agrees with **Calamint** in the shape of its flower; it is distinguished from the rest of this family by its dark green leaves, its lemon scent <term>odore citri</term>, and its flowers being crowded together on a single stalk emerging from each leaf axil, not scattered as in Calamint. *Mr. Rivinus* adds that the flowers do not form complete rings or whorls <term>verticillos</term>, and that they are white at the beginning and turn yellow as they mature.

19. **Ground Ivy** <note>original: *Hedera terrestris*</note> is distinguished from other whorled plants by its roundish leaves, its creeping runners <term>flagellis reptatricibus</term>, and its flower’s upper lip being split and turned back <term>reflexo</term>, with a three-part lower lip whose middle segment is wide and split. The flowers grow on shoots emerging from the leaf axils <term>alis</term>; they are not sparse and scattered as in Calamint, but are born more compressed and crowded together.

20. **Bastard Dittany** <note>original: *Pseudo-dictamnus*</note>, whose characteristics, according to *Tournefort* <note>Joseph Pitton de Tournefort (1656–1708), a French botanist known for defining the concept of the genus.</note>, include a flower with an arched and forked upper lip and a three-part lower lip (*Rivinus* says it is four-part).

21. **Skullcap** <note>original: *Cassida* or *Scutellaria*</note> has identifying marks: small, long flowers appearing one to each leaf axil; the upper lip is hooded <term>galeato</term> with two attached "ears" <term>auriculis</term>, and the lower lip is usually split; the calyx <note>the green outer cup of the flower</note> containing the seed has a lid <term>operculatus</term>, resembling the heel of a slipper or shoe. This single mark is sufficient for identification.

22. **Dragonhead** <note>original: *Dracocephalon*</note>, whose marks include a "gaping" flower <term>velut gulofus</term> with a cavity that gradually narrows (*Dr. Herman* <note>Paul Hermann (1646–1695), a physician and botanist who served in Ceylon.</note> says it is a large tubular flower, almost in the shape of a **Foxglove** <note>original: *Digitalis*</note>); its upper lip is hollowed out in the shape of a helmet, the lower is divided into three parts, and the leaves are like those of a Peach tree.

---

### VI.

->*Herbaceous whorled plants, with flowers lacking a helmet.*<-

1. **Ground Pine** <note>original: *Chamaepitys*</note> differs from the rest by its leaves, which mimic those of a Pine tree, and its resinous scent. Add to this that the lower lip of the flower is divided into three parts, the middle portion being split, while the place of the upper lip is occupied by small teeth. In this plant, the flowers appear one to each leaf axil.

2. **Bugle** <note>original: *Bugula*</note>. This has blunt leaves notched around the edges with larger, somewhat rounded indentations. The common species is "two-stemmed" <note>original: *διαυκαυλος* (diaucaulos)</note>, having some stems that are round and creeping, and others (which support the flowers) that are square and upright. *Mr. Rivinus* attributes a "helmet" <term>galeam</term> <note>the upper hood of the petal</note> to it, but it is barely perceptible unless inspected carefully. The lower lip of the flower is divided into three parts.

3. The identifying marks of **Wood Sage** <term>Scorodonia</term> <note>Now known as *Teucrium scorodonia*. The name suggests its garlic-like scent.</note> are its scent of **Garlic** <term>Allii</term>, leaves resembling **Sage** <term>Salviæ</term>, and flowers that emerge singly from each leaf axil <note>The point where the leaf joins the stem.</note>, extending into long spikes. *Tournefort* <note>Joseph Pitton de Tournefort (1656–1708), an influential French botanist.</note> classifies this plant as a species of **Germander** <term>Chamædryos</term>, which in my opinion is less correct; indeed, having single flowers in each leaf axil is a sufficient mark of generic distinction, as *Mr. Rivinus* <note>Augustus Quirinus Rivinus, a German botanist who argued for simpler classification based on flower petals.</note> also judges.

4. The identifying marks of **Water Germander** <term>Scordii</term> <note>Now known as *Teucrium scordium*.</note> are leaves like those of **Germander** <term>Chamædryos</term>, a scent of **Garlic** <term>Allii</term>, a marshy habitat, and a remarkably creeping growth habit. *Mr. Tournefort* also considers this a species of **Germander**, the marks of which are a five-part lip, with the middle segment larger than the rest, and in some species, hollowed out into the shape of a spoon.

In **Water Germander** <term>Scordio</term>, the flowers grow in whorls <term>verticillis</term> <note>A circular arrangement of flowers around the stem.</note>.

## THE FIFTEENTH GENUS,

### or Herbs

# WITH MANY-SEEDED NAKED FRUITS

->That is, those in which more than four seeds follow from each individual flower.<-

I consider as "naked seeds" <term>seminibus nudis</term> whatever does not naturally cast off its pods or private coverings—if they have any or seem to have any—but rather depart from the mother plant still clothed in them. <note>In modern botany, these are often "achenes," where the seed is so closely attached to its outer coat that they appear to be one unit.</note>

->I.<-

->*Many-seeded plants with a three-petaled flower.*<-

1. **Water-plantain** <term>Plantago aquatica</term> <note>Now known as *Alisma plantago-aquatica*. It is not a true Plantain despite the name.</note>, the identifying marks of which are leaves like a **Plantain**, a three-petaled flower, and seeds gathered into a triangle in the larger species, and into a prickly little globe in the smaller species.
2. **Arrowhead** <term>Sagitta</term> <note>Now known as *Sagittaria sagittifolia*.</note> is easily recognized by its leaves, which resemble the shape of a winged arrow. Seeds follow each flower, gathered into a head and densely packed together. *Mr. Tournefort* <note>Joseph Pitton de Tournefort, a French botanist known for his system of plant classification.</note> assigns the **Arrowhead** to the **Buttercup** <term>Ranunculus</term> genus; however, in my judgment, the three-petaled flowers and the arrow-shaped form of the leaves are sufficient to establish it as its own genus. He likewise assigns the **Water-plantain** to the **Buttercup**; I do not agree with him, because of its distinct characteristics—namely, the three-petaled flower and the plantain-like leaves—which are enough to constitute a new genus.

->I I.<-

->*Many-seeded plants with a four-petaled flower.*<-

**Tormentil** <term>Tormentilla</term> <note>Now classified as *Potentilla erecta*. Its name comes from "torment," as it was once used to treat stomach pain.</note> agrees in all respects with **Cinquefoil** <term>Pentaphyllo</term>, except for having a four-petaled flower.

->III.<-

->*Many-seeded plants with a five-petaled flower.*<-

1. **Buttercup** <term>Ranunculus</term>, the identifying marks of which are five-petaled flowers that fall away together with a five-leaved calyx <note>The green, leaf-like structure that supports the petals.</note>, and many seeds following each flower, gathered into a globe or a spike.

# METHOD OF PLANTS

2. ***Avens*** <term>Caryophyllata</term> <note>Now known as the genus *Geum*.</note> differs from its relatives by its seeds, which have long tails ending in hooked or feathery appendages that cling to things; a calyx divided into ten segments (five larger ones with five smaller ones placed between them); pinnate leaves <note>Leaves arranged like a feather on both sides of a common stalk.</note>; and, in some species, a root that smells of spices.

3. ***Strawberry*** <term>Fragaria</term> has a calyx divided in the same way into ten segments, leaves grouped in threes on the same stalk with visible veins, seeds growing upon a soft, edible pulp, and creeping runners.

The so-called ***Barren Strawberry*** <term>Fragaria sterilis</term> <note>Now *Potentilla sterilis*.</note> agrees with the **Strawberry** in the shape of its leaves and the count of three leaflets on one stalk; however, it differs so much in its fruit—not to mention that it lacks runners—that it is rightly considered a different genus. It should rather be referred to the **Cinquefoils** <term>Pentaphyllon</term>. Certainly, the count of five leaves on a single stalk is not exclusive or unique to that genus (which takes its name, "Pentaphyllum," from that very number). Indeed, there are plants that agree in almost all characteristics with **Cinquefoil** but have seven or even three leaflets; conversely, there are some with five leaflets that differ from **Cinquefoil** in all other traits.

4. ***Cinquefoil*** <term>Pentaphyllo</term> <note>Commonly known as *Potentilla*.</note> has veined leaves, with five or seven leaflets on the same stalk, and a calyx likewise divided into ten segments: five larger ones covering the fruit, and five smaller ones lying between them.

5. ***Cinquefoil-like plants*** <term>Pentaphylloides</term> differ from **Cinquefoil** by having lobed leaves that almost rival those of ***Agrimony*** <term>Agrimoniæ</term>.

---

## IV.

### *Many-seeded plants with whole leaves, a many-petaled flower, a three-leaved calyx, and fruit like a Buttercup.*

1. ***Lesser Celandine*** <term>Chelidonium minus</term> <note>Now known as *Ficaria verna*.</note> agrees with ***Liverleaf*** <term>Hepatica trifolia</term> in having a three-leaved calyx and a **Buttercup**-like fruit; it differs from the same by having a calyx that falls off with the flower <note>original: "calice cum flore deciduo"</note> as in the **Buttercups**, by its trailing stems, its somewhat round leaf shape, and its tuberous or lumpy roots.

2. ***Liverleaf*** <term>Hepatica trifolia</term> <note>Now *Anemone hepatica*.</note> has a calyx that remains after the flower has withered, no stem other than the flower stalk, leaves divided into three parts, and fibrous roots. By these marks, it differs from **Lesser Celandine**.

Mr. ***Tournefort*** refers these two genera to the ***Buttercups*** <term>Ranunculus</term>. However, in my judgment, the three-leaved calyx and the many-petaled flowers are sufficient to separate these plants from the **Buttercups**.

## V.
### *Many-seeded plants with finely divided leaves, a many-petaled flower, a five-leaved calyx, and an oblong Buttercup-like fruit.*

1. ***Fennel-leaved Black Hellebore*** <term>Helleborus niger ferulaceus</term> <note>Now known as *Adonis vernalis* or Spring Pheasant's Eye; it is not a true Hellebore.</note>, which has very finely divided leaves and a perennial root.
2. ***Flower of Adonis*** <term>Flos Adonis</term> or ***Eranthemum*** <note>Commonly known as Pheasant's Eye (*Adonis annua*).</note>, which has leaves divided in the same way but an annual root. If anyone does not think the distinction between a perennial and an annual root is a sufficient mark to divide these plants into two separate genera, they may, as far as I am concerned, reduce them to one.

## VI.
### *Many-seeded plants with a many-petaled flower and seeds arranged in a circle.*

***Dropwort*** <term>Filipendula</term> <note>Specifically *Filipendula vulgaris*.</note>, which has tuberous roots with oblong glands hanging from the ends of the root fibers; a simple flower calyx that is toothed or fringed; a six-petaled flower; and seeds collected into a head resembling a small barrel. *Tournefort* <note>original: "Tournef." A reference to Joseph Pitton de Tournefort, a leading French botanist of the era.</note>.

## VII.
### *Many-seeded plants with a naked flower.* <note>In historical botany, a "naked" flower often referred to one that lacks a calyx (sepals), or where the sepals are colored like petals.</note>

***Anemone*** <term>Anemone</term>, the defining characteristic of which we state to be a simple, non-branching stem, with leaves arranged only at a single point <note>A whorl of leaves on the stem.</note>, bearing a single naked, many-petaled flower at the top. Let the clever reader judge whether the ***Wood Anemone*** <term>Anemone sylvestris</term> (called the ***Wood Buttercup*** by some), to which the similarity of the roots can also be added, should not rather be referred to the **Anemones** than to the **Buttercups** <term>Ranunculus</term> solely because of the shape of its fruit; for it is a most certain sign of a generic relationship to have many attributes in common.

1. The seeds of the ***Wood Anemone*** are similar to those of the **Buttercup**, clustered into a round head, with no downy fluff <term>pappus</term> attached, surrounding, or enveloping them. <insert>see Page 190, Line 20.</insert>
2. The seeds of the ***Garden Anemone*** <term>Anemones sativæ</term> are clustered into an oblong head and surrounded by a thick, woolly down.
3. ***Pasque-flower*** <term>Pulsatilla</term> has "curled" seeds with long, feathery plumes attached; the flowers are usually six-petaled.
4. ***Clematis*** <term>Clematis</term> <note>Also known as Traveler's Joy or Virgin's Bower.</note>, whose characteristics are "curled" seeds with long, feathery plumes growing from them; a four-leaved or cross-shaped flower; and, in most species, a fiery, pungent taste.

## SIXTEENTH GENUS,

->*or Herbs*<-

# P O M E - B E A R I N G  P L A N T S.

<note>original: "POMIFERÆ". In modern botany, "pome" refers to fruits like apples, but here the author uses it to describe large, fleshy fruits with thick rinds, specifically the Gourd family (Cucurbitaceae).</note>

I call "Pome-bearing" those plants which produce the largest fruits of all (not every species, but some among them). These fruits are covered with a thick rind—which distinguishes them from the "Berry-bearing" plants, whose fruits are covered only by a thin membrane—and they have naked, single-petaled flowers with a five-part edge, which sit atop the fruit.

To this genus I also refer the ***Passionflower*** <term>Murucuja</term> <note>original: "Murucujam sive Passifloram". *Murucuja* is a Tupi Indian name for certain species of passionflower.</note> because of the similarity of its fruits, which are covered with a thicker rind, even though the flowers do not match the others.

1. ***Gourd*** <term>Cucurbita</term>: Characterized by soft leaves, a white flower, and a fruit covered with a rind that is harder and more wood-like than other pome-bearing plants. Its seed is shield-shaped <note>original: "thyreoides"</note>, appearing horned with two protruding angles at the top. *Tournefort* <note>original: "Tournefortius". Joseph Pitton de Tournefort (1656–1708), a French botanist famous for his system of plant classification.</note> adds that the fruit is usually divided into six compartments.

2. ***Pumpkin*** <term>Pepo</term>: Differs from the Melon in the size of the whole plant, its leaves, flowers, and fruits. It is distinguished from all other pome-bearing plants by its diamond-shaped seed, which is surrounded by a raised line around the edges. *Mr. Tournefort* <note>original: "D. Tournefort". The "D." is an abbreviation for *Dominus*, a title of respect like "Master" or "Doctor."</note> adds that the internal cavity of the fruit is almost always divided into three cells, which distinguishes it from the ***Squash*** <term>Melopepone</term>, whose fruit is usually divided internally into five parts and is striped or angled.

3. ***Colocynth*** <term>Colocynthis</term> <note>Also known as bitter apple or desert gourd; it was historically used as a powerful purgative.</note>: The inner pulp of this fruit is spongy, very light, extremely bitter, and not at all edible. The seeds are small, white, and hard; the leaves are cut into deep lobes.

4. ***Watermelon*** <term>Citrullus</term>: Its seeds are similar to the Pumpkin's but lack the raised line on the edge and are hidden deep within the flesh. It is more reliably distinguished from the others by its deeply divided leaves. *Mr. Tournefort*.

5. ***Melon*** <term>Melo</term>: Shares the characteristic of a white, narrow, oblong seed (resembling a pine nut) with the Cucumber, but differs from it by having a larger fruit that is not spiny, smells of musk, and has sweet flesh.

6. ***Cucumber*** <term>Cucumis</term>: Distinguished from the Melon (which it resembles) by its smaller fruit, which is often covered in spiny bumps. The seeds are contained in a plentiful, moist, gelatin-like pulp. The seed has a sort of prickle, making it easy to distinguish from a melon seed. *Magnol, Garden of Montpellier* <note>original: "Magnol. Hort. Monsp." Referring to Pierre Magnol, the botanist for whom the Magnolia is named.</note>.

7. ***Squirting Cucumber*** <term>Cucumis asininus</term> <note>Literally "donkey's cucumber." Now known as *Ecballium elaterium*, famous for ejecting its seeds forcefully when ripe.</note>: Differs from the Cucumber by its smaller fruit, which is bristling with crowded spines, its toxic juice, and the fact that it lacks tendrils.

5. <note>Likely a typographical error in the original for item 8.</note> ***Summer Squash*** <term>Melopepo</term>: Lacks tendrils; the internal cavity of the fruit is usually

<meta>catchword: usually [rumque]</meta>

...and is usually divided into five chambers, as observed by **Mr. Tournefort** <note>original: "D. Tournefort." Joseph Pitton de Tournefort (1656–1708) was a pioneering French botanist who developed a system of classification based on the shape of the flower's corolla.</note>.

9. ***Male Balsam*** <term>Balsamina mas</term> <note>Now identified as *Momordica balsamina*, or the Balsam Apple.</note>. The fruit is roughened with warty bumps, very small, with little flesh, and contains a single internal cavity which opens spontaneously when ripe. It contains seeds wrapped in a sort of hood or small cap <note>original: "calyptra seu pileolo"</note>, which are usually notched. The flowers are split all the way to the center into five segments <note>original: "lacinias"</note>; sometimes these segments are so separated from one another that it is doubtful whether the plant should be classified as having a single petal <term>monopetalos</term> or five petals <term>pentapetalos</term>.

10. ***Sicyos-like*** <term>Sicyoides</term> <note>A genus described by Tournefort, now usually referring to the bur cucumber (*Sicyos angulatus*).</note> *Tournefort*. The fruit is prickly like a hedgehog <note>original: "echinatus"</note> and somewhat similar to an almond; it contains a single broad or flattened seed inside.

11. ***Passionflower*** <term>Granadilla</term> or <term>Murucuia</term>. The fruit of this plant grows upon a very high stalk <note>original: "summo stylo"</note>, at the base of which the stamens emerge, crowned with tips. From the top, three structures rise like headed pins <note>original: "clavi capitati"; in modern terms, these are the three styles of the passionflower gynoecium</note>. When ripe, the fruit is filled with seeds that are wrinkled or marked with unequal sunken pits.

# THE SEVENTEENTH GENUS,

->or Herbs that are<-

# BERRY-BEARING.

In this section, I use the term "berries" <term>Baccæ</term> <note>original: "Baccas"</note> to refer to any fruits of herbs covered by a relatively thin membrane, containing an internal pericarp <term>pericarpium</term> <note>The part of the fruit that encloses the seeds, such as the flesh or pulp.</note> or pulp that is moist or soft, either surrounding the seeds or mixed among them. Some of these fruits are quite large, so the name "berry," as it is commonly understood, does not strictly apply to them in the most proper sense.

->I.<-

->*Berry-bearing plants with fruit composed of several grains.*<-

1. ***Cloudberry*** <term>Chamæmorus</term> or ***Ground-bramble*** <term>Chamærubus</term> <note>Specifically referring to *Rubus chamæmorus*.</note>. The characteristics of this plant are a five-petaled flower <term>pentapetalos</term> and a fruit composed of several grains <term>acini</term> <note>In modern botany, these "grains" are called drupelets.</note> tightly packed together, mimicking the fruit of the blackberry bush.

2. ***Dwarf Honeysuckle*** <term>Chamæpericlymenum</term> <note>Likely referring to the Bunchberry or Dwarf Cornel (*Cornus suecica*).</note>. Its characteristics include several grains, each attached to its own small stalk (not packed together into a single berry), which follow each individual flower. The leaves resemble those of the ***St. John's-wort*** <term>Ascyrum</term>, and the flower has four petals <term>tetrapetalos</term>.

->II.<-

->*Berry-bearing plants with fruit in clusters.*<-

->*1. Climbing plants.*<-

1. ***Rough Bindweed*** <term>Smilax aspera</term> <note>Commonly known as Sarsaparilla.</note>. It shares its tendrils <term>capreoli</term> with the ***White Bryony***, and its leaf shape with the ***Black Bryony***; however, it differs from both by having thorny stems. The flowers have six petals <term>hexapetali</term> and are attached at the base of the fruit, which is a berry containing one or more spherical seeds. **Mr. Tournefort** <note>Joseph Pitton de Tournefort (1656–1708), the influential French botanist.</note> refers the ***May Lily*** <term>Unifolium</term> of **Dodoens** <note>Rembert Dodoens (1517–1585), a Flemish physician and botanist.</note>, the ***Clustered Solomon’s Seal*** <term>Polygonatum racemosum</term> of **Cornut** <note>Jacques-Philippe Cornut (1606–1651), a French physician and botanist.</note>, and the ***Fertile Spiked Solomon’s Seal*** <term>Polygonatum spicatum fertile</term

### 2. Upright plants.

1. ***Berry-bearing Angelica*** <note>original: *Angelica baccifera*</note>, of a taller stature, with leaves approaching those of the ***Angelica***, smaller berries of a dark red color and sweet taste; it differs from the ***Baneberry*** <note>original: *Christophoriana*</note> and others by the fact that the calyx <term>calix</term> <note>The outer part of a flower that protects the bud.</note> or flower sits atop the berry.
2. The characteristics of the ***Baneberry*** <note>original: *Christophoriana*</note> are a five-petaled flower (though Tournefort <note>Joseph Pitton de Tournefort (1656–1708), a French botanist influential in the development of the modern genus concept.</note> says usually four-petaled) attached to the very bottom of the fruit, leaves like ***Masterwort*** <note>original: *Imperatoria*</note>, and poisonous or harmful fruit.
3. ***American Racemose Nightshade*** <note>original: *Solanum racemosum Americanum*</note>, or ***Pokeweed*** <note>original: *Phytolacca*</note> according to Tournefort. The flower's style <term>stylus</term> <note>The stalk of the female part of the flower.</note> develops into a berry, as Mr. Tournefort likes to say; the seeds are arranged like spokes within the berries, and the fruit grows in clusters <term>racemosi</term>.
4. ***Lily of the Valley*** <note>original: *Lilium convallium*</note>; its characteristics are bare little stalks supporting the flowers and fruit, small bell-shaped flowers that are naked <note>meaning without a calyx</note>, with the margin divided into six small segments, and red berries. Mr. Tournefort, in his *Elements of Botany*, page 69, writes that the shape of the flower constitutes a sufficiently notable difference ( *assez considerable* ) <note>original: French "assez considérable," meaning quite significant.</note> between ***Solomon’s Seal*** <note>original: *Polygonatum*</note> and ***Lily of the Valley***, which is enough to distinguish these genera; however, he himself does not exclude the ***Branching Broad-leaved Solomon’s Seal*** <note>original: *Polygonatum latifolium ramosum*</note> of Caspar Bauhin <note>C. B. refers to Caspar Bauhin (1560–1624), a Swiss botanist who classified thousands of plants.</note> (or the fourth kind of Clusius <note>Carolus Clusius (1526–1609), an influential doctor and botanist.</note>) from the ***Solomon’s Seal*** genus, even though, according to the testimony of Clusius and Jean Bauhin, it produces flowers very similar to those of ***Lily of the Valley***.
5. ***May Lily*** <note>original: *Monophyllon*</note>, characterized by four-petaled, star-shaped flowers arranged in a spike; the leaves rising from the ground are solitary (though there are two or three on the stem), and the berries are red, as in ***Lily of the Valley***.

Mr. Tournefort (as I have said) refers this herb to the ***Rough Bindweed*** <note>original: *Smilax aspera*</note> and joins with it the ***Spiked Canadian Solomon’s Seal*** of Cornut <note>Jacques-Philippe Cornut (1606–1651), a French physician and botanist known for his work on North American flora.</note>, under the title ***Spiked Smilax with a Solomon’s Seal leaf***.

### III.

### *Berry-bearing plants with more scattered fruit.*

1. ***Horse-tongue*** <note>original: *Hypoglossum*</note> differs from the ***Alexandrian Laurel*** by the "little tongue" or secondary leaf emerging from the middle of the leaf in addition to the berry. The pistil of the flower swells into a berry. — *Tournefort.*
2. ***Alexandrian Laurel*** <note>original: *Laurus Alexandrina*</note> differs from ***Horse-tongue*** by having the fruit or berry alone growing from the middle of the leaf, and from ***Butcher’s Broom*** by its larger, non-spiny leaves.
3. ***Butcher’s Broom*** <note>original: *Ruscus*</note> is distinguished from other plants where the seeds grow on the leaves <term>epiphyllospermis</term> by its smaller leaves, which rival those of the Myrtles and end in a sharp, spiny point.
4. ***Solomon’s Seal*** <note>original: *Polygonatum*</note> agrees with ***Lily of the Valley*** in its veined leaves and naked flower; but it is distinguished by its size, its stem clothed with many leaves, and its cylindrical flowers divided into six notches, which emerge from the junctions <note>original: *sinubus*, the "armpits" or axils of the leaves.</note> of the leaves—

5. **Mandrake** <note>original: *Mandragora*</note>: Its characteristics are a single-petaled flower divided into five parts, almost in the shape of a bell; it has no stems except for the stalks <term>pediculos</term> <note>The small stalks that support individual flowers or fruits.</note> supporting the flowers and fruit; the roots are thick.

6. **Herb Paris** <note>original: *Herba Paris*</note>: It is easily distinguished from all other plants by its unbranched stems, which bear leaves in a fixed pattern or from only one joint <note>This refers to the characteristic whorl of leaves.</note>, with a single flower and berry at the tip of each. The flower has four petals, and the calyx <term>calix</term> is also four-leaved.

7. **Mayapple** <note>original: *Pomum majale*</note>: This is a singular plant of its own kind, called **Duck’s Foot** <note>original: *Anapodophyllon*</note> by Morin <note>Jean Morin (1591–1659), a French botanist and florist.</note>; it is described by Mr. Banister <note>John Banister (1650–1692), an English cleric and pioneering naturalist in Virginia.</note> as a **Pome-bearing single-leafed Nightshade with navel-shaped leaves** <note>original: *Solanum pomiferum monophyllon, umbilicifolium*</note>, divided into six more-or-less deep segments. The fruit has the shape of an urn and encloses seeds lying one upon another, as if heaped together.

8. **Nightshade** <note>original: *Solanum*</note>: Its characteristics are single-petaled flowers, either five-parted or star-shaped in most species, with oblong tips in the center <term>umbilicus</term>, which by their union form a sort of boss <term>umbonem</term> <note>A shield-like central projection.</note>; the seeds are small and compressed, and the flower is attached to the very bottom of the fruit.

9. **Love Apple** or **Tomato** <note>original: *Pomum amoris* or *Lycopersicon*</note>: It differs from the **Nightshade** by its fruit being divided into many chambers <term>cellulas</term>. They agree in the shape of the flower.

10. **Eggplant** or **Mad Apple** <note>original: *Melongena* or *Malum insanum*</note>: This differs from the **Nightshade** because its fruit is solid, fleshy, and without a cavity, whereas the fruit of the **Nightshade** is soft, hollow, and succulent. (According to Mr. Tournefort).

11. **Caper** <note>original: *Capparis*</note>: The characteristics are a four-petaled flower, from the center of which emerges a pistil <term>pistillus</term> ending in a small globe, which develops into a pear-shaped fruit containing several seeds in its flesh (Tournefort). However, this plant belongs rather to the woody or tree-like genus.

12. **Berry-bearing Chickweed** <note>original: *Cucubalus* or *Alsine baccifera*</note>: Its characteristics are the five-petaled flowers of the **Chickweed** (*Alsine*) with split petals, and fruit contained in calyxes that swell into bladders <term>vesicas</term> with the segments turned backward; the fruits are oval and filled with many kidney-shaped seeds.

13. **Winter Cherry** or **Bladder Nightshade** <note>original: *Alkekengi* or *Solani halicacabi*</note>: The characteristics are a single-petaled, five-angled flower, and fruit hidden within the calyxes of the flowers, which swell into bladders.

14. **Capsicum** or **Indian Pepper** <note>original: *Capsicum* or *Piper Indicum*</note>: The flowers are like those of the **Nightshade**; the fruits have less flesh and are a type of capsule or pod <term>siliquæ</term>, divided lengthwise by a slightly fleshy membrane into three chambers, or sometimes only two; the seeds are compressed and mostly kidney-shaped. The whole plant, but especially the fruit and seeds, is burning and very sharp.

15. **Deadly Nightshade** or **Belladonna** <note>original: *Solanum lethale* or *Bella donna*</note>: It has bell-shaped flowers, concave and tubular, with the margin divided into five sharp segments; the fruit is larger, divided into two chambers, and is malignant and poisonous.

16. **Cuckoo-pint** <note>original: *Arum*</note>: Whose characteristics are a single-petaled, tongue-shaped flower,

METHOD OF PLANTS

# THE EIGHTEENTH GENUS,

->*or Herbs*<-

# MANY-PODDED PLANTS <note>original: *Multisiliquæ*</note>.

I call many-podded plants those whose individual flowers are followed by several distinct pods or seed vessels.

The distinguished man **Mr. Paul Hermann** <note>Paul Hermann (1646–1695) was a German-born physician and botanist who served as the director of the Leiden Botanical Garden.</note> calls these plants **multi-capsuled, single-valved, and many-seeded** <note>original: *multicapsulares, univalves polyspermas*</note> because, after each flower, they leave behind several capsules that gape open along their inner or upper length, while remaining closed on the opposite side, containing many seeds.

These can be divided into those that have thick and succulent leaves, and those with thinner and less juicy leaves. The latter can be further subdivided into those with a regular flower and those with an irregular flower.

## I.

->*Many-podded plants with thick and succulent leaves.*<-

1. **Pennywort** <note>original: *Cotyledon*</note> or **Venus’s Navel** <note>original: *Umbilicus Veneris*</note>, the characteristics of which are oblong tubular flowers with the rim divided into five segments; the fruit is composed of five sheaths <term>thecis</term> containing many tiny seeds; the leaves are somewhat round, and in some species, the stalk <term>pediculo</term> is attached at the center of the leaf.

2. **Stonecrop** <note>original: *Sedum*</note> or **Greater Houseleek** <note>original: *Sempervivum majus*</note>, the characteristics of which are lower leaves gathered into clusters resembling "ox-eyes"; the flowers are somewhat rose-like, spread out into several petals on curved shoots at the tops of the stems; the fruit is formed from many pods or "little horns" <term>corniculis</term>. The leaves covering the stems are very different from the lower ones.

3. **Lesser Stonecrop** <note>original: *Sedum minus*</note> differs from the preceding by its small size, the narrowness of its leaves, and by having fewer petals in the flower—specifically five or six—and fewer pods following the flower.

4. **Orpine** <note>original: *Telephium*</note>. In this plant, the leaves are not gathered into small heads as they are in the **Stonecrop** <note>original: *Sedo*</note>; for it produces a stem immediately from its first sprouting. Its flowers are gathered at the tops of the stems into umbels or bundles; they are five-petaled and star-shaped, and are followed by seed-sheaths, usually five in number.

<summary>This page introduces the eighteenth genus of herbs, the Multisiliquæ (many-podded plants), defining them by their distinct seed vessels and further classifying them by leaf succulence and flower symmetry. It specifically describes succulent varieties including Pennywort, Houseleek, and Orpine.</summary>

## II.

### Many-podded plants with thinner and less succulent leaves.

#### 1. With a Regular Flower.

**1.** **Peony** <note>original: *Paeonia*</note>, the characteristics of which are very large rose-like flowers, thick or tuberous roots, seed-horns <term>cornicula</term> that are curved back and woolly, and rather large, round seeds.

This plant belongs to the genus of monocotyledons <note>Plants that sprout with a single seed-leaf. Ray is noting an exception in his classification here.</note>. However, since no other monocotyledon is many-podded, we have seen fit to refer it to this group.

**2.** **White Hellebore** <note>original: *Helleborus albus*; now known as *Veratrum album*</note>, the characteristics of which are veined leaves, furrowed with ridges and appearing as if pleated; six-petaled flowers that are "naked," or lacking a calyx; usually three pods or sheaths follow each flower, containing seeds lying one above the other, similar to a grain of wheat and surrounded by a papery wing.

In my *Method* and *History of Plants*, being too trusting of Parkinson <note>John Parkinson (1567–1650), an English botanist and herbalist.</note>, I arranged this plant among the "Naked-seeded Herbs with three-cornered seeds." However, I have been informed by **Dr. Charles Preston, M.D.** <note>A Scottish botanist and correspondent of Ray.</note>—following **Mr. Tournefort** <note>Joseph Pitton de Tournefort (1656–1708), a French botanist famous for his system of plant classification.</note>—that it is actually *many-podded*. Dr. Preston even sent the fruit itself to me so that no room for doubt remained. Nevertheless, I am uncertain whether I have correctly placed it here, as the flower seems rather to be of the "stamineous" type <note>A term used by Ray for flowers that consist mostly of stamens and lack showy petals.</note>.

**Indian Mallow** <note>original: *Abutilon*</note> with soft leaves like **Marshmallow** <note>original: *Althaea*</note>; it differs from others of this genus by its flowers emerging from the leaf axils, and its two-valved cases like those of the **Hollyhock** <note>original: *Alcea*</note>, with individual seeds solitary in each. It is distinguished from the **Indian Hollyhocks** by its cases being disconnected and only touching, not fused together as they are in those plants. However, due to its agreement in other characteristics and its overall habit and outward appearance, it should probably be moved from here and joined with them.

Note that the pods in this genus are two-valved and contain solitary seeds; therefore, the defining characteristic of the "Many-podded plants" given at the beginning does not fit it—namely, that the cases should gap open only on the inner side and consist of a single layer, containing many seeds.

**3.** **Black Hellebore** <note>original: *Helleborus niger*; also known as the Christmas Rose</note>, the characteristics of which are "fingered" leaves <note>palmate leaves, like the fingers of a hand</note>, and tubular petals of the flowers, surrounding the stamens and the head like a crown. Those broad, showy leaves, which are commonly considered the petals of the flowers, seem rather to constitute the calyx, since they do not fall off or wither but last until the fruit reaches maturity.

**4.** **Winter Aconite** <note>original: *Aconito hyemali*; *Eranthis hyemalis*</note> has the leaves of an **Aconite** and the flower of a **Buttercup** <note>original: *Ranunculi*</note> in the center of the leaf.

**5.** **Goatsbeard** <note>original: *Barba capri*; likely *Aruncus dioicus*</note> has a five-petaled flower and triangular leaves, divided in the manner of the **Umbellifers** <note>Plants in the carrot/parsley family with umbrella-like flower clusters.</note>.

**6.** **Buttercup-like False Hellebore** <note>original: *Pseudo-helleborus Ranunculoides*</note> of **Mr. Bobart** <note>Jacob Bobart the Younger (1641–1719), an English botanist and curator of the Oxford Botanic Garden.</note>. The characteristics of which are flowers spread out in the manner of a Hellebore, naked, with tubes such as

<header>METHOD OF PLANTS</header>

Those which differ from **Black Hellebore** <note>original: *Helleboro nigro*</note> are gifted with several pods containing somewhat round seeds, and have individual leaves sitting on their own stalks; these are roughly circular in outline, some being whole and others jagged <note>original: *laciniata*; having deep, irregular divisions</note>.

To this genus **Mr. Bobart** <note>Jacob Bobart the Younger (1641–1719), an English botanist and superintendent of the Oxford Botanic Garden.</note> refers the following: 1. **Marsh Marigold** <note>original: *Caltham palustrem*</note>. 2. **Globe Flower** <note>original: *Ranunculum globosum*</note>, which we consider to be distinct genera. 3. **Mountain Crowfoot** with an Aconite leaf and a larger white flower <note>original: *Ranunculum montanum Aconiti folio*</note>. 4. **Mountain Crowfoot** with an Aconite leaf and a smaller white flower.

7. **Marsh Marigold** <note>original: *Caltha palustris*</note> has a flower like a Buttercup <note>original: *Ranunculi*</note>, but it is "naked" without a calyx <note>the green outer protective layer of a flower</note>; the pods are arranged in a radiating pattern, and the leaves are whole and somewhat round.

8. **Globe Flower** <note>original: *Ranunculo globoso*</note> has leaves like Aconite <note>Monkshood</note>, and a flower approaching that of a Buttercup; it is naked, with concave petals that are slightly turned inward so that they mimic a sitting globe—hence its name.

9. **Lesser Starry Water-Plantain** <note>original: *Plantago aquatica minor stellata*; now known as *Damasonium alisma*</note> agrees with the Lesser Water-Plantain in its leaves and its three-petaled flowers; it differs, however, in its thin, membrane-like pods which are arranged in a star shape, with many following each flower.

10. **Flowering Rush** <note>original: *Butomus* or *Juncus floridus*</note>. The characteristics of this are grassy, triangular leaves and naked stems supporting clusters <term>umbellas</term> <note>a flower cluster where stalks spread from a common center like umbrella ribs</note> of flowers at the top; it grows in water. <insert>see page 191, line 13.</insert>

### Plants with a Regular Flower and Two Pods <note>original: *Bifiliqua*</note>.

1. **Dogbane** <note>original: *Apocynum*</note>, the characteristics of which are twin pods for every flower, each being a single capsule with one valve, opening lengthwise from the inner side; within these are seeds with hanging downy fluff <note>original: *lanugine*</note>, resting upon a nourishing stalk in the manner of roof tiles <note>original: *imbricum modo*; overlapping</note>, as described by **Hermann** <note>Paul Hermann (1646–1695), a German physician and botanist.</note>. It pours out a milky sap, and the leaves grow in opposite pairs on the stems.

**Mr. Tournefort** admits in his *Elements of Botany, page 77*, that Dogbane possesses flowers of two kinds or forms. If, therefore, the generic characteristic must be taken from the shape of the flower, why does he not divide the plants called Dogbanes into two genera?

The same author makes **Silk-vine** <note>original: *Periploca*</note> a distinct genus from Dogbane, the characteristic of which is a flower cut all the way to the base into five segments <note>original: *lacinias*</note>, arranged in the shape of a star. Strictly speaking, he says, Silk-vine ought to be placed among the herbs with star-shaped flowers (*en rosette*). Why then does he not arrange it there? Instead, he advises that it should by no means be separated from Dogbane and Milkweed, despite the shape of the flower. Does it not follow from this that he himself recognizes that plants which differ in the shape of their flowers can still belong to the same genus, and that the form of the flower—if other features do not match—is not sufficient to distinguish genera? On page 112, he admits that the flower of **Viper’s Bugloss** <note>original: *Echii*</note> is not entirely regular, yet he does not believe that genus should be removed from Class 2, Section 4, a part of whose definition is having a regular flower.

2. **Milkweed** <note>original: *Asclepias*</note> differs from Dogbane in hardly any other respect than that the sap...

...since it does not yield a milky sap; for two pods follow each small flower, not one as I wrote in my *History of Plants* <note>original: *Historia*; referring to Ray's own *Historia Plantarum*</note>.

3. **Periwinkle** <note>original: *Clematis Daphnoides*; now usually classified as *Vinca*</note>. The characteristics of this plant are long, creeping runners; leaves with the color and consistency of ivy; a large flower; and pods that are paired at each flower, joined at both ends, narrow, and containing two or three oblong seeds with no attached down <note>original: *lanugine*; the fluffy hairs often found on seeds like those of a dandelion or milkweed</note>.

### 2. Many-podded plants with less succulent leaves and irregular flowers.

1. **Dittany** <note>original: *Fraxinella*; also known as the Burning Bush or *Dictamnus albus*</note>, whose characteristics include many stamens in the flower, which are very long and curved backward; flowers arranged in spikes; and individual sheaths enclosing a capsule which, upon maturity, opens into two parts or valves. These valves roll back, receding from one another, and eject large, black, shining seeds—as noted by **Mr. Tournefort** <note>Joseph Pitton de Tournefort (1656–1708), a French botanist whose system of classification was a contemporary rival to Ray's.</note>. It has pinnate leaves <note>leaflets arranged on both sides of a common stalk</note> like those of the **Ash tree** <note>original: *Fraxini*</note>, from which it takes its name.

2. **Monkshood** <note>original: *Aconitum*</note>; its characteristics are leaves that are roughly circular in outline and jaggedly divided; hooded flowers; and wrinkled seeds. Its quality, at least in most species, is harmful and poisonous.

3. **Stavesacre** <note>original: *Staphis agria*</note> agrees with the **Monkshoods** in its leaves and pods, and even in its medicinal powers; however, its flower resembles the **Larkspur**, to which it is more closely related by its seed than to Monkshood.

4. **Columbine** <note>original: *Aquilegiæ*</note>. Its characteristics are hanging flowers composed of alternating flat and horn-shaped petals (the "horns" being beaked or curved back); leaves divided in the manner of **Umbel-bearing plants** <note>original: *Umbelliferarum*; the family including carrots and parsley, characterized by umbrella-like flower clusters</note>; and black, shiny seeds. I consider the "star-flowered" Columbine and the "double-flowered" Columbine (composed only of horn-shaped petals) to be mere varieties, not distinct species.

5. **Larkspur** <note>original: *Delphinii*</note>. Its characteristics are leaves dissected into thin segments; flowers gifted with a spur; and black, three-sided seeds.

# Angiospermous herbs—those that bear seed vessels—with a single-petaled flower are either of a uniform or irregular shape.

<image-desc>A taxonomic chart categorizing "Angiospermous herbs" into two main groups using a system of nested brackets. The primary division is between plants with "Uniform or regular" flowers and those with "Difform or irregular" flowers. Each category is further subdivided by characteristics of the leaf or petal shape, and the type of seed vessel (one-capsuled, two-capsuled, or many-capsuled), with specific botanical examples like Bindweed and Snapdragon.</image-desc>

- **Uniform or regular flowers, of various genera:**
    - Flowers that are whole, or cut into less deep segments; such as **BINDWEED** <note>original: *Convolvulus*</note>, **TOBACCO** <note>original: *Nicotiana*</note>, etc.
    - Flowers appearing to have four petals, or four-petaled in form; such as **SPEEDWELL** <note>original: *Veronica*</note>, etc.
    - Flowers appearing to have five petals, or five-petaled in form:
        - **One-capsuled** <term>unicapsulares: plants where the seeds are contained within a single seed-vessel or pod</term>; in which the seat of the seeds is in the middle, protected on the outside by the vessel; **PIMPERNEL** <note>original: *Anagallis*</note>, etc.
        - **Two-capsuled** <term>bicapsulares</term>; where the vessel is divided into two compartments; as in **LESSER CENTAURY** <note>original: *Centaurium minus*</note>, etc.
        - **Many-capsuled** <term>multicapsulares</term>; where the vessel is divided into many—that is, more than two—compartments or cases; **GREEK VALERIAN** <note>original: *Valeriana Graeca*; also known as Jacob's Ladder</note>, etc.
- **Difform or irregular flowers:**
    - Of various shapes; **BIRTHWORT** <note>original: *Aristolochia*</note>, etc.
    - Helmet-shaped or lipped; **COW-WHEAT** <note>original: *Melampyrum*</note>, etc.
    - Representing a gaping mouth <note>original: *rictum exprimente*; referring to flowers that look like an open mouth, such as snapdragons</note>:
        - Provided with a spur <note>a slender, nectar-containing projection at the back of the flower</note>; **TOADFLAX** <note>original: *Linaria*</note>.
        - Lacking a spur; **SNAPDRAGON** <note>original: *Antirrhinum*</note>, etc.

# THE NINETEENTH GENUS,
#### or Herbs
# VESSEL-BEARING [ANGIOSPERMS] WITH A SINGLE-PETALED FLOWER.
## I.
## Of a Uniform or Regular shape.
### 1. Whole or divided into less deep segments.

These, besides the cup of the flower <term>calyx: the outer green part of a flower that protects the bud</term>, possess a vessel or capsule in which the seed is enclosed; this vessel is simple or singular for each individual flower, though it is sometimes divided into compartments <note>original: *loculamenta*</note>.

1. **HENBANE** <note>original: *Hyoscyamus*</note>, whose characteristics are: leaves arranged alternately on the stems, soft and greasy to the touch; the calyx is divided into five pointed teeth; the flower is divided into five segments and swells at the base into a "belly"; the female vessel <note>the seed pod</note> is shaped like a cup, has two capsules, and is covered by a lid which falls off of its own accord upon maturity; it possesses narcotic and poisonous properties.

2. **TOBACCO** <note>original: *Nicotiana*</note>, characteristics: the flower expands in width from an oblong tube, with a five-sided or five-parted edge; the female vessel is two-capsuled and filled inside with very tiny and numerous seeds; the leaves have even margins (meaning they are not notched or cut), and are greasy and woolly.

3. **GENTIAN** <note>original: *Gentiana*</note>, whose characteristics are: veined leaves, paired opposite each other on the stems; basket-shaped flowers <note>original: *calathoides*</note> with the edge usually divided into several segments that look like leaves; the follicles <note>seed pods</note> are two-capsuled, containing seeds that are flat and leaf-like in most species.

Mr. <note>original: *D.*, abbreviation for *Dominus* or Master</note> **Tournefort** <note>Joseph Pitton de Tournefort (1656–1708), a famous French botanist who was a contemporary and sometimes rival of the author</note> acknowledges that the flowers of the Gentians differ in form; nevertheless, he reduces all Gentians to the same genus, presumably so he would not be forced to include among the **Lesser Gentians** <note>original: *Gentianellis*</note> certain species that were larger than the Gentians themselves, which seemed absurd to him. But why, to avoid this inconvenience, could he not have given a new name to the Lesser Gentians, since he is otherwise not sparing with new names?

4. **THORN-APPLE** <note>original: *Stramonium*</note>, characteristics: the flower rises from an oblong tube and is basket-shaped; the seed receptacle is large and thorny, divided into four compartments; the seeds are compressed and usually kidney-shaped.

<margin>See page 195, line 19.</margin>
5. **BINDWEED** <note>original: *Convolvulus*</note>. Its characteristics are: a bell-shaped flower with a whole and usually turned-back edge; the seed receptacle is somewhat round and thin-skinned. It is known for climbing by its stems and for [being] with a milky juice...

...to flow <note>original: *scatere*; likely referring to the presence of milky sap</note>, and to have a seed vessel divided into three compartments <note>original: *loculamenta*</note> are characteristics that suit most species of this kind, though not all. **Mr. Tournefort** <note>Joseph Pitton de Tournefort (1656–1708), a French botanist</note> writes that he possesses several species of **Bindweed** <note>original: *Convolvulus*</note> whose fruits have only one cavity.

6. **Alpine Snowbell** <note>original: *Soldanella Alpina*</note>, characteristics: upright stems, round leaves, and rounded, upright seed pods <note>original: *siliquæ*</note>; but especially the bell-shaped flowers with a fringed margin.

7. **Bellflower** <note>original: *Campanula*</note>, whose characteristics are: a bell-shaped flower usually cut into five segments <note>original: *lacinias*</note> at the edges, sitting atop the fruit; a seed vessel divided into three compartments; and flowing with a milky juice <term>latex: a milky fluid found in many plants, often exposed when the stem is broken</term>: which is also common to the following five genera.

8. **Canterbury Bells** <note>original: *Medium* or *Viola Mariana*</note> differs from the **Bellflower** by its fruit being divided into five cells and the edges of the flower being less deeply cut. **Mr. Tournefort** considers the *Bellflower with Viper’s Bugloss leaves* <note>original: *Campanulam foliis Echii*; referenced from Caspar Bauhin's *Pinax*</note> to be a species of this.

*Blue Umbrella Throatwort* <note>original: *Trachelium umbellatum azureum*</note> of Pone is made a distinct genus by **Mr. Tournefort** because its fruit is membranous, with three rounded angles, and divided into three cells filled with very tiny seeds.

9. **Horned Rampion** <note>original: *Rapunculus corniculatus*</note>, characteristics: the flower is cut into five long, narrow segments; the flowers are densely crowded into spikes, bundles, or heads, and in some species, they are gathered into a sort of "aggregate" or total flower, which also has a cup <term>calyx: the green outer part of a flower</term> beneath it.

10. **Venus's Looking-glass** <note>original: *Speculum Veneris*</note> differs from others of this genus by its flower being cut into five wide segments and being more expanded than in the **Bellflower**, but especially by its seed vessel, which is oblong and extended into a pod.

11. **Cardinal Flower** <note>original: *Rapunculus galeatus* or *Flos Cardinalis*; called *Rapuntium* by Tournefort</note>. In some species, the flower is an open tube, expanded at the top into the shape of a channel, then cut into five parts like fingers. The tube of the flower is filled by a certain sheath <note>original: *vaginâ*</note> enclosing the style <term>style: the stalk of the female part of a flower</term> which rises from the middle of the cup. The fruit is similar to the **Common Rampion**.

In our *History of Plants* <note>original: *Historia Plantarum*</note>, page 731 and following, we reduced the five preceding genera to the same single genus because of the similarity of the seed vessel, the similar position of the flowers in relation to the seed vessel, and because they flowed with milk. However, due to the dissimilarity of the flowers and some differences in the fruit in some cases, we now separate them: although all agree closely with the genus mentioned above.

**Mr. Tournefort**, on page 92, Class 1, Section 7, includes the **Horned Rampion**, whose flower, when expanded, resembles a star of five rays and bears no similarity to a bell; even though part of the title of that Section is, *To have a bell-shaped flower...*

### 2. Enangiospermous Herbs with a uniform single-petaled flower resembling four petals, or "Tetrapetaloid."
<term>Enangiospermous: plants that have their seeds enclosed within a seed vessel or capsule, rather than lying naked.</term>

1. **Speedwell** <note>original: *Veronica*</note>, the characteristics of which are: a single-petaled flower divided almost to the base <note>original: *ad unguem*; literally "to the claw," referring to the narrow base of a petal</note> into four segments resembling as many leaves; its calyx <note>the green outer protective layer of a flower</note> does not fall off with the flower but remains until the seed reaches maturity; seed vessels are compressed and divided into two compartments like those of **Cress** <note>original: *Thlaspeos*</note>. It differs from Cress not only by its single-petaled flower but because its calyx remains after the flower has fallen, and because the flower stalks emerge from the leaf axils <note>original: *sinubus*; the angles formed between the leaf and the stem</note>. The flower is not perfectly regular or uniform, as one of its segments is narrower than the others.
2. *Smaller Henbit* <note>original: *Morsus gallinae minor*; likely referring to a type of Chickweed or Speedwell</note> differs from **Speedwell** by having a regular flower with equal petals and a more swollen, almost testicle-shaped fruit.
3. **Dodder** <note>original: *Cuscuta*</note>, the characteristics of which are: leafless stems; white, single-petaled flowers divided into four (rarely five) sharp segments, held by a green, succulent calyx that is likewise divided into four parts; and round fruits containing four oblong-rounded seeds.

### 3. Enangiospermous Herbs with a uniform single-petaled flower resembling five petals, or "Pentapetaloid."

->a. Single-capsuled plants, in which the seat of the seeds is in the middle, protected on the outside by a vessel.<-

1. **Pimpernel** <note>original: *Anagallis*</note>, the characteristics of which are: leaves growing in pairs opposite each other on the stem; single flowers in each leaf axil hanging from long, thin stalks; and seed capsules that, upon maturity, burst open horizontally or transversely across the middle <note>this refers to circumscissile dehiscence, where the top of the capsule pops off like a lid</note>.
2. *Cowslip* or **Primrose** <note>original: *Paralysis* sive *Primula veris*</note>, the characteristics of which are: stems bare of leaves; flowers expanding from a long tube into five two-cleft <note>forked</note> segments; and their calyxes are whole, long, concave, and channeled <note>original: *striati*</note>. The leaves are wrinkled and of a less thick texture than the leaves of the **Bear's Ear**. The number of segments in the flower is perhaps not constant, as is the case in almost every other kind of flower, but the usual and natural number is five <note>original: *quinarius*</note>.
3. **Bear's Ear** <note>original: *Auricula ursi*; a species of Primula</note> differs from the **Primrose** by having smoother and thicker leaves, a shorter flower calyx so that the tubes of the flowers appear almost naked, and the beginnings of some small leaves at the top of the stem from which the flower stalks emerge. <gloss>See page 191, line 24.</gloss>

4. **Rock-jasmine** <note>original: *Androsace*</note> is distinguished from **Bear’s-ear Primrose** <note>original: *Auricula ursi*</note> because the base <note>original: *fundo*; the bottom of the flower tube</note> of its flower is not at all perforated like that of the latter, as observed by **Mr. Tournefort** <note>Joseph Pitton de Tournefort (1656–1708), a French botanist</note>. **Mr. Hermann** <note>Paul Hermann (1646–1695), a German physician and botanist</note> ascribes to it round seed vessels; large, five-cleft, spreading calyxes; small flowers resembling five petals <note>original: *pentapetaloides*</note> arranged in an umbel <note>a cluster of flowers where the stalks spread from a common center like umbrella ribs</note>; and small, veined, **Plantain-like** leaves with notched edges <note>original: *crenata*</note>.

5. **American Cortusa**, the characteristics of which according to **Mr. Volckamer** <note>Johann Georg Volckamer (1662–1744), a German physician and botanist</note> are: perfect, uniform, single-petaled flowers, divided into five parts and arranged in a spike, which are very small; several seeds (or an uncertain number), small, oblong, shining, and black, enclosed in a simple, parchment-like seed-case <note>original: *pericarpio membranaceo*</note> that naturally splits open into two keel-shaped parts <note>original: *carinas*</note> upon reaching maturity.

6. **Yellow Loosestrife** <note>original: *Lysimachia lutea*</note>; its characteristics are willow-like oblong leaves and a somewhat round capsule (made of two small vessels, as noted by **Hermann**) whose tip opens into several parts at maturity.

To **Yellow Loosestrife**, **Mr. Tournefort** relates **Greater Yellow Moneywort** <note>original: *Nummulariam majorem luteam*</note> and **Yellow Wood Pimpernel** <note>original: *Anagallidem luteam nemorum*</note>. But in their overall appearance <note>original: *tota facie*; their general habit or growth form</note>, these plants differ too much from one another to be referred to the same genus.

7. **Moneywort** <note>original: *Nummularia*</note>, so called because its round leaf shape rivals a coin <note>original: *nummi æmula*</note>, is distinguished from others of this kind by its creeping runners and its individual flowers emerging from the leaf axils <note>original: *foliorum alis*; the "wings" or angles where the leaf meets the stem</note> (having round containers hidden within five-cleft calyxes, according to **Hermann**). These containers (as observed by **Mr. Preston** <note>likely George Preston, a Scottish botanist</note>) open into several pointed parts, containing many tiny seeds attached to a central core <note>original: *placentæ mediæ*; the placenta is the part of the ovary where seeds are attached</note>. The fruits are too small for me to have ever been able to observe these parts in them.

8. **Sea-milkwort** <note>original: *Glaux exigua maritima*</note>, the characteristics of which are: small flowers emerging from the leaf axils, naked <note>lacking a calyx or petals, or in this case, perhaps lacking a distinct corolla</note>, five-parted, leaving behind parchment-like capsules that open at the top into several parts and contain a central core inside loaded with several tiny seeds. **Mr. Tournefort**.

9. **Bogbean** or **Buckbean** <note>original: *Trifolium paludosum, Menianthes*</note>. It reveals itself by its leaves, which have the shape and size of Bean leaves and grow in threes on a single stalk; by its beautiful flowers in a cluster <note>original: *thyrso*</note>, which are white on the inside with curly, downy filaments; and by its somewhat round, two-valved seed containers with a single cavity inside. Its place of birth is in watery areas.

10. **Water Pimpernel** <note>original: *Samolus Valerandi*</note>, or **Lobelius’s third aquatic Pimpernel**, is characterized by somewhat round leaves that are not notched; small flowers mimicking five petals; and somewhat round capsules within five-parted calyxes, which open into several pointed parts and are filled with small, reddish seeds attached to a central core.

**Mr. Tournefort** distinguishes **Water Pimpernel** from **Yellow Loosestrife** because its fruit takes its origin from both the pistil and the calyx together, which is indeed a sufficient mark of distinction; but how it agrees with...

I do not see the general mark of this section—namely, that in the genera subject to it, the **style** <note>original: *stylus*; the stalk of the plant's female organ that receives pollen</note> turns into the fruit.

Its characteristics are a bell-shaped flower divided into five segments and a star-shaped calyx <note>the outer protective envelope of the flower</note>; the fruit is nearly spherical, opening from top to bottom into two hemispheres, enclosing a single, almost round seed. According to **Mr. Tournefort**.

12. **Water Violet** <note>original: *Viola aquatica*; specifically *Hottonia palustris*</note>; its characteristics are feathered leaves, mostly submerged in water, and bare stems with many showy flowers like the **Snowflake** <note>original: *Leucoii*</note>, which are single-petaled but split almost to the base into five segments so that they appear to have five petals. 13. **Wintergreen with a Chickweed flower** <note>original: *Pyrola Alsines flore*; now known as *Trientalis europaea* or Chickweed Wintergreen</note>, which bears many leaves at the top of a small stem like an umbel <note>a cluster where stalks spring from a single point</note>. The flowers sit individually on thin little stalks, star-shaped and single-petaled (as far as I remember), divided into five segments.

As I have never seen the fruit of this plant either, I am no less uncertain of its place than I am of the preceding one.

### b. Two-Chambered Plants.
<note>original: *Bicapsulares*; plants whose seed vessels are divided into two internal compartments</note>

1. **Lesser Centaury** <note>original: *Centaurium minus*</note>, the characteristics of which are flowers spreading from a long tube into five sharp segments, a cylindrical seed vessel divided into two compartments containing very tiny seeds, and a notable bitterness <note>a classic medicinal trait of the Gentian family</note>.

2. **Yellow Perfoliate Centaury** <note>original: *Centaurium luteum perfoliatum*; *Blackstonia perfoliata*</note>; its characteristics are leaves situated opposite each other on the stem and fused into one (as in the **Teasel**), yellow flowers divided almost to the base into eight segments (mimicking eight leaves), and roundish, two-valved capsules filled with very tiny seeds.

3. **Mullein** <note>original: *Verbascum*</note>; its characteristics are leaves arranged in an alternating order on the stems, flowers crowded into long clusters <note>original: *thyrsis*</note> that are not spread out horizontally but rather held in an upright position, and two-valved capsules that are conical or top-shaped <note>original: *turbinatae*</note>.

4. **Moth Mullein** <note>original: *Blattaria*</note> differs from **Mullein** in almost nothing except the spherical shape of the capsule (whereas the Mullein’s is top-shaped, as we said). One might add that the flowers are more spaced out in the spikes and the color of the leaves is a brighter green, though this is not constant or common to all species. <insert>see page 191, line 24.</insert>

2. **Wood Sorrel** <note>original: *Trifolium acetosum*, *Oxys*; now known as *Oxalis acetosella*</note> differs from all other plants by notable characteristics: namely, three heart-shaped leaves on the same stalk and an acidic taste; the flowers are borne singly on each stalk, and the seed vessel is five-sided (divided into five chambers according to **Tournefort** <note>Joseph Pitton de Tournefort (1656–1708), a French botanist who developed an early system of plant classification</note>). This vessel, when ripe, bursts open at the slightest touch and forcibly ejects the seeds. (The seeds are wrapped in a kind of covering or "membrane," which by its contraction expels them quite far from the fruit, according to **Tournefort**.)

3. **Mallow** <note>original: *Malva*</note>, the characteristics of which are a single-petaled flower divided nearly to the base <note>original: *ad unguem*; literally "to the nail"</note> into five segments, and seeds arranged in the form of a small wheel or a little cheese.

*Mr. Tournefort, in his "Elements of Botany," page 81, says that Morison and all the writers he himself had read affirm that Mallow flowers have five petals. But truly, if he had read our **History**, he could have found it observed by us long ago that the Mallow flower is single-petaled, on page 597 in the description of the **Curled Mallow** and on page 599 in the description of the **Common Mallow**.*

I have included this plant in my **Method** and **History of Plants** among the "many-seeded naked-seeded plants" <note>original: *plantis gymnospermis polyspermis*; referring to plants whose seeds appear to be uncovered</note>, not because I mistook the capsule for a grain out of ignorance, as **Mr. Tournefort** supposes. I knew well that **Caesalpinus** <note>Andrea Caesalpinus (1519–1603), an Italian physician and botanist who pioneered scientific classification</note> attributed individual little pouches to each Mallow seed and distinguished them from truly naked seeds, as is clear from the summary of the **Caesalpinian method** which I added to my **New Method of Plants, published in the year 1682**. However, I considered as "naked seeds" all those that, upon ripening, separate and fall away individually and spontaneously from their mother plant, as I have explained more fully elsewhere. But although it agrees with naked-seeded plants in this respect, since it agrees with the **Indian Hollyhock** <note>original: *Alcea Indica*</note> in the form of its flower, its pistil, the seeds themselves when stripped of their outer covering, and in the appearance of the leaves and the whole plant—as well as in its softening <note>original: *vi emolliente*; a reference to the mucilaginous, soothing properties of the plant</note> power—I acknowledge it should by no means be separated from it, according to the rule I prescribed for myself and others.

4. **Hollyhock** <note>original: *Alcea*</note> differs from **Mallow** by its dissected or jagged leaves.

5. **Marsh-mallow** <note>original: *Althaea*</note> differs from the same by its softer and more hoary <note>original: *incanis*; covered in white, fuzzy hairs</note> leaves. In the **History of Plants**, I made the more elongated and less round leaf the distinguishing mark of the **Marsh-mallow**, nor do I yet see a reason why I should reject it. For the plant first called **Marsh-mallow**, which is known by this name in the writings of physicians, in the apothecaries' shops, and among the common people themselves, has a more elongated leaf. Furthermore, the first species in any genus is the measure of the others. Secondly, the shape of the leaf seems to be of more value for distinguishing genera than color or softness. Even herbalists themselves count the **Venetian Tree Mallow** and our own species among the **Mallows**, even though they have soft and hoary leaves, because of the nearly round shape of their leaves. We indeed [refer to] the botanists who first observed them...

# CORRECTIONS AND ADDITIONS

Following those who preserved and described them, we included several species having sub-round leaves under the chapter on **Marsh-mallow** <note>original: *Althaea*</note> due to excessive haste and lack of thought.

**Tournefort** distinguishes **Marsh-mallow** from **Mallow** <note>original: *Malva*</note> for no other reason than to avoid departing from common usage. Thus, on page 104, he distinguishes **Buck’s-horn Plantain** <note>original: *Coronopus*</note> from **Plantain** <note>original: *Plantago*</note>, and on page 131, **Dragon Arum** <note>original: *Dracontium*</note> from **Cuckoo-pint** <note>original: *Arum*</note> because of their deeply lobed leaves; he does this, of course, because these genera are accepted and established by common usage. On page 94, he distinguishes **Bedstraw** <note>original: *Gallium*</note> from **Cleavers** <note>original: *Aparine*</note> by their smooth leaves; and **Crosswort** <note>original: *Cruciata*</note> from both by the number of leaves at each joint. For, strictly speaking (he says), they ought not to be distinguished. On page 87, he says **Cucumber**, **Watermelon**, and **Melon** <note>original: *Cucumis, Citrullus, Melo*</note> ought to constitute only one genus strictly speaking, if common usage did not oppose it. But why is he so scrupulous in these cases not to depart from common usage, when in others of greater importance he does not fear to innovate? Indeed, he boldly and without apology reduces **Dittany** to **Oregano**, **Ground Ivy** to **Calamint**, **Woad-leaved Pepperwort** and **Horseradish** to **Scurvy-grass**, and **Wood Sage** and **Water Germander** to **Germander** <note>original: *Dictamnum* to *Origanum*, *Hedera terrestrem* to *Calamintham*, *Lepidium glastifolium* & *Raphanum rusticanum* to *Cochleariam*, *Scorodonia* & *Scordium* to *Chamaedryn*</note>.

Allow me to subjoin what the most illustrious man, **Paul Hermann**, has to say about the division of **Mallows** in the recently published *Paradisus Batavus* on page 4:

> The plants commonly called **Mallow-like** (he says), or those noted by the names **Mallow**, **Hollyhock**, and **Marsh-mallow** <note>original: *Malva, Alcea, Althaea*</note>, can be divided into two primary groups. The first contains those that bear <term>naked seeds</term> <note>Seeds that appear to have no outer fruit or pod covering them</note>; the other contains those that have seeds enclosed in capsules. The plants of the first group are called, in an absolute sense, **Mallows**, **Hollyhocks**, and **Marsh-mallows**. Those of the latter are called **Indian Hollyhocks**. **Robert Morison** calls the species of the first group **Mallows** and **Hollyhocks**, but the latter group he calls **Marsh-mallows**.

It was also our opinion that the plants commonly called **Mallows**, **Hollyhocks**, and **Marsh-mallows** produce naked seeds, because their seeds, clothed in that outer covering which some maintain is a <term>capsule</term> <note>A dry fruit that opens to release seeds</note>, fall away or separate from the mother plant individually and of their own accord. But since more curious observers of plants—**Andrea Caesalpino** of the last century, and **Mr. Tournefort** of the present—maintain that the outer covering is a capsule containing the seed and not a part of the seed itself, I will not start a quarrel with their followers. For I do not think it of such great importance to contend fiercely over this matter; let everyone, as far as I am concerned, enjoy their own judgment. **Mr. Hermann** continues:

> *It seemed best to us to follow the opinion of **Morison**, which has been received by many moderns, and to enroll the **Marsh-mallow** of the apothecaries <note>original: *Officinarum Althaeam*; plants used in medical shops</note> (called by others **Ibiscus** or **Bismalva**) into the former group, namely the genus of **Mallows**, and to call it by the name of the **Soft and Hoary Mallow**, or as **Morison** preferred, the **Marsh Mallow**, because it does not differ from Mallows except that it is softer, hairier, more gray-white, and fuller of <term>mucilage</term> <note>A thick, gluey substance produced by plants, often used in medicine to soothe tissues</note>, and thus in all its parts...*
