### OF OBSCURE TERMS.

There is also a genus of plants called *Cotyledon* <note>original: "Cotyledon"; a genus of succulent plants with cup-shaped leaves</note>.

<term>CULM</term> <note>original: "Culmus"</note>. The stalk of Grains and Grasses, which is jointed, unlike the stems of other grass-leaved plants with "Stamineous" flowers <note>flowers consisting mainly of stamens, lacking prominent petals</note>. Hence the order of *Culmiferous Grass-leaved plants*, regarding which see page 124.

<term>DIFFORM or IRREGULAR FLOWER</term>. A flower whose parts are not similar to one another if it consists of a single petal; or, if it is composed of more than one petal, the petals differ from one another in shape, position, or both. See <term>UNIFORM FLOWER</term>.

<term>DIGITATE LEAF</term>. A leaf that is divided into several segments, like so many fingers, reaching all the way to the little stalk [petiole]. Such is the leaf of the Lupin, Hemp, etc. <note>From "digitus," the Latin word for finger</note>.

<term>DISK or DISCOID FLOWER</term>. A compound flower made up of many small tubular florets arranged into a single surface, whether it eventually dissolves into downy fluff [pappus] or not. It is either equipped with small "beards" or rays, or it lacks them. The former is said by Mr. Rivinus <note>Augustus Quirinus Rivinus (1652–1723), a pioneer in botanical classification</note> to be composed of "regular and irregular florets." That which lacks the ray-beards, he calls a composite of "regular florets" only. Mr. Tournefort <note>Joseph Pitton de Tournefort (1656–1708), a French botanist famous for his genus-based system</note> calls this a "flosculous" flower.

<term>ENANGIOSPERMOUS or ANGIOSPERMOUS PLANT</term>. A plant whose seeds are enclosed in a small vessel. The word is composed of the Greek *angeion* <note>original: "ἀγγεῖον"</note>, meaning "vessel," and *sperma* <note>original: "σπέρμα"</note>, meaning "seed."

<term>FLOSCULOUS FLOWER</term>. A discoid flower that lacks "beards" or rays.

<term>HELMETED FLOWER</term> <note>original: "Galeatus"</note>, also called by some a <term>LABIATE</term> <note>lipped</note> flower. A non-uniform, single-petaled flower usually split into two lips, the upper of which is called the <term>Galea</term> <note>Helmet</note>, which it resembles in shape. The lower lip is called the <term>Beard</term> by Mr. Rivinus.

<term>GLUME</term> <note>original: "Gluma"</note>. The husk or small leafy casing of the grain in Cereal crops.

<term>GYMNOSPERMOUS PLANT</term>. One that bears a naked seed. See <term>NAKED SEED</term> <note>From the Greek "gymnos" (naked) and "sperma" (seed)</note>.

<term>IRREGULAR FLOWER</term>. See <term>DIFFORM FLOWER</term>.

<term>MANE</term> <note>original: "Juba"</note>. A reed-like plume or head of flowers loosely spread out, such as is found in Millet.

<term>CATKIN, AMENT, or NUT-CONE</term> <note>original: "Julus, Amentum, Nucamentum"</note>. A cluster of small petal-less flowers, usually sterile, shaped like a worm and hanging from trees like a leather strap. Hence the *Catkin-bearing Trees* [Juliferae], for which see page 140.
Note: In the Willow genus, some individuals bear fertile catkins.

<term>LABIATE FLOWER</term>. See <term>HELMETED FLOWER</term>.

<term>LEGUME or LEGUMINOUS PLANTS</term>. Those which produce a "Butterfly-like" [papilionaceous] flower. See page 191. <note>This group includes peas and beans; the flowers resemble the wings of a butterfly</note>.

<term>STONE-PLANT</term> <note>original: "Lithophyton"</note>. See page 3. <note>Historically used for coral or calcified sea-growths that appeared to be "stone plants"</note>.

<meta>catchword: LOBOS <note>original: "ΛΟΒΟΣ"</note></meta>

<summary>This page continues a botanical dictionary, defining terms related to flower shapes (discoid, labiate, irregular), leaf structures (digitate), and seed types (angiosperm, gymnosperm). It references the classification systems of prominent 17th-century botanists like Rivinus and Tournefort.</summary>
<keywords>culm, irregular flower, digitate leaf, discoid flower, angiosperm, gymnosperm, catkin, legume, botanical terminology, Rivinus, Tournefort</keywords>

--- Page 244 ---
<meta>This page continues the alphabetical botanical glossary from page 199. It provides definitions for terms beginning with L, N, O, and P, focusing on leaf structures, seed types, and flower classifications. It maintains the system of referencing earlier pages for more detailed explanations of complex categories like the "Butterfly-shaped" flower.</meta>

->### INTERPRETATION<-

<term>LOBE</term> <note>original: "ΛΟΒΟΣ" (Greek); "Siliqua" (Latin pod)</note>. A segment of a leaf, or a larger partial leaf.
<term>LOBED leaf</term> <note>original: "LOBATUM folium"</note>, which is composed of such *lobes*.
<term>SPIKELET</term> <note>original: "LOCUSTA"; literally "locust," used here in botany for the small flower clusters of grasses</note>. The grain of paniculate grasses wrapped in its husk. See page 176.

<term>CATKIN</term> <note>original: "NUCAMENTUM"</note>. See <term>JULUS</term>.
<term>NAKED FLOWER</term> <note>original: "NUDUS FLOS"</note>. One that lacks a calyx <note>the green outer envelope of a flower</note>.
A <term>Naked Discoid Flower</term> is one that is not "rayed"—that is, it lacks the small "beards" or petals around the edge.
<term>NAKED SEED</term> <note>original: "NUDUM SEMEN"</note>. A seed that is not enclosed in a vessel or capsule. Sometimes it is entirely *naked*, and sometimes it is hidden within the perianth <note>the floral envelope</note>. A plant that bears naked seeds is called <term>GYMNOSPERMOUS</term> <note>from the Greek for "naked seed"</note>.

<term>STONE or PIT</term> <note>original: "OS" (bone), "OSSICULUM" (little bone)</note>. The hard, bone-like covering of seeds that is itself covered by fleshy pulp, such as is found in Cherries and Plums.

<term>PANICLE</term> <note>original: "PANICULA"</note>. A branched mane <note>a loose, branching cluster of flowers</note>, especially in Grains and Grasses. See page 176.
<term>BUTTERFLY-SHAPED FLOWER</term> <note>original: "PAPILIONACEUS FLOS"; from "papilio," the Latin for butterfly</note>. See page 101.
<term>DOWN or FLUFF</term> <note>original: "PAPPUS"</note>. The woolly hair attached to certain seeds, as in Hawkweed, Aster, and Thistle. A *Pappose* seed is one equipped with such fluff. Plants that produce these kinds of seeds are called *Pappose* and *Pappescent*.
<term>STALK or PETIOLE</term> <note>original: "PEDICULUS, PETIOLUS"</note>. That from which a leaf, flower, or fruit hangs.
<term>PINNATE or FEATHER-LIKE LEAF</term> <note>original: "PENNATUM aut PINNATUM FOLIUM"</note>. A leaf composed of several leaflets attached opposite each other on the same central rib, usually with a single leaflet at the end.
If these partial leaves [leaflets] are quite large, the entire leaf is called <term>LOBED</term>.
<term>PERFECT FLOWER</term>. See <term>PETAL-BEARING FLOWER</term>.
<term>PERIANTH</term>. See <term>CALYX</term>.
<term>PERICARP</term>. The same as "Flesh" [Pulp]. See <term>CARO</term>.
Sometimes it is used more broadly for any covering of the seed.
<term>PERSONATE or MASKED FLOWER</term> <note>original: "PERSONATUS FLOS"; from "persona," a mask</note>. A term used by Tournefort <note>Joseph Pitton de Tournefort (1656–1708), a French botanist</note> for a flower that resembles the "Labiate" [lipped] type, such as the flowers of Toadflax, Snapdragon, Lousewort, Cow-wheat, etc. Following him, we attribute personate flowers to the Purple Ageratum of Dalechampius <note>Jacques Daléchamps (1513–1588), a French physician and botanist</note> and to the Toothwort <note>original: "Clandestina"</note>.

<term>PETAL</term> <note>original: "PETALON" (Greek)</note>. A leaf of the flower.
<term>PETALED, PERFECT, or BRACTEATE FLOWER</term> <note>original: "PETALODES, PERFECTUS, BRACTEATUS FLOS"</note>. A flower constructed of stamens, a style, and a petal or petals, whether it has a perianth or lacks one. Depending on the number of petals of which it consists, a flower is called <term>Monopetalous</term> [1 petal], <term>Dipetalous</term> [2], <term>Tripetalous</term> [3], <term>Tetrapetalous</term> [4], <term>Pentapetalous</term> [5], <term>Hexapetalous</term> [6], or <term>Polypetalous</term> [many petals].

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical botanical glossary from page 200. It covers terms from P to S, focusing on flower structures, fruit types, and seed classifications. It cites prominent botanists like Tournefort, Rivinus, Jungius, and Spigelius to clarify technical definitions.</meta>

->## OF OBSCURE TERMS##<-

**PISTIL.** <note>original: "PISTILLUM"</note> See **STYLE.**

**FLAT-PETALED FLOWER.** <note>original: "PLANIPETALOS FLOS"</note> A composite flower made of pure flat florets that are nonetheless tubular at the bottom. See pages 27 and 29. <term>Tournefort</term> calls these "semi-florets" and the flower composed of them "semi-flosculous"; <term>Rivinus</term> names them a flower composed only of irregular florets.

**POME.** <note>original: "POMUM"</note> A larger fruit of trees consisting of flesh or succulent pulp. Hence **Pomiferous Trees**, which bear such fruit. See pages 143 and 153.
Regarding **Pomiferous Herbs**, see page 70.

**KERNEL or STONE.** <note>original: "Π Υ Ρ Η Ν" (Greek: Pyren)</note> A seed-kernel, from which a fruit is called **Apyrenous** <note>seedless</note> if it lacks a kernel, or **Monopyrenous**, **Dipyrenous**, **Tripyrenous**, **Tetrapyrenous**, or **Polypyrenous** depending on whether it contains one, two, three, four, or many kernels.

**RADIATE FLOWER.** <note>original: "RADIATUS FLOS"</note> See **BEARDS.** <note>referring to ray florets</note>
**REGULAR FLOWER.** <note>original: "REGULARIS FLOS"</note> See **UNIFORM FLOWER.**

**SEMI-FLORET, SEMI-FLOSCULOUS FLOWER.** <note>original: "SEMIFLOSCULUS"</note> See **FLAT-PETALED FLOWER.**

**POD.** <note>original: "SILIQUA"</note> A long or oblong seed-husk; specifically used for the husk or case of <term>leguminous</term> <note>bean-like</note> plants.
Regarding **Multi-podded** herbs, see page 76.

**SOLID SEED.** <note>original: "SOLIDUM SEMEN"</note> That which lacks a <term>pappus</term> <note>the tuft of hairs or "down" found on seeds like dandelions</note>.

**SEED.** <note>original: "SPERMA"</note> A seed. A **Gymnospermous** herb is one that bears naked seeds. **Enangiospermous** and **Angiospermous** refer to those whose seeds are enclosed in vessels. **Monospermous**, **Dispermous**, **Tetraspermous**, and **Polyspermous** refer to plants producing one, two, four, or many seeds.

**SPIKE.** <note>original: "SPICA, Σ Τ Α Χ Υ Σ" (Greek: Stachys)</note> According to the definition by <term>Joachim Jungius</term> <note>in "Isagoge phytoscopica," chapter 11</note>, it is a structure densely composed of flowers or seeds, resulting in an upright, oblong, or very sharp cone, as seen in **Plantain**, **Bistort**, and **Rye**. **Polystachion** refers to that which produces many spikes.

**STAMENS.** <note>original: "STAMINA"</note> These are the same as **Filaments** <note>original: "Capillamenta"</note>, which <term>Spigelius</term> <note>Adriaan van den Spiegel</note> describes thus: "There are Stamens in the middle of the flower, which is called the center <note>original: "umbilicus"</note>; these are oblong parts, thin like filaments, sometimes a little thicker, protruding slightly, and frequently provided with tips <note>anthers</note> at the summit; they surround the style, which is a similarly oblong but slightly thicker part emerging from the center."

**STAMINATE or APETALOUS FLOWER.** <note>original: "STAMINEUS, APETALOS FLOS"</note> One that consists only of stamens and lacks petals. Plants that produce such flowers are usually called **Apetalous**. See page 17.
A **Staminous Flower** is named, according to the mind of Jungius, as one that abounds in stamens, even if it possesses petals.

<meta>This page concludes the alphabetical glossary of botanical terms, completing the definitions from S to U. It provides foundational terminology for plant anatomy, such as the style, whorl, and seed vessel, while referencing the author’s larger work, "Historia Plantarum," and other contemporary botanists like Tournefort and Jungius.</meta>

->## INTERPRETATION OF OBSCURE TERMS ##<-

**STARRY HERB**. <note>original: "STELLATA HERBA"</note> See page 54.

**STYLE**. <note>original: "STYLUS"</note> An elongated part, thicker than the stamens, emerging from the center of the flower in the midst of the stamens and attached to the beginning of the fruit or seed.

*Mr. <term>Tournefort</term> calls this the Pistil.*

**LITTLE VESSEL**. <note>original: "VASCULUM"</note> The same as **CAPSULE**. From this, plants are called *Vasculiferous*, or *Angiospermous* <note>plants with seeds enclosed in a vessel</note> and *Enangiospermous*.

**WHORL**. <note>original: "VERTICILLUM"</note> A ring of flowers closely surrounding the stems or branches; so named from its resemblance to a *whorl* <note>original: "Verticillus"</note>, which is an instrument commonly used on a spindle to help it turn. From this, such flowers are said to grow *Whorl-wise*. Hence the name given to **Whorled** Herbs, about which see page 58.

**UMBEL**, **UMBELLIFEROUS PLANTS**. <note>original: "UMBELLA"</note> See page 47.

**NAVEL**. <note>original: "UMBILICUS"</note> The remnant of the flower that usually remains on those fruits to which the flowers were attached. Such fruits are called **Navelled** <note>original: "Umbilicati"</note> and the trees that produce them are called **Navelled Trees**, about which see page 142 and following.

*The navel of a flower signifies its center from which the style bursts forth.*

**UNIFORM** or **REGULAR FLOWER**. <note>original: "UNIFORMIS, REGULARIS FLOS"</note> One whose parts, if it consists of a single petal, are similar; or whose petals, if composed of several, match one another in shape and position. See **IRREGULAR FLOWER**.

**ONE-VALVED**. <note>original: "UNIVALVE"</note> Said of a seed vessel that opens from one side only. See **TWO-VALVED**.

->The remaining technical terms that I have used in this little work are sufficiently clear and do not seem to require explanation. If anyone wishes to know more on this subject, let them consult the *Interpretation of General Terms* prefixed to our *History of Plants* <note>John Ray's "Historia Plantarum"</note> and its first Book, <term>Jungius</term>’s *Introduction to Botanical Observation* <note>original: "Isagogen Phytoscopicam"</note>, and other herbalist writers.<-

General History of Plants <note>original: "Historia Plantarum generalis"</note>. *London* Folio 1686 & 1688, 2 volumes.

Francis Willughby’s History of Fishes with Figures. Revised, arranged, and supplemented by *John Ray. Oxford, in Folio,* 1686.

Methodical Synopsis of British Plants <note>original: "Synopsis Methodica Stirpium Britannicarum"</note>, in which both the characteristic marks of the Genera are presented, and individual Species are briefly described: With an Index and an epitome of their properties <note>original: "virium Epitome"; referring to the medicinal or practical uses of the plants.</note>. *London,* Octavo 1690.

The same Synopsis, with many Plants and curious Observations inserted throughout, with a Method and fuller History of Mosses, enlarged by about one hundred species and just as many types of Mosses and Fungi. *London* 1696.

Methodical Synopsis of Quadruped Animals and the Serpent Kind. *London,* Octavo 1693.

Three Physico-Theological <note>A movement that sought to prove the existence and attributes of God through the interpretation of the natural world.</note> Discourses, concerning. 1. The Primitive Chaos, and Creation of the World. 2. The General Deluge, its Causes and Effects. 3. The Dissolution of the World, and future Conflagration <note>The predicted end of the world by fire.</note>. With Practical Inferences therefrom. *London,* Octavo 1693.

A Collection of European Plants growing outside of Britain <note>original: "Stirpium Europæarum extra Britannias nascentium Sylloge"</note>. *London,* Octavo 1694.

*Letter to Mr. Rivinus <note>Augustus Quirinus Rivinus, a contemporary German botanist.</note> regarding the Method of Plants. Octavo 1696.*

*Dissertation on various Methods of [classifying] Plants. Octavo. London 1696.*

The Wisdom of God manifested in the Works of the Creation. In Two Parts. The First treats more briefly of the Heavenly Bodies, Elements, Meteors, Fossils, Vegetables, Animals, ( Beasts, Birds, Fishes, and Insects. ) The Second more particularly and fully : Of the Body of the whole Earth, its Figure, Motion, and Consistency. 2. Of the Bodies of Men, and other Animals, their admirable Structure, and the use of their several Parts ; as also, of their Manner of Generation. *London* 1701.

A Persuasive to a Holy Life, from the Happiness that attends it, both in this World, and that which is to come. Octavo 1700.

The Method of Plants, amended and enlarged, by John Ray, Fellow of the Royal Society. A special Method of Grasses, Rushes, and Sedges is added. By the same Author. *London* Octavo 1703.

*The Third Volume of the History of Plants, or a Supplement to the preceding two. In press <note>original: "Sub prelo"; indicating the book was being printed at the time of this publication.</note>.*
